*The Open Tao Te Ching, translated from the classical Chinese by Shalom Ormsby. Public domain (CC0).*

## Curator's Note

This is the Open Tao Te Ching, a new English translation made directly from the classical Chinese and dedicated to the public domain (CC0). It replaces Gia-Fu Feng and Jane English's 1972 translation, which is in copyright and was in this corpus by mistake.

The translation lives in [opencosmos-ai/taoteching](https://github.com/opencosmos-ai/taoteching), where every rendering decision is argued in the open, and its glossary is in the [Open Classical Chinese Character Atlas & Glossary](https://chinese-atlas.opencosmos.ai/glossary/). Some of its settled renderings differ from the familiar ones: 天 (*tiān*) is *sky*, not "Heaven"; 萬物 (*wàn wù*) is *the countless things*, not "the ten thousand things"; 常 (*cháng*) is *ever-present*; and the sage is never "he."

This document is generated from the translation and regenerated whenever it changes, so it is never more than a day behind. Each chapter gives the English verse, then the Chinese it translates. Where the translator has written notes, they follow under their own heading: they explain why a line reads as it does, and are the translator's reasoning, not the text. Readers can find each chapter, with every character glossed, at [opencosmos.ai/library/sources/taoism-tao-te-ching](https://opencosmos.ai/library/sources/taoism-tao-te-ching).

## Chapter 1

*Heshang Gong's title: 體道, "Embodying the Tao".*

The Tao that can be made a way is not the ever-present Tao.
The name that can be named is not the ever-present name.
The nameless is the beginning of sky and earth.
The named is the mother of the countless things.

Ever desireless, observe its subtlety;
Ever desiring, observe its boundaries.

These two have the same origin, but differ in name.
Together, they are called profound darkness.

Dark, and dark again, the gate of all subtleties.

The Chinese:

道可道，非常道；
名可名，非常名。
無名，天地之始；
有名，萬物之母。
故常無欲，以觀其妙；
常有欲，以觀其徼。
此兩者，同出而異名，
同謂之玄。
玄之又玄，眾妙之門。

### Notes on chapter 1

**道可道 → *The Tao that can be made a way*.** **The book opens on a paradox, and the paradox is in the grammar.** 道可道，非常道 (*dào kě dào, fēi cháng dào* — "the Tao that can be *dào*-ed is not the ever-present Tao") prints one graph three times in six characters: the name, the same word acting as a verb, and the name again. The line turns its own central word back on itself, so the ever-present Tao is denied in its own word. To keep the paradox, the English has to hold three things together:
- **the name**, *Tao*, which the line also teaches means *way*;
- **the turn**, the middle 道 being the same word, made to act;
- **the voice**, the Tao being what the verb is done to.

**How the second 道 is a verb.** Classical Chinese does not inflect; a word's job is its position. 可 (*kě* — can, may) always takes a verb and makes it passive — 可食 (*kě shí*) is *can be eaten*, edible — so whatever stands after 可 is an action. 道 (noun: the Tao) · 可 (can be) · 道 (verb: *dào*-ed). The next line is the same shape, and English can follow that one: 名可名, *the name that can be named*. The move was ordinary in Laozi's century — the 論語 (*Lúnyǔ* — the *Analects*) has 君君，臣臣 (*jūn jūn, chén chén* — "let the lord be a lord, the minister a minister") — so it is not a joke on two meanings but **one word turned on itself.** 說文 (*Shuōwén*) gives the noun as 所行道也 (*suǒ xíng dào yě* — "the road that is walked"), and the verb grows from it: to tread a way, to lead along it (later split off as 導, *dǎo* — to guide), to tell it in words.

**Why the voice is the point.** 可 + verb puts the subject on the receiving end (`glossary/ke-可.md`). The Tao is not doing the *dào*-ing; it is what would be *dào*-ed. So someone other than the Tao does it: a person who lays it out as a route, a course, a program to follow. The Tao's own manner is 自然 (*zì rán* — so of itself), and ch 25 ends on it: 道法自然, *"the Tao models itself on being what it is."* Being made a way is not something the Tao does of itself. It is done to the Tao, by human hands, and the line says that what comes of it is not the ever-present Tao. An English in another voice loses this. *The Tao that can become a way* makes the change the Tao's own, a claim about what the Tao does, where the Chinese speaks of what is done to it.

**How the English makes it a verb.** *Tao* is locked as a name (`glossary/dao-道.md`), and *"the Tao that can be Tao'd"* is not English. So the middle 道 is rendered by **what the name means**, and *made* turns it into a verb: *made a way*. *Made* is supplied scaffolding (`process/principles/supplied-verb-is-scaffolding.md`); *way* is 道's own word. The line reads *Tao · way · Tao*, carrying the word all three times the Chinese prints it, and a reader learns what the name means before learning anything else. *Made a way* is the ordinary English passive of *make it a way*, as in *she was made a judge*, and nothing in it is spare. **The precedent is already in the book**: where 道 is an ordinary way and not the name, this manuscript renders it *way* — 天之道 and 天道 (*tiān zhī dào*, *tiān dào* — the way of heaven) are *"the way of nature"* at ch 9, 47, 73, 77, 79 and 81; 人之道 (*rén zhī dào*) is *"the way of people"* at ch 77; 聖人之道 (*shèng rén zhī dào*) is *"the way of the sage"* at ch 81. The lock forbids *the Way* as a stand-in for the Tao; a lowercase *a way* is the common noun doing its own job.

**Where other translations let it go.** English versions keep one or two of the three and give up the rest. What goes most often is the turn.
- **The middle 道 becomes speech.** Waley (1934), *the Way that can be told of*; Lau (1963), *the way that can be spoken of*; Feng and English (1972), *the Tao that can be told*. The word appears twice, not three times, and the paradox becomes a claim about language: the Tao cannot be put into words. That is the next line's subject (名可名, *the name that can be named*), so the opening line is folded into its partner.
- **A different word takes the middle.** Legge (1891), *the Tao that can be trodden*, keeps the road and the passive, but the reader hears two words where the Chinese has one.
- **The turn is kept by translating the name.** Carus (1898), *the Reason that can be reasoned*, turns the word on itself exactly as the Chinese does, but only by making the Tao *Reason*: the Logos of John 1:1, which the Chinese Union Bible renders with 道 (`process/overlay-audit.md`).
- **The walker is kept, and the name is lost.** Le Guin (1997), *the way you can go*, names the person the line implies, but the Tao is gone from the sentence and *go* is a different word from *way*.

None of these keeps all three. *The Tao that can be made a way* does: the name, the same word in the middle, and the passive.

**What the line says, and who says it with us.** *Made a way* — laid out as a route, a course, a program to follow:
- 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses the second 道 with the noun itself: 謂經術政教之道也 — *"it means the **way** of classical learning and political instruction."* A Tao that can be laid out and taught.
- 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*, the oldest reader we carry): the ever-present has 無定理 (*wú dìng lǐ* — "no fixed pattern"), 是以不可道也…然而可論 — *"therefore it cannot be **dào**-ed… and yet it can be discussed."* On a reading of *spoken* that sentence contradicts itself; on *made a way* it is exact. A fixed course is the thing it cannot be.
- 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) is half with us: 可道之道，可名之名，指事造形，非其常也 — *"the Tao that can be dào-ed and the name that can be named point at affairs and **make forms**; they are not its constant."* 造形 (*zào xíng* — to make a form) is the making; 指事 (*zhǐ shì* — to point at affairs) is the designation, and that half we lose.

**And the two lines do two things, as the Chinese does.** Line 1 asks whether the Tao can be made a way; line 2, 名可名, whether it can be named. A speech reading folds the first into the second.

**What it costs, named rather than hidden.** **The speech sense goes.** It is real: the 詩經 (*Shījīng* — the Book of Songs) has 中冓之言，不可道也 (*"the words of the inner chamber cannot be told"*), and 河上公 closes his own gloss on this line with 不可稱道 (*bù kě chēng dào* — "it cannot be spoken of"). **This is a line where the commentators diverge and the English picks a side** — the route reading of 河上公's lemma gloss and 韓非, over 王弼's pointing — which `divergence-stays-open` would refuse. It is taken here on Shalom's call, because the route reading is the one that lets the English keep the paradox. *Made a way* is also longer than 道可道's three syllables, and a little longer than its partner line, *the name that can be named*. And it brushes the English idiom *make a way*, to clear a path; in this sentence the Tao is what is made, so the idiom does not take hold.

**What was refused, and why.**
- ***spoken*** — *speak* is 言 (*yán* — speech)'s English at ch 5, 17, 27, 56, 66 and 73, and it makes ch 1 rhyme in English with ch 56's 知者不言 (*"Those who know do not speak"*), where the Chinese uses a different character. It also makes 韓非 contradict himself.
- ***told*** — the strongest alternative: it carries speech *and* directions (*tell someone the way*). It loses the word *way*, which is the point of the line.
- ***followed*** — the book says the Tao *is* followed, and praises it: 惟道是從 (*wéi dào shì cóng* — ch 21, *"follows only the Tao"*), 從事於道 (*cóng shì yú dào* — ch 23). *Follow* is also 從 (*cóng*)'s, 隨 (*suí*)'s and 徒 (*tú*)'s word already.
- ***conceived as Tao*** — keeps three *Tao*s, but moves the act inside the head, where no commentator puts it; turns line 1 into line 2's naming; and is seminar register.
- ***mapped*** is 圖 (*tú* — to plan)'s word at ch 63; ***traced*** chimes with 跡 (*jì* — footprints) at ch 27, *"leaves no tracks."*
- ***become a way*** — lighter, and wrong in voice. It has the Tao turn into a way of itself, where the Chinese has the Tao made one. It breaks the parallel with 名可名, which English keeps passive. And *become* is the English of a verb the line does not print, 為 (*wéi* — to do, to serve as, to become).
- ***made into a way*** — the same passive with a spare word. *Made* already does the work *into* was added to do.

*The Literal column for this line was changed with it — it read "can be spoken", which was one reading set down as the gloss.*

*End of chapter 1.*

## Chapter 2

*Heshang Gong's title: 養身, "Nourishing the self".*

When the world knows beauty as beauty, ugliness arises.
When the world knows good as good, the bad arises.

Therefore presence and absence give birth to each other,
Difficult and easy complete each other,
Long and short measure each other,
High and low depend on each other,
Sound and tone harmonize each other,
Front and back follow each other.

Therefore the sage dwells in the work of non-doing
and carries out the teaching without words.

The countless things arise, and the sage does not begin them.
They are born, and the sage does not possess them.
The sage acts, yet relies on nothing.
The work is done, and the sage does not stay in it.

Only because the sage does not stay does it not leave.

The Chinese:

天下皆知美之為美，斯惡已。
皆知善之為善，斯不善已。
故有無相生，難易相成，
長短相形，高下相盈，
音聲相和，前後相隨。
是以聖人處無為之事，
行不言之教。
萬物作而弗始，
生而弗有，
為而弗恃，
功成而弗居。
夫唯弗居，是以不去。

### Notes on chapter 2

**夫唯弗居，是以不去 → "Only because the sage does not stay does it not leave."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`. Was: "Because the sage does not stay, it does not leave.")* 唯 (*wéi*) is *only*, and the bare *because* had dropped it. Not staying is the whole reason the work stays, not one reason among several. *Because* renders 是以 (*shì yǐ* — therefore), moved to the front where English wants it, and the clause after it inverts. The frame reads the same in all nine of its lines.

*End of chapter 2.*

## Chapter 3

*Heshang Gong's title: 安民, "Settling the people".*

By not exalting the exceptional, the people have no cause to contend.
By not prizing rare goods, the people do not become thieves.
By not displaying the desirable, the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder.

This is how the sage governs:
emptying their hearts and filling their bellies,
weakening their ambition and strengthening their bones,
so the people are ever unknowing, ever desireless,
and the knowers never push to act.
Do the not-doing, and nothing is left ungoverned.

The Chinese:

不尚賢，使民不爭；
不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜；
不見可欲，使民心不亂。
是以聖人之治，
虛其心，實其腹，
弱其志，強其骨。
常使民無知無欲。
使夫智者不敢為也。
為無為，則無不治。

### Notes on chapter 3

**使民心不亂 → *the people's hearts are not thrown into disorder*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-21. `glossary/luan-亂.md`.)* Was *"not disturbed"*, which read psychologically in a chapter that is political throughout — contending, thieving, governing, 無不治. **亂 is the governance word**, and this chapter holds it with 治 (*zhì*) twice: 聖人之**治** three lines later and 無不**治** at the close. 說文 defines 亂 *as* 治, and the graph is 𤔔, silk between two hands, plus 乙 — *"what orders it."* The hearts are not a mood here; they are the thing that comes untidy when you show people what to want.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods," and the line was circular before.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* *(was: "By not valuing the precious, no one becomes a thief.")* 不貴難得之貨，使民不為盜 (*bù guì nán dé zhī huò, shǐ mín bù wéi dào*) is a **causal claim about what a ruler does** — the goods are hard to get, the ruler prizes them, people steal. *"Do not value the precious"* puts the value in the object, so it argues in a circle and **the ruler drops out of the sentence**, which is the one place the sentence points. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) keeps the cause where the Chinese has it: 貴貨過用，貪者競趣，穿窬探篋，沒命而盜 — *"prize goods beyond their usefulness, and the greedy race for them: they tunnel through walls, rifle chests, and steal at the cost of their lives."*

**貨 (*huò* — goods) was wearing 貴's word, in a line where 貴 is the verb.** *Precious* belongs to 貴 (*guì*) at ch 70, 72 and 75; here 不貴 is *does not prize*. 貨 is now locked to *goods* book-wide — see `glossary/huo-貨.md`, which reads the three cowrie characters apart: 貨 is 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell) under 化 (*huà* — a body turning over), **a shell that changes hands**; 寶 (*bǎo* — treasure) is a hoard under a roof; 貴 is a position on a price scale.

***"Rare" and not "scarce," and the reason is this chapter's third line.*** *Scarce* means **a need going unmet**. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) names the goods — 好珎寶，黃金棄於山，珠玉捐於淵, *"fine treasures; gold left in the mountain, pearls and jade abandoned in the deep"* — and **nobody needs jade**. If the wanting were a real shortfall, honestly felt, the ruler could not be blamed for it. But line three says where the wanting comes from: 不見可欲，使民心不亂 — *"do not display what can be desired, and the people's hearts are not disturbed."* **Display, then appetite, then theft.** 說文 agrees at the level of the graph: 盜 (*dào* — thief) is 私利物也。从㳄 — *"to take private profit from a thing; it follows 㳄 (*xián* — drool)"* — **a person salivating over a dish.** The chapter blames the first link.

**The triad was lopsided in the Chinese and our English had flattened it.** The three objects are 賢 (*xián* — the talented, one character), 難得之貨 (four), 可欲 (*kě yù* — what can be desired, two): **the middle line is deliberately the heaviest.** *"The exceptional / the precious / the desirable"* imposed a neat symmetry by shrinking the longest object to two words.

**民 restored to the middle clause.** All three clauses are 使民X — 使民不爭 / 使民不為盜 / 使民心不亂 — and ours had *"the people"* in the first and third and *"no one"* in the second. This uses no word the stanza does not already carry, and **settles nothing about the deferred 民/人 call** (`WORKLIST` T4-1). 不貴 also reads *prizing* now, matching ch 20's 貴食母 and ch 64.

**The second movement had the opposite grammar from the Chinese.** *(2026-08-31, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T1-3.)* *(was: "Therefore the sage / Empties hearts and fills bellies / Weakens striving and strengthens the bones of the people. // Without creating desire or cunning, / Without causing the cunning to act, / Without effort, the sage leaves nothing out of order.")* 常使民無知無欲 / 使夫智者不敢為也 / 為無為，則無不治 are built on 使 (*shǐ* — to cause), 使, and 為 (*wéi* — to do / to handle). The English was built on three *"Without"*s, an anaphora nothing in the Chinese repeats. **The Chinese sage acts; the English sage merely abstained.** The Chinese is one continuous movement under 是以聖人之治, and the English had it as two stanzas.

**為無為 → *"Without effort"* broke the 無為 lock on the one line the lock's own entry cites as its proof.** `glossary/wuwei-無為.md`: *"為無為 (3, 63) — three characters: do the not-doing … 無為 is something you **actively do** … continuous, **effortful**, and difficult."* The line now reads ch 63's English exactly — **"Do the not-doing"** — so the book's home formula says one thing in both places. *(`check_locks.py` could not see the breach: its forbidden list held `"effortless action"`, not `"without effort"`. Both `"effortless"` and `"without effort"` are now on 無為's list and verified firing.)*

**治 (*zhì* — to govern / to order) frames the chapter, and had been dropped from the hinge.** 是以聖人之治 — *"therefore, the sage's governing"* — read only *"Therefore the sage."* 治 opens the second movement and is the chapter's last word; the ring was broken. 無不治 now reads **"nothing is left ungoverned,"** which restores an echo the Chinese has: 無不治 here against 無不為 (*wú bù wéi*) at ch 37 and 48, already rendered *"nothing is left undone."* Ch 65 — 民之難治 (*mín zhī nán zhì* — "the people are hard to govern") — already renders 治 as *govern* three times. 說文解字 on 治 is a **river name**, 水 (*shuǐ* — water) with 台 for sound; governing in this word begins as channelling water, not as forcing it.

**The old English read as manipulation, and the Chinese does not.** Every state the movement names is elsewhere the sage's **own**: 無知 (*wú zhī* — without knowing) is asked of the reader at ch 10, 能無知乎 (*"can you be unknowing?"*); 常…無欲 (*cháng… wú yù* — ever without desire) is the reader at ch 1 and the Tao itself at ch 34, both already rendered **"Ever desireless"**; and 不敢為 (*bù gǎn wéi* — does not push to act) is the sage's own posture at ch 64, 67 and 69. **The English had made asymmetric what the Chinese makes symmetrical, and the asymmetry is what read as coercion.** Three collocations did the work — *"keeping X without knowing"* (an English idiom for *behind someone's back*), *"weakening their will"* (the vocabulary of interrogation), *"keeping X from Y"* (restraint imposed). See [`collocation-carries-a-verdict`](https://github.com/opencosmos-ai/taoteching/blob/main/process/principles/collocation-carries-a-verdict.md).

**And the mechanism is subtraction, which ch 57 states outright.** 我無為，而民自化 … 我無欲，而民自樸 — *"I do not do, and the people transform themselves … I am desireless, and the people become plain of themselves."* The operative character is 自 (*zì* — of themselves). All three of stanza 1's 使 clauses take a **not** as their cause, and 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) spells it out: 故可欲不見，則心無所亂也 — *"so when the desirable is not displayed, the heart has nothing to disorder it."* Nothing is put into anyone. The movement's two 使 clauses are now handled as stanza 1 already handles its three: result of the arrangement, not an act performed on persons.

**河上公 reads the movement as a body, not a population.** He opens it 聖人治國與治身同也 — *"the sage's governing of the state and the governing of the self are one and the same"* — and glosses 實其腹 as 懷道抱一守五神 (*"harbor the Tao, embrace the one, guard the five spirits"*) and 強其骨 as 愛精重施，髓滿骨堅 (*"cherish the vital essence and be sparing in spending it; the marrow fills and the bones grow firm"*). *Govern* holds both readings; it does not shut the inner one out. **What is not smoothed:** this is still a ruler arranging the conditions under which other people want things, and 河上公 titles the chapter 安民 (*ān mín* — "settling the people"). Paternalist is not sinister, and the chapter owns the first.

**弱其志 → "ambition," and 弱 keeps *weaken*.** 說文 on 志: 意也, *"intent"* — 心 (*xīn* — heart) with 之 (*zhī* — to go), the heart going toward something. 王弼: 志生事以亂 — *"ambition generates affairs, and so brings disorder"* — and 心虛則志弱也, *"when the heart is emptied, the ambition weakens,"* which is why the four clauses are one gesture and not four. The lock licenses **weaken** wherever 弱 takes an object, and it does here; the coercion was in *will*, not in *weaken*. **志 is still split against ch 33's *will*** — `WORKLIST` T2-7.

**常 → "ever," restoring a dropped lock term.** 常使民無知無欲 had no *ever* at all, the same fault as ch 28's three 常德. The 常 entry licenses plain *ever / always* adverbially, and 常…無欲 is already **"Ever desireless"** at ch 1 and ch 34.

**敢 applied; it had been dropped outright.** 不敢為 → **"never push to act,"** joining ch 30, 64, 67, 69, 73 and 74.

***智者 → "the knowers," and "cunning" is gone from the chapter.*** *"Cunning"* had covered both 知 (*zhī* — to know) and 智 (*zhì* — knowing-how) in consecutive lines, erasing the distinction exactly where the chapter draws it, and it renders no character it owns — it also wears 巧 (*qiǎo*) at ch 19 and 57. **無知 now reads *unknowing***, ch 10's word for the same compound (能無知乎 — *"can you be unknowing?"*, asked of the practitioner), **and 智者 reads *the knowers*.** *(Shalom's word, against two of mine.)*

**The commentators diverge on who the 智者 are, and the English must not settle it.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) prints 智者 and glosses 智者謂知為也 — *"the 智者 are those who know how to handle"* — the operators, whom the line restrains. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) prints 知者 with the phonetic note 知音智 (*"知 is read* zhì"), and glosses 思慮深，不輕言 — *"deep in deliberation, they do not speak lightly"* — almost word for word what he says of the unambiguously approving 知者 at ch 56, 知者貴行不貴言也. **王弼 has two graphs and two figures; 河上公 has one graph and one figure.** *"Those who know how"* and *"the clever"* both pick 王弼's side. ***The knowers* picks neither** — a bare nominalization, which is exactly what 者 (*zhě*) does in Chinese, leaving the line itself to say whether knowing is good here. The fork is recorded in `sources/variants.yaml` and `notes/manuscript.md`.

***"Those who know" was tried and refused.*** It is **知者's English at ch 56** (知者不言 — *"Those who know do not speak"*) **and ch 81** (知者不博), and in both it names the sage's side. The *string* collides; the *family resemblance* does not, and **河上公 makes that resemblance on purpose.** *The knowers* also chimes with *unknowing* one line above — same root, opposite pole — which is what 河上公's text does with one graph twice. **The book-wide 智 split stays open**: disparaged at ch 18, 19 and 65, neutral at ch 33. `WORKLIST` T2-2.

**Still open on this chapter.** 心 (*xīn* — heart) is dropped from 使民心不亂 in stanza 1, where it also sets up 虛其心 in the movement below; and 亂 (*luàn*) reads *perturbed* there against ch 64's *chaotic* for the same character. 說文 glosses 亂 as **治也** — *"to put in order"* — the tangle and the untangling being one act read from both ends, which is the pair this chapter opens and closes on.

**心 restored to line 3, and 亂 → "disturbed."** *(2026-08-31, with T1-3.)* *(was: "By not displaying the desirable, the people are not perturbed.")* 使民心不亂 (*shǐ mín xīn bù luàn*) had **dropped 心 (*xīn* — heart) at its first appearance**, two lines before the chapter empties it — 虛其心. That is the joint that makes 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*)'s anatomy visible: 心懷智而腹懷食，虛有智而實無知也 — *"the heart harbors clever knowing and the belly harbors food: empty what has 智, fill what has no 知"* — and 骨無知以幹, *"the bones have no knowing, and so they are the frame."* **Knowing lives in the heart, which is why 虛其心 and 常使民無知 are one instruction and not two policies.** *Perturbed* rendered nothing at all.

***"Disturbed," and not "disordered" or "confused."*** 亂 elsewhere in the book is *chaos* (18), *disorder* (38), *chaotic* (64), and the 說文解字 gloss is startling — **亂，治也**, *"亂 means to put in order"* — the graph being hands working tangled silk (𤔔) with the tool that untangles it (乙). **So 亂 and 治 are one act read from both ends, and this chapter opens on the first and closes on the second.** English cannot hold that in one word, and the choice was between the ring and the organ. **The organ wins**: *disordered hearts* is clinical and odd, and 亂 here is something done **to** the heart from outside — 王弼: 故可欲不見，則心無所亂也, *"when the desirable is not displayed, the heart has nothing to disorder it."* Display, then appetite, then theft. ***Confused* was refused on a stronger ground**: it puts the damage in the **knowing**, and this chapter has just spent two lines separating what the heart holds from what disturbs it. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) pairs 亂 with 惑 (*huò* — led astray) — 不邪淫，不惑亂也, *"no depravity or license; no bewilderment or disorder"* — which is the nearest the evidence comes to *confused*, and it is still agitation rather than misunderstanding. *(Shalom's word.)*

***"Not," not "never" — and the triad's negation is still uneven.*** The three opening clauses carry the identical negation, 不爭 / 不為盜 / 不亂, and our English gives them three shapes: *"have no cause to contend" · "do not become thieves" · "are not disturbed."* Plain *not* makes two of the three match. **The remaining offender is line 1**, where *"have no cause to"* asserts a causal claim 不爭 does not make — still open.

**Rider for ch 26.** *Disturbed* now carries 亂 here, and ch 26's *"their equanimity is undisturbed"* is wearing it for 燕處超然 (*yàn chǔ chāo rán* — "dwells at ease, aloof"), which contains no 亂. Ch 26 is already owed a visit for 靜 (`WORKLIST` T2-5) and 君 (T2-6); this goes with them.

*End of chapter 3.*

## Chapter 4

*Heshang Gong's title: 無源, "The sourceless".*

The Tao is empty, and using it, it never fills.
Fathomless, it seems to be the ancestor of the countless things.

It blunts the sharpness, untangles the knots,
dims its own light, is the same as the dust.

Submerged, it seems to be here.
I do not know whose child it is.
It seems older than any god.

The Chinese:

道沖，而用之或不盈。
淵兮，似萬物之宗。
挫其銳，解其紛，
和其光，同其塵。
湛兮，似或存。
吾不知誰之子，
象帝之先。

### Notes on chapter 4

*Rewritten 2026-08-31 — the first Pass D chapter. `WORKLIST.md` T1-2, and it closes T2-14c's deferred question. Four things were wrong and one whole line was missing.*

**道沖 was inverted, and given 器's word.** 沖 (*chōng*) is **empty**; 不盈 (*bù yíng*) is **never fills**. The line read *"The Tao is a vessel that never runs empty"* — **both halves flipped**, and *vessel* is locked to 器 (*qì*). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) states the mechanism: 沖而用之，用乃不能窮…滿以造實，實來則溢 — *"empty, and using it, the use cannot be exhausted… fill it to make it solid, and when solidity comes it overflows."* **Emptiness is the capacity; the old line made the Tao a reservoir that never drains, which is the opposite metaphysics.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 或 as 常 (*cháng* — always): 道常謙虛不盈滿.

**淵 was dropped, and with it a frame.** 淵兮，似X and 湛兮，似X are **two matched frames** around the quatrain; the English rendered only the second, so the symmetry was invisible and the 湛 line arrived as a new topic with nothing to rhyme against. 說文解字 on 淵: 回水也…左右，岸也，中象水皃 — *"eddying water; the left and right are the banks, the middle depicts the water."* A pool of turning water between two banks. 河上公: 道淵深**不可知**也 — *"deep as an abyss and cannot be known"*, which is what **fathomless** means.

**湛 is not "still" — it is submerged.** 說文: **沒也**, *"to sink under"* (水 with 甚 for sound). That matters, because it makes the line **answer the quatrain** rather than start a new thought: the Tao has just blunted its own edge, dimmed its own light and merged with the dust, and now it is **under**.

**兮 (*xī*) never hedges, and that decided where the doubt goes.** Across its twelve occurrences the pattern is **[asserted quality] 兮，[hedged predicate]** — ch 15 runs seven in a row (豫兮**若**冬涉川, 猶兮**若**畏四鄰, 儼兮**其若**客). So 湛 is **stated**; 似 hedges 存 alone. An earlier draft read *"Submerged. It seems to be."*, which let English's ellipsis reach backward and take *submerged* as the missing complement — putting the doubt on the submersion, which the Chinese asserts. *(Caught by Shalom.)* Both frames now take a comma, matching how the manuscript already handles 兮 at ch 15.

**存 is not "exist" and not "remain."** It is **being-still-there**, against 亡 (*wáng* — to perish): ch 41 pairs them, 若存若亡, and 河上公 glosses this line 長存**不亡**. *Remain* imports a **depletion frame the first line explicitly denies** — leftovers are what survive consumption, and 用之或不盈 says the Tao is not consumed. *Exist* is unavailable: it already serves 有 (*yǒu*) at ch 32, 39 and 64, and 有 is half a locked pairing. **"It seems to be here"** reads in English as *presence*, not location, which is exactly 存. *(Shalom's line.)*

**吾不知誰之子 was not translated at all** — *"I do not know whose child it is."* The book's one flat admission of ignorance about the Tao's parentage, and it was missing. **It is also the only unhedged line in the chapter**, which is why the closing line can follow it as a hedge without going slack.

**帝 was erased, and that erasure deleted the chapter's argument.** See `glossary/di-帝.md`, now locked. The short version: **帝 (*dì*) is not a god this text is importing — it is a god the text is demoting**, and English translation has only ever inflated it (*God*, *the Lord*, *the Creator*) or deleted it, as we had. 帝 reaches Laozi as **the Shang high power that the Zhou deposed and replaced with 天** (*tiān*) when they invented 天命 (*tiān mìng* — the Mandate of Heaven) to justify the conquest; and by 288 BCE living kings were grabbing the title (東帝 / 西帝), with 秦始皇帝 fixing it to the throne in 221. **Read with 誰之子 above it, the line takes the floor out of legitimation:** authority in this culture descends — the Zhou king rules as 天子, *the child of 天* — and a thing with **no parent** standing **before any god** leaves the chain of descent with nothing at the bottom.

***"Any god," not "the high god."*** The definite article asserts a **singular supreme deity at the top of a hierarchy**, which the scholarship on Shang religion has not settled — and it smuggles that in where no reader weighs it, since articles are not words people notice. **The definite article confers status exactly as a capital does.** *Any* also makes the stronger claim the argument needs: precede only *the* high god and a claimant can answer *"my line descends from a different power."* *(Caught by Shalom.)*

**象 is the comparison, not the noun — and this was argued the other way first.** 象 (*xiàng*) is the book's word for **image** at 無物之象 (14), 其中有象 (21), 執大象 (35) and 大象無形 (41), and 似 is the dedicated hedge, already used twice here — so a draft read the last line *"An image, older than any god."* **The grammar defeats it: in all four noun uses 象 is marked as one, by 之, by 有, or by 大, and here it stands bare before a noun phrase, which is verb-plus-object.** Both commentaries read it as a comparison. Ch 4 is also 象's first appearance, so an English *image* would land where no reader can hear the thread.

**One sentence, not two, because English cannot strand a subject.** The four phrases are one sentence in the Chinese — 挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵 — with the subject elided, as classical Chinese elides freely. A draft broke them into two sentences and left the second without one: *"Dims its own light, merges with the dust."* That is the fault standing rule 5 names in its reasoning about em-dashes, reached with a full stop instead of a dash. The couplet now runs on a comma with a **lowercase continuation line**, which is this manuscript's convention at ch 2, 7, 16, 19, 25, 31, 34, 43, 47, 48 and 49. *(Caught by Shalom.)* **Ch 56 needs no such repair**, because its version is imperative and each line stands as a complete sentence — the nouns match, the grammar differs because the subject does.

**同 → *the same as*, not *merges with*.** *(2026-09-03, `WORKLIST.md` T2-26, the rider ch 23 left.)* 同 (*tóng* — the same) is the antonym of 異 (*yì* — different), printed against it in ch 1's own clause 同出而異名, and ch 23's six occurrences were repaired first. **河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses this very line 不當自别殊也** — *"one should not set oneself apart as separate and distinct"* — where 别 (*bié* — to separate) and 殊 (*shū* — distinct) are 同's opposites. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) makes the couplet a matched pair**: 和其光 is 無所**特顯** (*"nothing specially displayed"*), 同其塵 is 無所**特賤** (*"nothing specially despised"*) — do not stand out above, do not hold yourself apart from below. ***Merges with* read as self-dissolution**, losing yourself into dust; the Chinese says do not consider yourself too good for the common muck. **The cost:** *is the same as the dust* is the one stative in a run of actions (*blunts, untangles, dims*), which is the price of one English for one character across ch 4, 23 and 56.

**誰之子 → "whose child," never "whose descendant."** 說文解字 on 孫 (*sūn* — grandchild): **子之子曰孫。从子从系。系，續也** — *"the 子 of a 子 is called 孫; from 子 and 系 (to connect), and 系 means to continue."* **Chinese separates the generations, and has a word for descendants — 子孫 — which this book uses at ch 54** (子孫以祭祀不輟). Ch 4 declines it and writes bare 子, whose 說文 entry is simply 象形, a **pictograph of an infant**. The distinction is load-bearing: **天子 (ch 62) is the *child* of 天, one generation, direct** — and ch 52 pairs 母/子, mother and child. *Descendant* would soften the claim into *"its ancestry is long and untraceable"*, when the claim is that **there is no parent at all.**

**The quatrain keeps the Tao as its subject**, closing the question deferred from Pass C. With 道沖 restored the subject chain runs unbroken — Tao → 淵兮 → the four lines → 湛兮 → 吾不知 → 象帝之先 — which is 王弼's reading: 銳挫而無損…同塵而不渝其真, *"the sharp is blunted and nothing is lost… it shares the dust and does not alter its truth."* Ch 56 keeps its imperative; the nouns match, the verb forms differ, and the divergence is now argued rather than inherited.

**Not attested at Guodian** (~300 BCE) — this chapter rests on the silks and later. The 或/若 fork at 湛兮似或存 is recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`: 河上公 reads 似若存, and the Siku 王弼 carries 〔案或一作若〕. Both are hedges of the same force, so nothing turns on it.

*End of chapter 4.*

## Chapter 5

*Heshang Gong's title: 虛用, "The use of emptiness".*

Sky and earth are not concerned with humaneness: they treat the countless things as straw dogs.
The sage is not concerned with humaneness: they treat everyone as straw dogs.

Isn't the space between sky and earth like a bellows?
Empty but never depleted, the more it moves, the more it yields.

Speaking of this is a dead end.
Instead, hold to the center.

The Chinese:

天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗；
聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗。
天地之間，其猶橐籥乎？
虛而不屈，動而愈出。
多言數窮，不如守中。

### Notes on chapter 5

**以百姓為芻狗 → "they treat everyone as straw dogs."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call, `glossary/baixing-百姓.md`. Was: "the people.")* *The people* is 民 (*mín*)'s, and 百姓 (*bǎi xìng*) is the whole population. *Everyone* answers the line above it: sky and earth treat the countless things as straw dogs, and the sage treats everyone the same way.

*不仁 revised 2026-08-28 under the 仁 lock (`glossary/ren-仁.md`). The verse had read "lack benevolence," which was wrong twice: the word, and **lack** — 不仁 is a refusal, not a deficit.*

**The line is not about cruelty, and both commentators say so.** 王弼 names what 仁 would require: 仁者必造立施化，**有恩有為** — *"the 仁 one must construct and impose transformation; there is 恩 (ēn — favour with a debt attached) and there is 為 (wéi — doing)."* So 不仁 is the absence of **management that keeps accounts**, not the absence of care.

河上公 is blunter still: 聖人**愛養**萬民，不以仁恩，法天地行自然 — *"the sage **loves and rears** the people, not by humane favour, but modelling sky and earth in acting so of themselves."* The sage of this chapter is not indifferent.

**A 芻狗 (*chú gǒu*) is a dog plaited from straw for a sacrifice** — dressed and honored through the rite, thrown away after. 河上公 gives the point in five characters: 不貴望其報也, *"expecting no repayment."* The straw dog is not contempt. It is what you are to something that plays no favorites and keeps no ledger.

*English "humane" now means chiefly "not cruel," so "are not humane" would deliver the one reading the commentaries forbid. Hence the longer phrase.*

**守中 → "hold to the center," and *in silence* rendered nothing.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 守 (*shǒu*) is locked to *hold to* (`glossary/shou-守.md`): 說文 守官也，从宀从寸…寸，法度也 — a roof over a regulation, **the only member of the holding family with no hand in its graph**. What you 守 is a post you are answerable for, which is why the English takes a preposition. The line's *"in silence"* rendered no character and is gone; 多言 (*duō yán* — much speech) two lines above already carries the contrast.

*End of chapter 5.*

## Chapter 6

*Heshang Gong's title: 成象, "Taking form".*

The spirit of the valley is deathless.
This is the dark female.
This dark gateway birthed the sky and the earth.
Unceasing yet barely perceptible, it can never be exhausted.

The Chinese:

谷神不死，
是謂玄牝。
玄牝之門，
是謂天地根。
綿綿若存，
用之不勤。

*End of chapter 6.*

## Chapter 7

*Heshang Gong's title: 韜光, "Sheathing the light".*

The sky is lasting, the earth enduring.
Sky and earth can last and endure
because they do not live for themselves,
and so they live long.

So the sage puts their body last, and their body comes first;
puts their body outside, and their body survives.

Is it not because they have no private self?
And so their private self is fulfilled.

The Chinese:

天長地久。
天地所以能長且久者，
以其不自生，
故能長生。
是以聖人後其身而身先，
外其身而身存。
非以其無私邪？
故能成其私。

*End of chapter 7.*

## Chapter 8

*Heshang Gong's title: 易性, "An easy nature".*

The most masterful are like water.
Water is masterful at benefiting the countless things and does not contend.
It dwells in what the crowd loathes,
and so is nearly the Tao.

In settling, masterful at choosing ground.
In the heart, masterful at staying deep.
In giving, masterful at humaneness.
In speech, masterful at trust.
In government, masterful at order.
In affairs, masterful at what can be done.
In moving, masterful at timing.

Only because it does not contend
is there no blame.

The Chinese:

上善若水。
水善利萬物而不爭，
處眾人之所惡，
故幾於道。
居善地，
心善淵，
與善仁，
言善信，
政善治，
事善能，
動善時。
夫唯不爭，
故無尤。

### Notes on chapter 8

**政善治 → *In government, masterful at order*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-23. `glossary/zhi-治.md`.)* Was *"In governing."* **The decision was about part of speech, not consistency.** The seven first slots of this stanza are a genuine mix in the Chinese, and the English renders each by **its own** part of speech — 居 (*jū* — to dwell), 與 (*yǔ* — to give) and 動 (*dòng* — to move) as verbs; 心 (*xīn* — heart), 言 (*yán* — speech) and 事 (*shì* — affairs) as nouns. **政 was the one slot rendered against its own**, and the book settles it elsewhere: its only other two lines are 其政悶悶 and 其政察察 at ch 58, where 其 (*qí* — its) can take nothing but a noun. 說文 agrees on the register — 政，正也。从攴从正, a hand holding a rod (攴 *pū*) making things straight.

**And it is what had pushed 治 onto *order*.** 政 and 治 are near-twins — modern Chinese fuses them into 政治 (*zhèngzhì* — politics) — so with both wearing verbs the line stuttered. With 政 nominal, 治's flexion to *order* here stands on its own reason: the object is the institution, not a people. 河上公 reads 治 in this chapter through water alone: 无有不洗清且平也, *"there is nothing it does not wash clean and level."*

**居 → *settling*, not *dwelling*, and the reason is four lines above.** 處 (*chǔ*) holds *dwell* at 處眾人之所惡 — *"it dwells in what the crowd loathes"* — in this same chapter, which is the sharpest kind of collision. 說文 separates them cleanly: 居，**蹲也**, *"to squat,"* on 尸 (*shī* — a seated body); 處，**止也。得几而止**, *"to stop; having got a stool (几 *jǐ*), one stops."* 居 is taking up a place; 處 is coming to rest where a seat has been set. **居's other lines are not yet consistent** — `WORKLIST.md` T2-57.

**Nine 善 (*shàn* — masterful), rendered nine ways, and one of them deleted outright.** *(2026-09-02, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T2-8 and T3-2.)* The chapter is 善's showcase — nine occurrences in thirteen lines, more concentrated than anywhere else in the book — and the lock had been applied to none of them. What stood instead was *supreme goodness · a solid foundation · limitless depth · pure kindness · trustworthy · good order · skillful · good timing*, plus a **deletion**: 水**善**利萬物 read *"it nourishes the countless things,"* with the 善 gone. **The Chinese is a list of trades; the English had made it a list of virtues.**

**善 governs a verb, everywhere in the book, and that decides this chapter's grammar.** X善Y admits two parses — 善 as a verb taking Y (*"masterful **at** Y"*) or 善 as an adjective modifying Y (*"masterful Y"*) — and nothing in these seven lines settles it. **The other eighteen instances do.** 善行 · 善言 · 善計 · 善閉 · 善結 · 善救 ×2 · 善為 ×2 · 善貸 · 善攝 · 善建 · 善抱 · 善下 · 善戰 · 善勝 ×2 · 善用 · 善應 · 善謀 — *travel, speak, reckon, shut, tie, rescue, handle, give, nurture, establish, embrace, go below, fight, overcome, use, respond, plan.* **Eighteen verbs, zero nouns.** And ch 8 sets the pattern itself four lines above the stanza with 善**利** (*lì* — to benefit), which is unambiguously verbal. The adjectival parse also collapses on its own terms: it yields *masterful order · masterful ability · masterful timing*, which read, and *masterful ground · masterful depth · masterful humaneness · masterful trust*, which do not. **A reading that survives three of seven loses to one that survives all seven.**

**Two of the seven objects name a *place*, and English needs a verb there.** *(Caught by Shalom: *"masterful at ground"* communicates nothing.)* The finding above says 善 governs a **verb** — and the first draft then rendered all seven objects as bare nouns, which is the finding applied to the argument and not to the English. *Masterful at X* requires X to name an **activity**: it holds for 時 (*shí* — timing), 能 (*néng* — able), 仁 (*rén* — humaneness), 信 (*xìn* — trust) and 治 (*zhì* — order), all of them qualities or practices, and it collapses for 地 (*dì* — ground) and 淵 (*yuān* — a deep pool), which are **places**. So a stance verb is supplied at exactly those two: **choosing ground** and **staying deep**.

**This is house practice, not a new licence.** Ch 66 does it already, in the same construction: 善下之 (*shàn xià zhī*) reads *"masterful at **staying** below them"* — 下 (*xià* — below) is a position, and the English supplies the verb. Ch 61's 以靜為下 takes *staying low* the same way. **The supplied word is scaffolding, not a character's English**, which is why *staying* can serve 下 and 淵 without either losing its own word.

**The verbs were chosen against the reverse check, and two obvious ones were rejected by it.** *Keeping trust* was declined because *keep* is 全 (*quán* — whole)'s declared render and the manuscript already carries **nine unbacked *keeps***; *bringing order* was declined because *bring* belongs to 生 (*shēng* — to give birth) and is already unbacked seven times. **擇 (*zé* — to choose) and 選 (*xuǎn* — to select) have zero occurrences in all 81 chapters**, so *choosing* takes nothing from anyone. *Staying deep* follows 說文's 淵: **回水也…左右，岸也**, *"swirling water… left and right are the banks"* — banked water that **stays**, which is why *going deep* was wrong for it and why *limitless* was backwards.

**The cost, named:** *choosing* imports agency the water image does not have (河上公 has water *flowing down* to the ground, not selecting it). What licenses it is that the seven couplets are the **person's** application — 上善之人如水之性 — where agency belongs, as it does to 與 (giving), 言 (speech) and 政 (governing) in the same stanza. And *deep* is 深 (*shēn* — deep)'s adjective in five other lines, with no 深 in this chapter; that overlap rides with T2-24, where 淵 is still open.

**幾 is an adverb of degree, and both drafts before this one made it a verb.** 故幾於道 first read *"And is therefore **one with** the Tao"* — identity asserted where the character asserts a hair's breadth — and the repair over-corrected into *"it **comes near** the Tao,"* which installed a distance and sent water walking across it. *(Caught by Shalom: it implies the Tao is somewhere else.)* **幾於道 has no verb in it at all.** 說文解字 on 幾 (*jī*): **微也。殆也。从𢆶从戍。戍，兵守也。𢆶而兵守者，危也** — *"minute; verging. From 𢆶 (yōu — fine silk threads) and 戍 (shù — a garrison guard). Threads under armed guard: that is danger."* Its second gloss is 殆 (*dài*), the character locked to **danger** on 2026-08-31.

**The manuscript already knew this in three other places, and only ch 8 moved.** Ch 69 輕敵**幾**喪吾寶 reads *"**nearly** costs me my treasures"*; ch 64 **幾**成 reads *"**just short of** completing them"*; ch 20 相去**幾**何 reads *"**how much** distance?"* Three degrees, one journey, and the journey was ours.

**The construction is sameness, not location.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses the line 水性**幾與道同** — *"water's nature is **nearly the same as** the Tao"* — where 幾 modifies 同 (*tóng* — the same), an adverb sitting on a stative verb. And the book prints the frame without the degree word **seven times in ch 23**: 同於道 (*tóng yú dào* — "the same as the Tao"). So 幾於道 is 同於道 with a hair's breadth inserted, and 於 (*yú*) is the all-purpose relational particle — *with respect to*, never *toward*. **The Tao is not placed anywhere, so nothing can travel to it.**

***Like the Tao* was proposed and declined on three deletions and a collision.** It drops 故 (*gù* — therefore), which is the chapter's inference and occurs twice here; it drops 幾, the only word keeping the line honest; **and *like* is 若's word, printed in this chapter's own first line** — 上善**若**水. It also moves the claim: *"it dwells in what the crowd loathes, like the Tao"* predicates the **dwelling** of the Tao, where the Chinese predicates **nearness** of water.
**上善 → "the most masterful," following 河上公's person-reading.** *(Shalom's call.)* 上 (*shàng* — highest) is settled at ch 38, where 上德 / 上仁 / 上義 / 上禮 all read *the highest*, so *"Supreme"* was the outlier. And *good* is reserved by the lock for chapters 2, 20 and 58, where the book **attacks** the category (皆知善之為善，斯不善已 — *"when all know good as good, the not-good arises"*) — using it here would make this chapter endorse what ch 2 dismantles. 河上公: **上善之人如水之性** — *"the person of the highest 善 is like the nature of water"* — which is 善人 (*shàn rén* — the masterful) at ch 27, 49 and 62. **The cost:** it decides that 上善 is a person rather than the quality, which the Chinese leaves open. ***True* was considered and rejected** — 真 (*zhēn* — genuine) is a live character in this book (21, 41, 54), and 上 is a graded rank word whose middle rung is printed at ch 41 (上士/中士/下士 — upper, middle and lower 士). *(A first draft of that argument claimed the chapter stages an 上/下 descent lexically. **It does not — 下 (*xià* — below) has zero occurrences here.** The descent is carried by low nouns, 地 and 淵, and by 所惡; the explicit pair lives at ch 66 and ch 76. Caught by Shalom.)*

**利 → "benefiting," and *nourishes* was another character's English.** `--english` found it: *nourish* appears at ch 34 (衣**養**萬物) and ch 51 (**養**之覆之), both 養 (*yǎng* — to nourish), which is **not in this chapter**. 利 (*lì* — to benefit) already reads *benefit* at ch 19, 56, 73 and 81 — including 81's 利而不害, *"benefits and does not harm,"* the same 而 (*ér* — and) construction as this line. 說文 makes it a blade: **銛也。从刀** — *"sharp; from 刀 (dāo — a knife)."*

**惡 is *loathe*, not avoidance.** 處眾人之所惡 had read *"where the crowd will not go."* 河上公 marks the reading with a *fanqie* pronunciation note — **惡烏路反**, fixing it as *wù*, the verb *to detest*, not *è*, the adjective *bad* — and glosses it 衆人惡卑濕垢濁, *"the crowd loathes the low, the damp, the dirty and the turbid."* The line's force is that water occupies what everyone finds disgusting.

**仁 → "humaneness" is simply the lock**, and *"pure kindness"* breached it while inventing *pure*. `check_locks.py` stayed silent because *kindness* is not on 仁's `forbidden:` list — the same blind spot that hid ch 38's *clutches at*. 河上公 on 與善仁: **萬物得水以生，與虚不與盈也** — *"the countless things get water and live; it gives to the empty and does not give to the full."*

**地 → "ground," matching ch 50's 死地** (*sǐ dì* — "deadly ground"). *Solid* and *foundation* each rendered nothing; the reverse check returns ch 8 as the only line in the book carrying *foundation*.

**能 → "what can be done," built from *can*.** 能 (*néng* — able) has **32 lines in 17 chapters, and 31 of them are the plain modal *can*** — 能無離乎, 故能長生, 天下莫能與之爭. This is the **only** place in the book where it is a noun, and *ability* was a Latinate abstraction imported for that one line, stacking two nouns of the same kind beside *masterful*. 說文 makes it a bear — **熊屬。足似鹿…能獸堅中，故稱賢能** (*"a kind of bear, feet like a deer… the 能 beast is solid within, therefore we call the worthy-and-capable 賢能"*) — so the sense runs from **packed-in capacity** to capability, and nothing in it moves. 河上公 reads the line as versatility: **能方能圓，曲直隨形** — *"it can be square, it can be round; bent or straight, it follows the shape."* ***Action* was proposed and fails twice**: 動 (*dòng* — to move) is the action word in the very next line, and *action* already wears 行 (*xíng* — to conduct oneself), 作 (*zuò* — to start up), 事 (*shì* — affairs, which is locked) and nothing at all across four other chapters.

**"Always blameless" lost both halves.** 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) has **zero occurrences here**, so *always* rendered nothing. And 尤 (*yóu* — blame) is a **hapax**, its only appearance in all 81 chapters, meaning fault-finding rather than moral purity; *blameless* fails the hymn test. 河上公: **天下无有怨尤水者也** — *"there is no one in the world who resents or blames water."* Kept agentless, as 無尤 is, where 河上公 supplies the agents.

**夫唯不爭 matches ch 22**, which shares the formula: *"Only because they do not contend…"* there, *"Only because it does not contend / is there no blame"* here. *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call: both had read a bare "Because…", which dropped 唯 (*wéi* — only). The frame reads *Only because* in all nine of its lines. `glossary/wei-唯.md`.)*

**居 and 處 both land on dwelling words, and the seam is named rather than forced.** 說文 makes them near-twins — 處 (*chǔ*) is **止也。得几而止** (*"to stop; to find a stool and stop"*), 居 (*jū*) is **蹲也** (*"to squat"*) — and ch 38 already uses them as stylistic variants in parallel clauses (see `notes/manuscript.md`). Here 處 keeps *dwells*, its English at ch 24, 31, 38 and 76, and 居 takes ***settling***, which is 說文's squat and leaves the two distinguishable.

**Left open: 淵 (*yuān*) has three Englishes and none of them is what it is.** *Fathomless* (4), *limitless depth* (8), *the deep abyss* (36). 說文: **回水也…左右，岸也** — *"swirling water… left and right are the banks."* **It has banks**, which is why a fish cannot leave one at ch 36, and why *limitless* is precisely backwards. *Depth* is a holding move; the term is now on `WORKLIST.md` as T2-24.

**A fork logged, which may not be a fork.** 河上公's text prints 正善治, our base prints 政善治. See `notes/manuscript.md`.

**河上公 reads the ground line through the feminine**, and it is worth a reader's note rather than a rendering: 水性善喜於地…**有似於牝**，動而下人也 — *"water's nature delights in the ground… **it resembles the female** (牝 *pìn* — the female animal), moving downward, below people."* That puts ch 8 in the same family as ch 6's 玄牝 (*xuán pìn* — the dark female) and ch 61's 牝常以靜勝牡 (*"the female always overcomes the male by stillness"*).

*End of chapter 8.*

## Chapter 9

*Heshang Gong's title: 運夷, "Keeping level".*

Rather than keep filling what you hold, stop.
Hammer a point ever sharper, and it will not keep for long.

Gold and jade fill the hall, and no one can guard them.
Grow arrogant with wealth and status, and you leave yourself the fault.

The work done, the body withdraws. This is the way of nature.

The Chinese:

持而盈之，
不如其已；
揣而銳之，
不可長保。
金玉滿堂，
莫之能守；
富貴而驕，
自遺其咎。
功遂身退，
天之道。

### Notes on chapter 9

**The chapter's spine is three things you cannot keep, in three different characters, and the English had kept one.** *(Closed 2026-09-20, `WORKLIST.md` T2-51 · T2-1.)* 持 (*chí* — to hold; 說文 握也) opens it at 持而盈之 and was **not rendered**; 保 (*bǎo* — 說文 養也, *to rear*) closes the couplet at 不可長保 and was **not rendered**; only 守 (*shǒu* — 說文 守官也) survived, as *guard*. All three are now on the page, four lines apart and visibly different.

**The verse also invented a vessel, and 器 (*qì* — vessel) is not in this chapter.** It was not arbitrary — 河上公 glosses the line 持滿必傾, *"hold it full and it must tip over,"* which points at the 欹器 (*qī qì*), the tilting vessel of the ancestral temple. But 器 is **locked** to *vessel / tool / implement* across nine chapters, none of them this one, so the image was a locked English on a chapter without its character. **The referent is named grammatically instead** — *what you hold* — per `name-the-referent`, which fires here because 之 (*zhī*) is a light particle where English *it* actively selects.

**不如 (*bù rú* — not as good as) had been flattened to a comma**, and is now the construction it is: *rather than X, stop*.

**保 takes bare *keep* here, a declared flexion** (`glossary/bao-保.md`). 保's other three lines all take a **cherished** object — the Tao at 15 and 62, the three treasures at 67 — and all three are positive. **Ch 9 is the only negative instance and the only one whose object is not cherished**, and *keep safe* in English requires something valued for its own sake. A hammered point being destroyed by overwork is not that. The lock had never been tested here: ch 9's verse rendered 保 nowhere, so the 2026-09-06 decision was argued from this chapter's **gloss table** rather than its verse.

**銳 (*ruì*) is a point, not an edge.** 說文: 芒也。从金兌聲 — *"it is 芒 (máng, the awn of grain), on the metal radical."* A taper to nothing, not a cutting edge. The edge is 刃 (*rèn*), which occurs **once in the whole book**, at ch 50. 王弼 reads it the same way: 既揣**末**令**尖** — *"having tapered the **tip** to make it **pointed**."* And 揣 (*chuǎi*) as *hammer* is 說文's own secondary gloss — 一曰**捶**之, *"one source says: to beat it."*

**What fails is the point, not its sharpness.** 王弼: 勢必**摧**䘐 — *the momentum must snap it*; 河上公: 先揣之，後必**弃捐** — *"work it first, and afterwards it must be discarded."* It breaks or is thrown away; it does not go quietly blunt. **Blunting is 挫's** (*cuò*, 說文 摧也) at 挫其銳, ch 4 and 56 — where it is the **remedy**, not the affliction. An English saying the point *"cannot be kept sharp"* would make ch 9's disease and chapters 4 and 56's cure the same sentence.

**咎 (*jiù*) → *fault*, following our own ch 46.** 說文 gives 災也 (*disaster*), and the graph is 人 (a person) with 各, which 說文 glosses 相違也, *at odds* — the falling-out and its consequence in one word. *Disaster* is nonetheless unavailable: **ch 46 sets 禍 (*huò*) and 咎 in a parallel couplet** — 禍莫大於不知足 / 咎莫大於欲得 — and gives *disaster* to 禍 and *fault* to 咎. The pair is only legible if they differ. 遺 (*yí* — to leave behind) is now rendered, matching ch 20 and ch 52.

**身 → *body*, and 退 restored.** 功遂身退 had read *"cease striving"* — 身 deleted, and *striving* is 爭's (*zhēng*) word. 河上公 reads the line as leaving office: 不**退身**避位則遇於害, *"if one does not withdraw the body and vacate the position, one meets harm."* He quotes the same shape back at ch 44, 名遂則**身退**也, which ties the two chapters together.

*End of chapter 9.*

## Chapter 10

*Heshang Gong's title: 能為, "What can be done".*

Housing your aliveness and embracing the one, can you keep these from parting?
Gathering the breath to softness, can you be like an infant?

Washing and clearing the dark mirror, can you be without blemish?
Loving the people and governing the state, can you be unknowing?

When the gate of the sky opens and closes, can you be the hen?
Clarity reaching the four quarters, can you be non-doing?

Giving birth to things and rearing them,
giving birth without possessing,
acting yet relying on nothing,
growing them without ruling them –
this is called profound integrity.

The Chinese:

載營魄抱一，
能無離乎？
專氣致柔，
能如嬰兒乎？
滌除玄覽，
能無疵乎？
愛民治國，
能無知乎？
天門開闔，
能為雌乎？
明白四達，
能無為乎？
生之畜之，
生而不有，
為而不恃，
長而不宰，
是謂玄德。

### Notes on chapter 10

**Five of this chapter's Englishes were attached to characters that are not in it.** *(2026-09-01, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T1-1.)* 全 (*quán* — whole), 萬物 (*wàn wù* — the countless things), 鑑 (*jiàn* — a mirror) — **all zero occurrences here** — plus 無為 and 無知, each wearing the other's English. **Every one is invisible to `check_locks`**: its evidence gate keys off the character being *present*, so a locked English on a chapter that lacks the character cannot fire. `--english` is the only thing that finds this class.

**The book's two great negations had swapped lines.** 愛民治國，**能無知乎** read *"can you lead without doing?"* and 明白四達，**能無為乎** read *"can you be unknowing?"* — four lines apart, each carrying the other's word. *Unknowing* has not left the chapter; **it has moved up two lines onto 無知**, where ch 3 settled it. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads this 無知 as **無以智**, *"without cleverness,"* and links it outright to ch 19's 絕聖棄智: 玄覽無疵猶絕聖也，治國無以智猶棄智也 — *"'the dark mirror without blemish' is like 'cut off sagacity'; 'governing the state without cleverness' is like 'discard cleverness.'"* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads it differently — 治國者布施惠德，**無令下知**也, *"one governing the state spreads kindness and lets none below know of it"* — but that requires supplying a second party the grammar does not have. **無為 keeps the lock's word**, used predicatively as ch 37 already does (*"The Tao is ever non-doing"*).

**疵 was not mistranslated; it was deleted.** 能無疵乎 asks *"can you be without blemish?"* — 說文解字: **病也**, under 疒, the sickness radical. Ours asked *"can you see what truly is?"*, which renders nothing at all. **國 (*guó* — the state) was dropped too**, from 愛民治**國**, in a chapter whose whole second couplet is about governing.

***"The dark mirror" was challenged and survives, and my objection to it was wrong.*** *(Caught by Shalom.)* I had argued that *mirror* renders 鑑 / 監 (*jiàn*), which our text does not print — the ch 52 襲/習 fault. **說文 defeats that: 覽，觀也。从見、監，監亦聲** — *"覽 means to look at; from 見 (to see) **and 監**, and 監 is also the phonetic."* **監 is a constituent of the very character we print**, and 監 is a person bending over a water basin at their own reflection, the ancestor of 鑑. The mirror is the character's own base, not an imported variant. **And the draft *"the dark seeing"* failed on the verb**: 滌除 (*dí chú* — wash and clear) needs a washable surface, and 河上公 says exactly what gets washed — 當**洗其心**使潔淨也, *"wash the heart and make it clean."* **疵 confirms it**: a blemish sits on a surface, and 王弼's gloss is more surface-like still — 能不以物**介**其明，**疵之**其神乎, *"can you keep things from **coming between** you and your clarity, or **blemishing** your spirit?"* **The cost, recorded:** both commentators gloss 覽 with *activity* verbs (觀 · 覽知萬事 · 極覽), so **the mirror is a reading of the graph, not of the lemma.**

**專 → "gathering," on the graph against a commentator.** 說文 makes 專 a **spindle whorl** — 一曰專，紡專 — thread wound onto a core. 河上公 agrees: 專守精氣使不亂 (*"concentrate and guard the essential breath so it is not disordered"*). **王弼 goes the other way** — 專，**任**也, *"專 means to entrust oneself to"* — nearly the opposite. **The character decides**, per the tie-breaking order, and the divergence is recorded rather than averaged.

**氣 → "breath," not "life energy."** 河上公's reading here is bodily and concrete: 呼吸精氣 (*"breathing the essential 氣"*), and 治身者愛氣則身全 (*"one who governs the body loves the 氣 and the body is whole"*). *Energy* is the register ch 28 has just been cleared of. **The book-wide call is still owed** — `WORKLIST` T2-4, where 氣 also reads *vital breath* (42) and *vital energy* (55).

**能為雌乎 → "can you be the hen?"** — the rider ch 28 left. 為 is *serve as / be*, not *embody*, and *"the flow of the feminine"* invented **flow** and abstracted the bird away. **王弼 ties the hen straight to this chapter's last question:** 雌**應而不倡，因而不為** — *"the hen responds and does not lead off; she goes along and does not act."* 河上公 pairs her with the other female graph — 治身當如**雌牝**安靜柔弱 — and gives the political half: 治國應變和而不唱, *"governing the state, respond to change harmoniously and do not lead off."* **The line's own graph is contested**; see `notes/manuscript.md`.

**嬰兒 → "an infant," closing T2-22.** It read *"a newborn"* here and *"an infant"* at ch 20 and ch 28, while 赤子 (*chì zǐ* — a red child) reads *"a newborn"* at ch 55. One character, one English, each way. 王弼: 能若嬰兒之**無所欲**乎 — *"can you be like an infant that has no wants?"*

***"Things," not "the countless things."*** 生之畜之 has **no antecedent anywhere in this chapter** — 萬物 does not occur — and both commentators supply one: 河上公 道生**萬物**而畜養之, 王弼 則**物**自生. So the English must supply one too, and **物 (*wù* — things)** is what the glossary carries as the secondary character, where 萬物 is a locked compound this chapter does not contain.

**長 → "growing," which also repairs ch 51.** 長而不宰 read *"leading without mastering,"* but 長 (*zhǎng*) here is the causative *make grow* — and **ch 51 already renders it *"grows"* four lines earlier** (長之育之 → *"grows and raises them"*), so that chapter was running two Englishes for one character in one stanza. 河上公: 道**長**養萬物，不**宰割**以為器用 — *"the Tao grows and nourishes them and does not **butcher** them into **vessels** for use"* — 宰 with 割 and 器, both of them ch 28's words. 說文 on 宰: **辠人在屋下執事者。从宀从辛** — *"a criminal under a roof doing service,"* from a roof and 辛, the tattooing knife. **Ch 51 takes the same change**, since T2-15 closed these two as a matched pair and they must stay matched.

**魄 → "aliveness": *"Housing your aliveness."*** *(Shalom's word, 2026-10-15. Full argument: `glossary/po-魄.md`.)* *(was: "housing your soul," from 2026-09-01.)* **"Housing" did the watchlist's work with a verb, and the noun was still the watchlist's word.** Every early source puts 魄 on the body's side: 杜預 (*Dù Yù*) 魄，**形**也, *"魄 is the form"*; 孔穎達 (*Kǒng Yǐngdá*) **附形之靈**為魄, *"the life clinging to the form,"* and then a newborn's senses, moving limbs and cry, 初生之時，耳目心識，手足運動，啼呼為聲，此則魄之靈也; 鄭玄 (*Zhèng Xuán*) **耳目之聰明**為魄, *"the sharpness of ear and eye."* **Aliveness** carries all three, comes in degrees as the 魄 does (左傳 魂魄**強**), and carries no theology, no breath and no energy. **The couplet now names the two halves the 禮記 pairs**: 氣也者神之盛也，魄也者鬼之盛也, *"breath is the fullness of spirit, the 魄 the fullness of ghost,"* aliveness in line 1 and the breath in line 2, and the infant line 2 asks for is 孔穎達's own picture of the 魄. ***Life force*, *vitality* and *vigor* were refused**: the first is the popular English for 氣; *vital* is 精's and 氣's (21, 42, 55); *vigor* leans toward virility, which is 精's at ch 55.

**Two claims below are corrected, and stay where they were made.** The pair 魂魄 is **not a Han invention**: the 左傳 has it (人生始化曰魄，既生魄，陽曰魂) and so does 韓非子 解老 on ch 60 (魂魄去而精神亂). What is Han in 河上公's gloss is the **organ map**, 魂在肝，魄在肺. And **"housing" does not follow 王弼**: his 營魄 is the house and the person dwells in it (言人能處常居之宅, *"a person who can dwell in the house where they always live"*). The direction *housing* takes, a person holding the 魄, is 王逸 (*Wáng Yì*)'s on 楚辭 遠遊's 載營魄而登霞兮 (抱我魂靈而上升也, *"embracing my soul I rise"*) and 河上公's 當愛養之, *"you must cherish and nourish it."* The verb stands on 營's graph and on those readings.

**載營魄 → "housing your soul," and the decisive fact is a character that is not in this book.** *(Shalom's line, 2026-09-01.)* *(was: "Being embodied"; then a draft, "carrying the body's soul.")* **魂 (*hún* — the cloud-soul) occurs zero times in all 81 chapters.** 魄 and 營 each occur once, both here. So 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*)'s reading — 營魄，**魂魄**也…魂在肝，魄在肺, *"營魄 is the 魂 and the 魄… the 魂 is in the liver, the 魄 in the lungs"* — is a **Han two-soul system imported onto a text that never uses the other half of the pair.** That is why a draft rendering *"the body's soul"* read as jargon: it answered a question neither English nor this book asks.

**王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) needs nothing imported, and the graphs back him.** 載猶**處**也。營魄，人之**常居處**也。一，人之**真**也 — *"載 is like 'to dwell.' 營魄 is a person's constant dwelling place. 一 is a person's genuine self."* **A person's constant dwelling place is the body.** 說文解字: **營，市居也。从宮** — a walled residence; **魄，陰神也。从鬼白聲** — the yin spirit, with a ghost for its radical, the one billeted in the flesh, not the one that leaves; **載，乘也。从車** — to ride, with a cart in the graph. **So 營魄 is not two souls. It is one thing: the quarters your animating part is camped in.**

**The rendering does the watchlist's work with a verb rather than a label.** CLAUDE.md flags 精/魄 → *soul*, and the corrective for 魄 is that it is the **corporeal** one. *"The body's soul"* said so with a possessive and read as jargon; **housing** says so with an action, and it renders 營's own graph. ***These*** carries 能無離乎 onto the two things the line has just named, which is how both commentators read it: 王弼 抱一清神，**能常無離乎**; 河上公 抱一使**不離於身**.

**Four candidate Englishes were blocked, and it is worth recording which.** *Spirit* is 神 (*shén*)'s at ch 6, 39, 60. *Flesh* is free and Pauline — *the flesh* against *the spirit*, Romans 8 — the hymn test. *Quarters* is taken four lines below by this chapter's own 四達. And ***body* is 身 (*shēn*)'s** at ch 13, 54 and 76; 身 does not occur in ch 10, so nothing clashed inside the chapter, but the noun was avoided rather than borrowed. ***Embodying* was refused too**: it is this manuscript's junk-drawer verb, wearing 為 at ch 28 until this pass removed it and still wearing 執 at ch 35 (`WORKLIST` T1-12).

**This also gives the chapter its floor.** Question 1 is the bodily ground, question 2 the breath, then the mirror, then governing, then response, then non-doing — **it moves outward from the flesh**, and the old *"Being embodied"* left it starting nowhere.

**天門 keeps *the gate of the sky*, and its strain case gains a second reading.** 河上公 gives both: 天門謂**北極紫微宮** (*"the Purple Tenuity Palace at the north pole"*) and, for the body, 天門謂**鼻孔**，開謂喘息，闔謂呼吸也 — *"天門 means the **nostrils**: 開 is breathing out, 闔 breathing in."* 王弼 takes neither: 天門謂天下之所由從也 — *"that by which the world proceeds."* Logged at `notes/translation.md` → 天 family, strain cases.

**The en-dash stays.** `WORKLIST` T4-3 is deferred, and this line's fault was its words, not its punctuation.

*End of chapter 10.*

## Chapter 11

*Heshang Gong's title: 無用, "The use of absence".*

Thirty spokes share one hub.
In what is not there,
the cart has its use.

Knead clay to make a vessel.
In what is not there,
the vessel has its use.

Cut a door and a window to make a room.
In what is not there,
the room has its use.

So presence gives the advantage,
and absence gives the use.

The Chinese:

三十輻共一轂，
當其無，
有車之用。
埏埴以為器，
當其無，
有器之用。
鑿戶牖以為室，
當其無，
有室之用。
故有之以為利，
無之以為用。

### Notes on chapter 11

**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D11 · T3-3). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; the 埏/挻 fork in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **The repetition is the argument.** 當其無 and 有X之用 repeat letter for letter three times; only 車 / 器 / 室 change. Our English changed everything else instead, so the click never happened. Eleven lines for eleven, the middle line of every stanza identical.
- 無 → **in what is not there** (its locked wording), not *emptiness* — 虛 is not in this chapter. 有 → **presence**, not *filled space*. This is the chapter `glossary/wu-you-無有.md` names as its own test case.
- 當 → **right where**, not *through*. 說文 田相值也, fields matching: it locates, it is not instrumental.
- 利 → **advantage**, the covered lock in `wu-you-無有.md`, **applied here for the first time anywhere** — the word had zero occurrences in the book. 利 wants its own entry: nine chapters, three jobs.
- **No check could find the central fault**: both tools indexed segments into a *set* of chapter numbers, so three occurrences in one chapter collapsed to one and were dropped as "not shared". **This chapter is where that was found and repaired** — `DISCOVERIES.md` §6 · `PLAN.md` → *What Chapter 11 taught the tools*.

*End of chapter 11.*

## Chapter 12

*Heshang Gong's title: 檢欲, "Reining in desire".*

The full spectrum of colors makes the eyes blind.
The full spectrum of tones makes the ears deaf.
The full spectrum of flavors makes the palate dull.

Galloping in pursuit of prey makes the heart wild.
Rare goods make actions corrupt.

Therefore the sage acts for the belly, not for the eye.
They let go of what is out there and take what is here.

The Chinese:

五色令人目盲；
五音令人耳聾；
五味令人口爽；
馳騁畋獵，
令人心發狂；
難得之貨，
令人行妨。
是以聖人為腹不為目，
故去彼取此。

### Notes on chapter 12

**故去彼取此 → "They let go of what is out there and take what is here."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-13.)* *(was: "Rejects the hungry gaze, chooses gut wisdom.")* 故去彼取此 (*gù qù bǐ qǔ cǐ* — "therefore let go of that and take this") is a **stock closing tag** — five characters, the last line of ch 12, ch 38 and ch 72, and **彼 (*bǐ* — that, yonder) occurs nowhere else in the book.** All three now carry the same English, ch 72's, where the axis was first argued.

**The old line translated the referents and deleted the deixis.** 彼 and 此 (*cǐ* — this) are **spatial** words — *yonder* and *here* — and the chapter's own pair is 目 (*mù* — eye) against 腹 (*fù* — belly): the organ that reaches outward and can never be filled, against the organ that is already here and can be satisfied. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) states it exactly: 為腹者，以物養己；為目者，以物役己 — *"one who acts for the belly uses things to nourish themselves; one who acts for the eye uses things to enslave themselves."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 去彼目之妄視，取此腹之養性 — *"let go of that, the eye's reckless looking; take this, the belly's nourishing of one's own nature."*

***"Gut wisdom" was forbidden by this chapter's own locked entry.*** `glossary/xin-心.md` carries a paragraph headed *"Why 'belly' and not 'gut'"* which names *trust your gut* as the import that must not happen — and **cites ch 12 as its evidence.** The chapter used the word anyway, one line below its own correctly rendered *belly*. Two things were wrong with it: it invents 智 (*zhì* — knowing, wisdom), a character not in this chapter, and it swaps the chapter's actual contrast — **inner need against outer craving** — for a modern one, *intuition against analysis*. It is the same failure as *"here, now"* at ch 21: see [`imported-register`](https://github.com/opencosmos-ai/taoteching/blob/main/process/principles/imported-register.md).

**The checker could not see it, and now can.** 腹 sits inside 心 (*xīn* — heart) as a `covers:` character, and **`covers:` records a `render:` but never a `forbidden:` list** — so *gut* was unforbidden book-wide. `"gut"` is now on 心's `forbidden:` list, which fires here because 心 is present in this chapter.

***What "the hungry gaze" was worth, and why it still goes.*** It was the most vivid phrase in the chapter. But 目 is already *"the eye"* in the line directly above, so the image is not lost — only not repeated — and *hungry* was borrowed from 河上公's gloss 妄視, a commentator's word rather than the text's.

**難得之貨 → "rare goods."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* *(was: "Rare treasures make actions corrupt.")* **"Treasures" is 寶 (*bǎo*)'s word** — ch 62, 67 and 69 — and 寶 never appears in this chapter. 說文 reads the two apart: 寶 is 珍也, a *precious thing*, its graph 宀 (*mián* — a roof) over 王 (jade) and 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell), **a hoard that does not move**; 貨 (*huò*) is 財也, *property*, 貝 under 化 (*huà* — a body turning over), **a shell that changes hands**. Locked to *goods* book-wide: `glossary/huo-貨.md`.

**This chapter is why "scarce" was refused for 難得.** *Scarce* means a need going unmet — and the chapter's whole hinge is 為腹不為目 (*wèi fù bù wèi mù*), 腹 (*fù* — the belly), the organ that **can** be satisfied, against 目 (*mù* — the eye), the one that cannot. **Scarcity is a fact about bellies. This chapter is about eyes.**

**Still owed here, not fixed:** 妨 (*fáng* — to hinder, obstruct) reads *"corrupt"*, a moral word for an obstruction word. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 難得之貨，塞人正路 — *"goods hard to come by block a person's straight road."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 妨，傷也 — *"妨 means to harm."* That is naturalistic-razor territory and its own item.

*End of chapter 12.*

## Chapter 13

*Heshang Gong's title: 猒恥, "Shrinking from disgrace".*

Favor and disgrace are both a shock.
Prize great trouble as your own body.

What does it mean that favor and disgrace are both a shock?
To be favored is to be below.
Getting it is a shock.
Losing it is a shock.
This is what is meant: favor and disgrace are both a shock.

What does it mean to prize great trouble as your own body?
The reason I have great trouble is that I have a body.
If I had no body, what trouble would I have?

So one who prizes their body as a way to serve the world can be trusted with the world.
One who loves their body as a way to serve the world can be trusted with it.

The Chinese:

寵辱若驚，
貴大患若身。
何謂寵辱若驚？
寵為下，
得之若驚，
失之若驚，
是謂寵辱若驚。
何謂貴大患若身？
吾所以有大患者，
為吾有身，
及吾無身，
吾有何患？
故貴以身為天下，
若可寄天下；
愛以身為天下，
若可託天下。

### Notes on chapter 13

**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D13 · T1-10 · T3-7). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; two forks in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **One word per character, and the argument appears.** 身 ×6 had four Englishes, 患 ×4 had two, 貴 ×3 had two. Now **身 → body ×6 · 患 → trouble ×4 · 驚 → shock ×5 · 貴 → prize ×3 · 下 → below ×1.**
- 無身 → **if I had no body** (T1-10). *The separate self dissolves* was Advaita, and it broke **有/無 on the one line in the book where the pair is applied to a person**. 王弼: 歸之自然也.
- **The closing couplet — Shalom's call, Reading B.** 以身為天下 → *the body as a way to serve the world*, supported by ch 26's 以身輕天下 (same 以身 + verb + 天下 shape) and by 河上公: 能愛其身，**非為己也**，乃欲為萬民之父母. **The cost is 王弼's whole chapter**, which reads it as immunity rather than devotion: 不以寵辱榮患損易其身，然後乃可以天下付之也. Reading A was drafted and withdrawn because **in English it lands as egotism** — a construal can be defensible in the Chinese and still arrive as a different claim.
- 寄/託 → **trusted with**, both (T3-7). Near-synonyms; **王弼 swaps them in his own commentary**, and 說文 defines each by the other. Two English verbs in a parallel frame read as an escalation the text does not make. 貴/愛 stay varied, because 王弼 *does* distinguish those: 無以**易**其身 (will not sell it) against 無物可以**損**其身 (will not let it be harmed).
- 若驚 → **a shock**, not *cause alarm*: 若 is *like*, not *cause*. 是謂 → **this is what is meant**, not *this is why* — 謂 is *to call*, and eight other chapters read *"This is called."*
- **Open:** T2-1 — 身 is settled inside this chapter only; it still reads three ways at ch 7, 9, 44 and 54.

*End of chapter 13.*

## Chapter 14

*Heshang Gong's title: 贊玄, "In praise of the dark".*

Look, but you cannot see it – its name is the invisible.
Listen, but you cannot hear it – its name is the inaudible.
Reach, but you cannot touch it – its name is the intangible.
These three defy comprehension.
Therefore, they mix into one.

It doesn’t have a bright top,
Or a murky bottom.
Continuously flowing, it cannot be named
And returns to no-thing.
This is the shape of no-shape, the image of no-thing.
This is called the elusive.

Meet it, and you cannot see its face,
Follow it, and you cannot see its back.

Grasp the ancient Tao, and steer what is present now.
If you can know the ancient beginning,
this is called the thread of the Tao.

The Chinese:

視之不見，
名曰夷；
聽之不聞，
名曰希；
搏之不得，
名曰微。
此三者不可致詰，
故混而為一。
其上不皦，
其下不昧。
繩繩兮不可名，
復歸於無物。
是謂無狀之狀，
無物之象，
是謂惚恍。
迎之不見其首，
隨之不見其後。
執古之道，
以御今之有。
能知古始，
是謂道紀。

### Notes on chapter 14

**能知古始，是謂道紀 → "If you can know the ancient beginning, / this is called the thread of the Tao."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-11.)* *(was: "Know the primordial source, / The thread of the Tao.")* **古始 (*gǔ shǐ* — the ancient beginning) had become *the primordial source*.** *Source* is on 母 (*mǔ* — mother)'s forbidden list and is the register the naturalistic razor strips; 古 is plainly *ancient* and 始 is *beginning*, the word ch 1 gives it. **Two characters had also gone missing.** 能 (*néng* — can) is the plain modal in 31 of its 32 lines. 是謂 (*shì wèi* — "this is called") is the formula this chapter already renders twice above (*"This is called the elusive"*). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the line as possibility, not command: 故雖在今可以知古始也, *"so although it is now, one can know the ancient beginning."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) prints 以知古始 (*yǐ zhī gǔ shǐ* — "by this, know the ancient beginning"). That drops 能 and makes the knowing follow from the line before. The English follows our base's 能. 紀 (*jì*) keeps *thread*: 說文 **絲別也**, *"the separate end of a silk thread,"* the end you pick up to unwind the rest.

**其上不皦，其下不昧 — 昧 → *murky*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-20. `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* Rode in with ch 41's 明道若昧, since one character takes one English. The line had read *"a dark bottom"*, and *dark* belongs to 玄 (*xuán*), which is absent from this chapter. 皦 (*jiǎo*) keeps *bright* and still has no entry.

**執古之道 → "Grasp the ancient Tao," and 搏 gives back the word it had taken.** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* 執 (*zhí*) is 說文 **捕罪人也**, *"to seize a criminal"* — a reaching hand and a set of manacles — and it is locked to *grasp* (`glossary/zhi-執.md`). The line had read *"Hold"* on the argument that *grasp the Tao* risks reading as *comprehend the Tao*. **The real collision was inside this chapter:** 搏之不得 (*bó zhī bù dé*) read *"you cannot **grasp** it"* thirteen lines above, so 搏 (*bó* — 說文 索持也, *"to search out and grip"*) was wearing 執's English on 執's own page. That line now reads *"Reach, but you cannot **touch** it."* **得 (*dé* — to get) is the generic completion verb here, not a lexical *obtain*, and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) proves it from inside his own gloss** — he uses 得 as a bare modal in the two lines above (不可**得**視而見之 / 不可**得**聽而聞之) and frames the triad by what is absent: 無**色**曰夷 · 無**聲**曰希 · 無**形**曰微. Colour, sound, form: sight, hearing, **touch**. Chinese has 見 (*jiàn* — to see) and 聞 (*wén* — to hear) for the first two senses and no dedicated verb for succeeding by hand, so it reaches for 得; English has one. **The cost, recorded:** 得 renders *get* at chapters 13, 23, 31 and 61 and *received* at 39, and this line departs from that. *Grasp* and *hold* were both unavailable — the first is 執's, standing in this chapter, and the second is 持's. **And ch 35's 執大象 was settled as *Grasp the great image* in Pass D**, so keeping *Hold* here split one character across the two chapters that print the same construction: 執 + a name for the Tao + a consequence for the world.

**夷 · 希 · 微 — the chapter names three characters, and the English gives their meanings rather than their words.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* This stanza is a **definition passage**: 名曰夷 · 名曰希 · 名曰微, *"its name is called X,"* three times. Each of the three is rendered here by what it means in this line, not by the word it carries elsewhere in the book.

| | 說文解字 | here | elsewhere |
|---|---|---|---|
| **夷** (*yí*) | 平也 — *"level."* 大 (a person) with 弓 (a bow) | the invisible | **level** — ch 41, 53 |
| **希** (*xī*) | the graph is 爻 (crossed threads) over 巾 (cloth): **loose-woven fabric you can see through** | the inaudible | **barely heard** — ch 41 · **sparse** — ch 23, 43, 70, 74 |
