| **微** (*wēi*) | 隱行也 — *"to move concealed,"* on 彳 (the step radical) | the intangible | **faint** — ch 15, 64 · **hidden** — ch 36 |

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies exactly these three readings, and the English follows him:**

> 無**色**曰夷 · 無**聲**曰希 · 無**形**曰微
> *"Colourless is called 夷. Soundless is called 希. Formless is called 微."*

Colour, sound, form — the three ways a thing presents to the senses, and the stanza denies all three in turn. He runs the same sentence three times: 言一無采色，不可得視而見之 · 言一無音聲，不可得聽而聞之 · 言一無形體，不可搏持而得之.

**The alternative was weighed and declined.** Rendering the words themselves — *"its name is the level · the sparse · the faint"* — would turn all three into live threads running through nine other chapters, and **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) argues for it**: at ch 41 he defines 希 by quoting this stanza outright, 聽之不聞名曰希, which makes 大音希聲 and this line **one word**. It was declined because **it costs this chapter its clarity, and chapter 14 is early** — a reader meeting three bare adjectives here has nothing yet to hang them on. **Carrying the connection is a job for these notes, not for the verse**, and the notes at chapters 15, 23, 36, 41, 43, 53, 64, 70 and 74 each point back here.

*End of chapter 14.*

## Chapter 15

*Heshang Gong's title: 顯德, "Integrity made visible".*

The ancients who were masterful in service
were faint, subtle, dark, and unobstructed,
so deep they could not be read.
Only because they could not be read
do I force a likeness:

Careful, like wading across a river in winter.
Hesitant, like someone wary of the neighbors on all four sides.
Dignified, like a guest.
Loosening, like ice about to melt.
Solid, like uncarved wood.
Open, like a valley.
Mixed, like muddy water.

Who can be muddy, and by stilling it slowly come clear?
Who can be at rest, and by moving it slowly come to life?

Those who keep the Tao safe like this have no wish to be full.
Only because they are never full
can they stay covered, and never newly made.

The Chinese:

古之善為士者，
微妙玄通，
深不可識。
夫唯不可識，
故強為之容：
豫兮若冬涉川；
猶兮若畏四鄰；
儼兮其若客；
渙兮其若冰之將釋；
敦兮其若樸；
曠兮其若谷；
混兮其若濁。
孰能濁以靜之徐清？
孰能安以動之徐生？
保此道者不欲盈。
夫唯不盈，
故能蔽而不新成。

### Notes on chapter 15

**猶兮若畏四鄰 → "Hesitant, like someone wary of the neighbors on all four sides."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "Watchful, aware of danger from all sides.")* **The danger was invented.** There is no 殆 (*dài* — danger) in this chapter and no threat in the Chinese, so no check could ever have seen it; it surfaced only because `--english "danger"` had to be run before locking that word elsewhere.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies what the line is actually about:** 其進退猶猶如拘制，若人犯法**畏四鄰知之**也 — *"their advancing and retreating is hesitant as if held back, like someone who has broken the law **fearing the four neighbours will find out**."* **Not peril from every side — the fear of being seen.** 鄰 (*lín*) is a neighbour, and 四鄰 is the ordinary phrase for the households around you.

**畏 (*wèi*) flexes here, and it is worth marking.** It reads **fear** in six other lines (17, 20, 53, 72, 74 ×2), always fear *of a thing* — authority, death, what people fear. Here 河上公's gloss is 畏四鄰**知之**, fear *that they will find out*: social exposure, not a threat. *"Fearing the neighbors"* would name them as the danger; *"wary of"* keeps the watching, which is the chapter's whole register. 畏 has no glossary entry yet, and this is the line that will decide its shape.

**The chapter was reworked whole on 2026-09-06** *(Pass D)*, because its closing line had stopped meaning anything. What follows is what changed and why.

**故能蔽而不新成 → "they can stay covered, and never newly made."** *(was: "They can become weathered, and have no interest in appearing new.")* **We had been reading 敝 (*bì* — worn out) where our base text prints 蔽 (*bì* — to cover, to screen).** Same sound, different character. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) prints 蔽 and glosses it 蔽者**匿光榮**也 — *"蔽 means **hiding one's radiance and glory**"* — and glosses the second half 新成者**貴功名** — *"the newly-completed means **prizing merit and fame**."* The line is about staying out of sight, not about patina.

**The 說文解字 (*Shuōwén Jiězì*, c. 100 CE) settles what kind of covering this is, and it is not a person hiding.** 蔽 is built on 艸 (*cǎo* — grass, growing plants): 蔽蔽，**小艸**也。从艸敝聲 — *"蔽蔙: **small grasses**. From 艸, with 敝 as the phonetic."* The covering is **vegetation** — undergrowth, foliage, shade. Its twin 敝 is built on 㡀 (*bì* — cloth in tatters) and 攴 (*pū* — to strike): 帗也。一曰**敗衣** — *"a cloth; one definition says **worn-out clothing**."* **One is plant cover, the other is a rag.** That the two share a phonetic is exactly why manuscripts confuse them, and it is why our base's choice of 蔽 has to be honoured rather than quietly read as 敝.

**This also answers the motive question, by dissolving it.** 能 (*néng*) is **can**, a capacity, not a wish — the line does not say these people *want* to be hidden, and reading it that way puts a strategy into a text that has none. 盈 is 滿**器**也 — *"a full **vessel**"*, on the 皿 (*mǐn* — dish, container) radical. A full vessel is a finished vessel, and a finished thing is a thing there is something to say about. Someone who never fills up has nothing that needs showing, so **being overlooked costs them nothing.** That is a capacity, not a virtue, and the chapter recommends no concealment anywhere in its seven similes.

**新 (*xīn*) is an axe, and that is why this line sits six lines below 樸.** 說文: 取木也。从**斤**新聲 — *"**to take wood**. From 斤 (*jīn* — an axe)."* The *new* sense is derived from freshly-cut timber. 樸 (*pǔ* — uncarved wood) is wood the axe has not finished with; 新成 is wood it has. **The etymology is not the reading** — 新 plainly means *new* by the Warring States, and we render it so — but it explains why the chapter's last image answers its middle one.

**The strongest evidence against this reading, and why it does not win.** Ch 22 has 敝則新 (*bì zé xīn* — "worn out, then new"), which we render *"Be worn out, and be renewed"* — the worn-out character paired with 新, looking very like ch 15's formula. But our base prints **敝** at ch 22 and **蔽** at ch 15; the text distinguishes them, and the worn-out character was available. And under the wear reading the two chapters collide: worn-out-becomes-new is the good outcome at 22, worn-out-and-not-new the good outcome at 15. Under the covered reading there is no clash.

**保此道者 → "Those who guard the Tao like this."** *(was: "One who holds the Tao.")* 此 (*cǐ* — this) is **anaphoric** — it points back at the two 孰能 (*shú néng* — who can) questions just asked, and 河上公 expands the phrase to 保**此徐生**之道, *"guards this Tao of gradually bringing to life."* English *"this Tao"* would partition instead of point, implying a second Tao somewhere. Attaching the pointer to the manner keeps the reach and loses the implication. 保 (*bǎo*) also moves from "holds" to **"guard"**, matching ch 9's 不可長保.

**不可識 (*bù kě shí*) appears twice, in adjacent lines, and had two Englishes** — *"fathomed"* then *"known"*. Now **"could not be read"** both times. This is `DISCOVERIES.md` §6's fault in miniature.

**An intermediate rendering, *"could not be made out,"* was retired within a day, and the reason is worth keeping.** It read as slang, and worse, it **invented a parallel**: *made out* in lines 3 and 4 chimed with *newly made* in the last line, but 識 (*shí*) and 新成 (*xīn chéng*) share no character and no root. **Where the Chinese does not repeat, the English must not either** — the mirror of `DISCOVERIES.md` §6, and nothing in the harness looks for it. `--formulas` finds a flattened repetition; an invented one is invisible. `WORKLIST.md` T5-14.

**識 is the speech-side knowing, and four candidates were tested against the whole manuscript before *read* won.** 說文: 常也。一曰**知**也。从**言**戠聲 — *"constant; one definition says **to know**. From 言 (*yán* — speech)."* Built on the speech radical, 識 is telling **what a thing is** — identification, not sensation.

- **"named" is the one to refuse hardest.** 名 (*míng* — name) runs 21 lines across 9 chapters, and **ch 14, the adjacent chapter, has 繩繩兮不可名 — *"it cannot be named."*** 不可名 and 不可識 are the same grammar one chapter apart, on **different characters**. An English that read *"could not be named"* here would assert a formula the text does not have — the invented-repetition fault (`WORKLIST.md` T5-14) in a far worse place than the one it replaced.
- **"defined"** is free of collisions but wrong in register: you define a term, not a person, and it turns the ancients into concepts. Abstraction drift, per the overlay watchlist.
- **"clearly perceived"** fails twice — 明 (*míng*) is locked to *clear-seeing / clarity* across twelve chapters, and flexes to *see clearly* and *clear* but never to a verb of perceiving, and 清 (*qīng*) takes *clear* four lines below in *"come clear"* — and *perceive* is sensory where 識 is not.
- **"known"** is 說文-licensed and has no local clash, since 知 (*zhī*) is absent from ch 15. But **"know" carries 58 English lines**, nearly all of them 知, and 識 appears in only two chapters. Handing the book's most-worked verb to a rare character muddies the reverse direction for no gain.

**"read" is free** — the only two hits on a whole-manuscript reverse search are false positives (*thread*, *already*) — plain, and exactly 識's job: telling what something is. It is metaphorical applied to people, but it is standard English rather than idiom, which *"made out"* was not.

**夫唯 (*fú wéi*) likewise appears twice** — 夫唯不可識 and 夫唯不盈 — and had *"Because they cannot be known"* against *"Because they don't seek to become full."* Both now read **"Only because"**, with the clause after each inverted, *"do I force a likeness"* and *"can they stay covered"*, and the invented *seek* is gone: 不盈 is simply *not full*. *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call. Was "Precisely because" from 2026-09-06, an intensifier where 唯 (*wéi*) is an exclusive. `glossary/wei-唯.md`.)*

**靜 and 安 had been swapped.** 孰能濁以**靜**之徐清 had 靜 (*jìng* — stillness) as *"sit"*, while 孰能**安**以動之徐生 gave *"still"* to 安 (*ān* — at rest). 靜 is **stillness** in seven other chapters. The two questions are a strict grammatical mirror — 孰能 [state] 以 [action] 之 徐 [result] — and *"move in ways that gradually stir life"* padded the second out of parallel with the first. Now: *"by stilling it slowly come clear"* / *"by moving it slowly come to life."* 生 (*shēng*) lands as **come to life**, not "stir life."

**涉 (*shè*) is 氵 (water) + 步 (*bù* — a pair of footprints): walking *through* water.** *"Crossing a frozen river"* let the crossing be made on ice or a bridge, which removes the reason for the caution — the danger is the cold water and the untested footing, and the whole simile depends on it. *"Fording"* carried that but reads as arcane; **"wading across"** keeps the legs in the river and supplies the direction English wants, which bare *"wading a river"* leaves open. *(Shalom's calls, 2026-09-06.)*

**Three smaller restorations in the similes.** 將 (*jiāng* — about to) had been dropped from 冰之將釋: the ice is **about to** melt, and the not-yet is the point in a chapter of not-yet things. 涉 (*shè*) is to **ford** or wade, so 冬涉川 is crossing a river *in winter*, not crossing a *frozen* river — the danger is the cold water, not thin ice. And all seven similes now carry **"like"**, matching 若 (*ruò*), which appears in all seven; *"as if wary of"* had broken the series at the second line.

**微妙玄通 → "faint, subtle, dark, and unobstructed."** *(was: "subtle-fine and dark-penetrating —", then "connected through", then briefly "went everywhere".)* Four characters, four parallel English terms, no hyphenated compounds and no em-dash — the dash was flagged by `check_locks.py`.

**通 (*tōng*) is a road word, which is what the first attempts missed.** 說文: 達也。从**辵**甬聲 — *"to get through (達). From 辵 (*chuò* — the walking-and-road radical)."* It is **motion past obstruction**, not a static link; *connected* drifted toward the mechanistic register the watchlist names, and *went everywhere* kept the reach but dropped the barrier, describing the result rather than the thing.

**通 shares both its radical and its definition with 道.** 說文 on 道: 所行道也。从**辵**从𩠐。**一達謂之道** — *"the road one walks. From 辵 and 首 (*shǒu* — head). **A single 達 — a single getting-through — is called a 道.**"* So 道's definition **contains** 達, and 通's definition **is** 達. They are siblings in one field: passage. **The honest limit:** 甬 is merely phonetic in 通, so the character was not built to evoke 道 and this is no pun. But the semantic kinship is real, and it means the last quality in this opening line already stands in the field the chapter's fourth block names outright at 保此道者.

**That kinship is why the passage sense had to be kept, and it decided the word.** The near candidates were all spoken for: **open** is 曠 seven lines below (*"Open, like a valley"*) plus 兌 at 10, 52 and 56; **clear** is 明 (locked, twelve chapters) and 清 four lines below; **unblocked** is 塞 at 52 and 56 (*"Block the openings"*); **far-reaching** takes *far* from 遠 at 25 and 65. *Obstruct* is free on a whole-manuscript reverse search.

**Why the Latinate register is accepted here but was refused for 識.** *Identified* was rejected because it imports a **wrong operation** — Latin *idem facere*, matching a thing against a known set — on top of its register. *Unobstructed* imports the **right** one: a road with nothing in it, which is precisely 辵 + 達. Register alone does not decide a word when the semantics are exact. It also keeps the line's four items grammatically parallel, as the Chinese is, where *went everywhere* put a verb phrase after three adjectives. **The one risk** is that English *unobstructed* often describes what one can see *through*, which would contradict 深不可識 in the very next line; the *dark* immediately before it blocks that reading.

**A thread worth pulling later: the book is full of road-words.** Besides 道 and 通, the 辵 radical carries 遠 (*yuǎn* — far), 還 (*huán* — return), 逝 (*shì* — pass away), 過 (*guò* — pass over), 隨 (*suí* — follow), 迎 (*yíng* — meet), 迷 (*mí* — go astray), 進 (*jìn* — advance), 遇 (*yù* — encounter), 遂, 遺 and 達. Not yet a note in `notes/reading.md`; recorded here so it is not lost.

**士 (*shì*) → "in service," settled 2026-09-07 across ch 15, 41 and 68** *(Shalom's call; the full argument is in ch 41's notes).* 古之善為士者 opens this chapter; 善為士者 opens ch 68; 上士 / 中士 / 下士 run through ch 41. The manuscript currently renders 士 as **"masters"** here, **"student"** at 41, and **"warrior"** at 68 — three words for one character, and ch 68's *"The master warrior is not martial"* cancels itself. A 士 is a man in service at court, the lowest rank of the nobility, which fits this chapter's deferential and unreadable figure exactly. 說文 gives 士，事也 — *one who handles affairs* — so *student* was never available; *officer* was declined as bureaucratic. **Note the seam:** 士 named a male class, and the English is deliberately neutral.

**古之善為▢者 is shared with ch 65**, which reads *"The ancients who were masterful at the Tao."* The frame now matches; only the object differs, as in the Chinese. *(`--formulas 15`.)*

**Not checked, and worth checking: whether the opening character is contested.** Guodian (~300 BCE) carries this chapter complete, and `sources/variants.yaml` records no forks for it, which means nobody has looked rather than that none exist. 河上公 glosses 士 as 謂得道之君也, *"this refers to a ruler who has attained the Tao"* — importing 道 to make 士 work, which is the kind of strain that sometimes marks a variant underneath. Logged as an open question, not as a claim.

**保此道者 → "Those who keep the Tao safe like this."** *(2026-09-08, Pass E, `WORKLIST.md` T2-19 — the holding family.)* *(was: "Those who guard the Tao like this.")* 保 (*bǎo*) is 說文 **養也**, *"to rear"* — 人 (*rén* — a person) beside an abbreviated 孚 (*fú*), a hand over a child — and it is locked to *keep safe* (`glossary/bao-保.md`). **The earlier move to *guard* was argued from ch 9's literal gloss table, not its verse**, which at the time rendered 保 nowhere and gave *guard* to **守** (莫之能守). Two characters, one English, in the chapter cited as the match. *(Ch 9 was rebuilt on 2026-09-20 and now renders 保 as bare* **keep** *— a declared flexion, and the lock's first real test there.)* 此 stays anaphoric, pointing back at the two 孰能 questions — 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 保**此徐生**之道, *"keeps safe this Tao of gradually bringing to life."*

**微 (*wēi*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 微妙玄通 renders **微** as *faint*. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 搏之不得，名曰微, which our English gives as *"its name is the intangible."* 說文解字 has 微 as 隱行也, *"to move concealed,"* built on 彳 (*chì* — the step radical) — something going by without being caught. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses ch 14's line 無**形**曰微, *"formless is called 微."* Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for the sake of that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried in the notes: *the intangible* there and *faint* here are one character. Also ch 36 (是謂微明) and ch 64 (其微易散).

*End of chapter 15.*

## Chapter 16

*Heshang Gong's title: 歸根, "Returning to the root".*

Go totally empty.
Hold steadily to stillness.
The countless things arise together,
Relying upon this, I observe their return.

Things come to their fullest,
Each returns again to its root.
Returning to the root is called stillness.
This is called returning to what is given.
Returning to what is given is called the ever-present.
Knowing the ever-present is called clear-seeing.

Not knowing the ever-present brings reckless action and disaster.

Knowing the ever-present, you contain everything.
Containing everything leads to impartiality.
Impartiality leads to supreme authority.
Supreme authority leads to the sky.
The sky leads to the Tao.
The Tao leads to what endures.
And to the end of your days, no danger will find you.

The Chinese:

致虛極，
守靜篤。
萬物並作，
吾以觀復。
夫物芸芸，
各復歸其根。
歸根曰靜，
是謂復命。
復命曰常，
知常曰明。
不知常，
妄作凶。
知常容，
容乃公，
公乃王，
王乃天，
天乃道，
道乃久，
没身不殆。

### Notes on chapter 16

**致虛極，守靜篤 → "Go totally empty. / Hold steadily to stillness."** *(2026-09-05, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D16 · T1-6.)* *(was: "Attain emptiness. / Embrace stillness.")* **Two of the couplet's six characters had no English at all.** 極 (*jí* — the far end) and 篤 (*dǔ* — steady) were both dropped, and 守 (*shǒu* — to hold to) was wearing 抱 (*bào* — to embrace)'s word.

**Both lines hide a gait.** 說文解字 makes 篤 **馬行頓遟**, *"a horse's gait, halting and slow,"* and 致 **送詣也** — 夊 (*suī* — a dragging foot) beneath 至 (*zhì* — to arrive), *"to send all the way there."* Not two achievements: one instruction about how far and how slowly. *Attain* and *embrace* had made both of them prizes.

**極 measures the reacher, not the emptiness** — its original graph 亟 (*jí*) is a standing body with a stroke at the crown and one at the heel. That is what dissolves the paradox the line seems to pose. And **虛 must not become *emptiness***: that is śūnyatā's English, and 空 (*kōng*), the character Chinese Buddhism uses for it, has zero occurrences in this book. Ch 16 is the only place 虛 is forced into a noun slot, so it is the only place the import can happen. Full argument in `glossary/ji-極.md` and `glossary/xu-虛.md`; the rejected candidates and the *hold to* decision are in `notes/translation.md`.

**Guodian (~300 BCE) carries this couplet and nothing else from the chapter** — bundle A, unit A.3, standing alone as its own slip-unit. Two forks logged: 致 / 至 and 觀復 / 觀其復, both in `notes/manuscript.md`.

**容 got one English, and the tail-head chain closed.** *(2026-09-05, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D16.)* *(was: "Knowing the ever-present creates the capacity to embrace the totality. / Embracing all leads to impartiality.")* 容 (*róng* — to contain) had **two Englishes one line apart** where the Chinese repeats the identical character, breaking 頂真 (*dǐng zhēn* — the tail-head chain) at its first link; the other four links were already clean. 說文解字: 盛也。从宀、谷 — *"to hold, as a vessel holds. From 宀 (mián — a roof) and 谷 (gǔ — a valley)."* Both commentators gloss it with 無所不包 — 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) 無所不包通也, 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) 无所不包容也 — which is what licenses *everything*. The one fix removed three imports: *create* (生 *shēng*'s), *embrace* (抱 *bào*'s), *totality* (nothing's).

**乃 (*nǎi* — then) keeps *leads to*, on Shalom's call.** Both commentators read the chain as conditional consequence, using 則 (*zé* — if/then): 王弼 無所不包通**則**乃至於蕩然公平也, 河上公 無所不包容**則**公正無私. English *leads to* carries that — the sunrise leading to light, not a machine producing an output.

**Two invented words removed.** *"The open sky"* ×2 — 天 (*tiān*) is locked to *sky* as a tier and *open* rendered nothing. And 久 (*jiǔ*) → **what endures**, not *what lasts*: ch 7's 天長地久 splits the pair in one line, 長 (*cháng*) → *lasting*, 久 → *enduring*, and 長且久 repeats it.

**夫物芸芸，各復歸其根 → "Things come to their fullest. / Each returns again to its root."** *(2026-09-05, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D16 · T1-13.)* *(was: "Multitudes flourish, / Each returns energy to its root.")* Four faults in two lines. **物 (*wù* — things) had been deleted**, hiding that this is the chapter restating the 萬物 of three lines above. ***Multitudes* is 眾 (*zhòng* — the crowd)'s word** and 眾 has zero occurrences here — invisible to the checker twice over, since 眾's `forbidden:` list carries *"the multitude"* and this line said *Multitudes*. ***Energy* is 氣 (*qì* — vital breath)'s**, also absent, the last survivor of the purge done at ch 28 and ch 10. And **復歸 lost a character**.

**芸芸 is a peak, not a motion.** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 芸芸者華葉盛 — *"芸芸 means flowers and leaves at their fullest."* The line sits immediately before the turn, and that adjacency is the chapter's teaching: maximum display, then the return. *In full leaf* was tried and rejected — 河上公's gloss explains the word vegetally, but 物 is general, and committing the English to foliage makes all things plants. *Prime* was rejected too: it is 壯 (*zhuàng*)'s word, 壯 is absent here, and ch 30 and ch 55 both read 物壯則老 as the identical sentence *"When things reach their prime, they decay"* — borrowing it would make ch 16 look like a quotation.

**復歸 → *returns again*, following ch 28.** The compound runs seven lines (14, 16, 28 ×3, 52) and ch 28's Pass D rewrite settled it to one shape: *"Return again to the infant / the endless / the uncarved wood."* 歸 carries *return*, 復 carries *again*. 說文解字 keeps them distinct — 復 往來也 (*"going and coming"*), 歸 女嫁也 (*"a woman marrying,"* going to the house that is now hers). *Returns home* was proposed and dropped: *home* does render 歸, but it matches no other line in the formula.

**根 is a stump.** 說文: 木株也 — the stock left in the ground when the growth is gone. Not an origin. That is why 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) can gloss the whole movement 凡有起於虛，動起於靜 — *"all presence arises from emptiness, all movement arises from stillness"* — and why 河上公 can say 枯落 (*"wither and fall"*) and 更生 (*"born again"*) in one breath. **歸根 is not a euphemism for dying**: 吾以觀復 has the speaker *watching* the returning, and no one watches their own death.

**是謂復命，復命曰常 → "returning to what is given."** *(2026-09-05, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T2-18.)* *(was: "returning to what **was** given.")* One word, and it settles a line four candidates had failed. **復命 is a name, not a further step** — the chapter describes one event and names it four times over, each name becoming the next line's subject: 各復歸其根 → 歸根**曰**靜 → 是謂**復命** → 復命**曰**常 → 知常**曰**明. Nothing new enters at 復命.

**The present tense is the whole of the change.** *What was given* put the giving in the past, in a naming chain whose other members — 靜 (*jìng* — stillness), 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) — are timeless. *What **is** given* is ongoing: what any thing is given, always. That reads straight into 常 on the next line, where a past-tense clause fought it.

**The giver stays present and unnamed, which is right rather than a compromise.** 命's graph has a mouth in it — 說文解字: 使也。从口从令, and 令 is 發號也, *"to issue a call."* What this edition strips is **naming** the speaker (*mandate* names Heaven, *destiny* names a plot); the passive admits the speech without naming who spoke, exactly as the Chinese does. Full argument, down to the radicals, in `glossary/fuming-復命.md`.

**Three candidates were rejected on evidence.** ***The allotted course*** — *course* is a path you run, and the chapter's event is a thing **finishing** one; it also passes the hymn test, which is the warning sign. ***Returning the charge*** and ***returning the message*** — both take 復命 transitively (hand it back, the envoy idiom), which **neither commentator supports**, and both need an antecedent the chapter never supplies. ***Returning to what is*** — *what it is* is already 自然 (*zì rán* — of itself)'s English at ch 25, and **ch 51 sets 命 and 自然 against each other in one clause**: 夫莫之命而常自然, *"no one 命s it, and it is always 自然."* That rendering would collapse the book's own antithesis.

**Chapter complete** (`WORKLIST.md` D16, closed 2026-09-05).

**没身不殆 → "and to the end of your days, no danger will find you."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "Not even death threatens this.")* **This was a mistranslation, not merely a mismatch.** 没身 (*mò shēn* — "to the end of one's body") is an idiom for **all one's life**, which is exactly how ch 52 renders the identical four characters. The old line read 没身 as *death itself* and handed the sentence to the Tao rather than to the person who has just climbed the ladder 公 → 天 → 道 (*gōng* impartiality → *tiān* the open sky → *dào*).

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) settles the subject:** 無殃無咎…乃與天地俱没，**不危殆**也 — *"no calamity, no blame… then one **sinks away together with sky and earth**, not in peril."* The sinking is the person's, and so is the safety.

**殆 is 歺 (*è*) — the bare-bone radical, the death element in 死 (*sǐ* — to die) and 殃 (*yāng* — calamity) — with 台 for sound.** 說文解字: 危也, *"peril."* It reads **danger** in all five of its occurrences now (16, 25, 32, 44, 52), and *danger* renders nothing else in the book.

*End of chapter 16.*

## Chapter 17

*Heshang Gong's title: 淳風, "Unspoiled ways".*

About the greatest leaders, those under them know only that they exist.
Good leaders are widely loved and praised.
Poor leaders are feared.
The worst leaders are despised by all.

Where trust runs short, there is no trust.

The greatest leaders speak sparingly.
When their work is done,
Everyone says, “We did this by ourselves.”

The Chinese:

太上，下知有之；
其次，親而譽之；
其次，畏之；
其次，侮之。
信不足焉，有不信焉。
悠兮其貴言。
功成事遂，
百姓皆謂：「我自然」。

### Notes on chapter 17

**太上，下知有之 → "About the greatest leaders, those under them know only that they exist."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "little is known.")* 下 (*xià* — below) is the subject, and the old line dropped it. *Those under them* mirrors ch 75's 其上 → *"those over them"*, so the book's two words for the vertical read as a pair. *Their subjects* was weighed and declined: it brings a sovereign the 民 entry already refuses, and it names the very relation this chapter says the greatest rule makes disappear, since its people end by saying *"We did this by ourselves."* It also read like the variant 不知有之 (*"do not know they exist"*), which is not our base.

**百姓皆謂 → "Everyone says."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call, `glossary/baixing-百姓.md`. Was: "The people all say.")* This is the one line in the book where the people speak in their own voice, and what they say is that they were not governed. It cannot use 民 (*mín*)'s *the people*, the book's word for them as the governed. *Everyone* already holds 皆 (*jiē* — all).

**信不足焉，有不信焉 → "Where trust runs short, there is no trust."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14. Was: "When leaders don't trust the people, no one trusts the leaders.")* Seven characters, verbatim at ch 23, and the two chapters had carried two different Englishes since the first draft. **The old line had the arrow backwards, which mattered more than the mismatch.**

**信 (*xìn* — trust) is not an attitude the ruler holds.** `glossary/xin-信.md` is locked on this: 信 names a **符契** (*fú qì*) — a **split tally**, a token broken in two so the halves can be matched later — so it is *a correspondence that can be checked*, not a warm inner disposition. 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads the line accordingly: 君信不足**於下**，下則應之以不信而**欺其君**也 — *"the ruler's trustworthiness is insufficient **toward** those below; those below respond with untrust and **deceive** their ruler."* **The people's deceiving mirrors a ruler who could not be relied on, not a ruler who was suspicious.** *"Leaders don't trust the people"* had the failure running the wrong way, and made 信 the inner state the entry rejects.

**No subjects are supplied, because 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) does not read this as being about a ruler at all.** On this very line, in this very chapter: 夫御體失性則疾病生，輔物失真則疵釁作。信不足焉，則有不信，**此自然之道也**。已處不足，非智之所齊也 — *"govern the body and lose its nature, and sickness arises; assist a thing and lose its truth, and flaws and cracks appear. Where trust is insufficient, there is untrust. **This is the way of things being so of themselves.** Once one stands in insufficiency, it is not something cleverness can set right."* That is **emergence, not reciprocity** — nothing is given back, the deficiency produces its own consequence the way disease follows a violated nature. An agent-free English holds his reading and 河上公's at once; the old one held only 河上公's.

**The near-tautology is the argument.** 不足 (*bù zú* — not enough; 足 is *enough*, as at ch 44 and 46's 知足, "know when you have enough") gives way to 不信 (*bù xìn* — no trust). **A shortfall of trust does not stay partial; it goes to zero.** There is no slightly-healthy body in 王弼's analogy either.

*(Ch 17 is attested at Guodian, ~300 BCE, bundle C, where the slips run continuously into ch 18 with no chapter division.)*

*End of chapter 17.*

## Chapter 18

*Heshang Gong's title: 俗薄, "When custom wears thin".*

When the great Tao is discarded, humaneness and duty appear.
When cleverness and erudition arise, great hypocrisy appears.
When kin are out of harmony, devotion and tenderness appear.
When states grow clouded and fall into disorder, loyal ministers appear.

The Chinese:

大道廢，有仁義；
智慧出，有大偽；
六親不和，有孝慈；
國家昏亂，有忠臣。

### Notes on chapter 18

**國家 → "states."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call, with ch 54. Was: "nations.")* 國 (*guó*) is *state* throughout the book.

**國家昏亂 → *nations grow clouded and fall into disorder*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-21.)* 亂 was *chaos*, a **cosmological** word in English where 亂 is political and domestic; see `glossary/luan-亂.md`. The provisional line of 2026-09-20 is now settled.

**國家昏亂 → *nations grow clouded and fall into chaos*.** *(2026-09-20, `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* 昏 (*hūn* — clouded) had been **absorbed into 亂's English** and not rendered at all; the line read *"When nations fall into chaos."* Two characters, one word.

**⚠ This line is provisional.** 亂 (*luàn*) still reads *chaos* here, and `glossary/luan-亂.md` recommends **disorder** against it — 說文 defines 亂 as **治也**, *to bring to order*, and ch 64 prints the pair 治之於未亂. The entry is `status: open` pending 治, so the swap is owed, not taken. `WORKLIST.md` T2-55.

*Revised 2026-08-28 under the 仁 and 慈 locks (`glossary/ren-仁.md`, `glossary/ci-慈.md`).*

**孝慈 had lost half of itself.** The verse read *"filial piety"* for 孝慈, so 慈 (*cí* — tenderness) had no English at all. The two graphs point opposite ways: 孝 is 老 (*lǎo* — old) abbreviated over 子 (*zǐ* — child), **the child bearing up the elder**; 慈 is 心 (*xīn* — heart) under a phonetic carrying *to grow*, the heart increasing toward its offspring. 河上公 makes it a circuit rather than a list: 乃有孝慈**相牧養**也, *"then there is 孝慈, tending each other."* Hence **devotion and tenderness**.

**六親 → "kin," and the number is deliberately not in the English.** 王弼: 六親**父子兄弟夫婦**也 — *"the six kin are parents and children, brothers, husband and wife."* Three **pairs**, counted as six **persons** — so the number enumerates people while the line is about relations, and English cannot carry both without a gloss inside the verse. *Families* was the wrong unit (households, not relations); *the six kin* makes the reader stop for a number that is doing no work in the argument.

**The scare quotes are gone from 忠臣.** The Chinese is straight, and the irony is structural — all four lines have one shape, and the shape is the claim. Quotation marks were the edition's voice telling the reader what to hear.

**大道 → the great Tao**, restoring 大, which ch 34 and ch 53 already carry.

**On what the chapter is doing.** 河上公: 大道之時，家有孝子，戶有忠信，仁義**不見**也 — *"in the time of the great Tao, every family had devoted children and every household loyalty and trust, and humaneness and duty **were not visible**."* Not absent. Unnamed, because nothing had gone wrong that would make anyone name them. See `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 19 for the Guodian fork, and for the Yongle Dadian's joining of this chapter to the next.

*End of chapter 18.*

## Chapter 19

*Heshang Gong's title: 還淳, "Back to the unspoiled".*

Cut off sagehood, abandon cleverness, and the people benefit a hundredfold.
Cut off humaneness, abandon duty, and the people return to devotion and tenderness.
Cut off cunning, abandon profit, and there are no thieves.

These three, taken as cultural form, are not enough.
So give them something to belong to:
see the undyed silk, embrace the uncarved wood,
diminish the self, diminish desire.

The Chinese:

絕聖棄智，民利百倍；
絕仁棄義，民復孝慈；
絕巧棄利，盜賊無有。
此三者以為文不足，
故令有所屬：
見素抱樸，
少私寡欲。

### Notes on chapter 19

*Revised 2026-08-28 under the 仁 and 慈 locks, with the Guodian fork recorded at the same time. Fork in `sources/variants.yaml`; reasoning in `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 19. This closes `PLAN.md` → G1.*

**絕 → cut off, 棄 → abandon, and they are two different violences.** 絕 is 斷絲也 — *Shuowen*: *"to break silk thread,"* from 糸 (*mì* — silk), 刀 (*dāo* — knife), 卩. A blade on a thread. 棄 is a child over a basket held in two hands, the element glossed 逆子 (*nì zǐ* — an inverted child): **casting out a newborn.** The verse had spent one English word, *abandon*, on both, and had merged the third couplet's two nouns into one phrase.

*Cut off* rather than *sever*, because 絕 must also serve ch 20's 絕學無憂: English *sever* wants a physical connection as its object and balks at abstractions, while *cut off* takes them and keeps the blade. Ch 20 is swept to match. *Abandon* for 棄 is already the book's word at ch 27 (無棄人) and ch 62.

**And the second couplet turns on that.** 棄 casts out the child; the line's payoff is 民復孝慈 — the people **return to devotion and tenderness**, which is the parent-child bond itself. Throw the child away and the childhood comes back.

**These are goods, not evils, and 王弼 says so plainly.** 聖智，才之善也；仁義，人之善也；巧利，用之善也 — *"sagehood and knowing are the best of talent; humaneness and duty are the best of persons; cunning and profit are the best of use."* Three matched pairs of **goods**, held to be insufficient as 文 (*wén* — cultural form, writing), not three vices. Hence *"These three, taken as cultural form, are not enough"* — the earlier *"insufficient decorations for society"* had invented **edicts** and lost 文.

**故令有所屬 → "so give them something to belong to."** 屬 (*shǔ*) is attachment, belonging. 王弼: 故令人有所屬，**屬之於素樸寡欲** — *"attach them to the undyed, the uncarved, and few desires."* The chapter does not end on a prohibition; it ends by handing over something to hold.

**抱 → embrace**, correcting a lock breach: 抱 is *embrace* and 守 is *hold fast to*, and the two are never swapped. **百倍 → a hundredfold**, restored; it had been flattened to *greatly*.

**The oldest witness does not make this attack.** At Guodian (~300 BCE) the passage carries neither 聖 nor 仁 nor 義; the pairs cut off there are different ones, and only 絕巧棄利 is shared. We keep the received text, as at ch 25, and record the fork.

*End of chapter 19.*

## Chapter 20

*Heshang Gong's title: 異俗, "Apart from custom".*

Cut off learning and there is no worry.

Between a respectful yes and a careless yeah,
how much distance?
Between good and bad,
how far apart?
What people fear must be feared.
How wild it is, and without end!

The crowd is merry, as if at a great feast,
as if climbing a terrace in spring.
I alone am moored, and show no sign,
like an infant who has not yet learned to smile,
listless, as if with nowhere to return.

The crowd all have more than enough.
I alone seem to have missed out.
I have the heart of a fool!
How muddled!
The worldly are bright. I alone am clouded.
The worldly are sharp. I alone am dull.

Calm, like the sea.
Blown along, as if never stopping.

The crowd all have something to use themselves for.
I alone am stubborn, and look coarse.
I alone differ from others:
I prize feeding from the mother.

The Chinese:

絕學無憂。
唯之與阿，相去幾何？
善之與惡，相去若何？
人之所畏，不可不畏。
荒兮，其未央哉！
眾人熙熙，
如享太牢，
如春登臺。
我獨泊兮，其未兆；
如嬰兒之未孩；
傫傫兮，若無所歸。
眾人皆有餘，
而我獨若遺。
我愚人之心也哉！
沌沌兮！
俗人昭昭，
我獨昏昏。
俗人察察，
我獨悶悶。
澹兮，其若海；
飂兮，若無止。
眾人皆有以，
而我獨頑似鄙。
我獨異於人，
而貴食母。

### Notes on chapter 20

**昏昏 (*hūn hūn*) → *clouded*, not *dark*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-20. `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* 說文: **日冥也。从日氐省。氐者，下也** — *"the sun gone dark; from 日 (the sun) and an abbreviated 氐, and 氐 means below."* The sun under the line: dusk. *Dark* belongs to 玄 (*xuán*), six verse lines including ch 1's 玄之又玄, and there is no 玄 here. With this line and ch 57, **玄 has its word to itself again** — `--english "dark"` is 6 lines, 6 backed.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) glosses this with the same compound he uses for 昧 at ch 41** — 我獨若昏 → **如闇昧也** — so for him 昏 and 昧 name nearly one state. The English keeps them a step apart, *clouded* against *murky*, which is the distance that reading suggests. He reads the other half as 明且達也, *"bright and penetrating,"* and 王弼 as 耀其光也, *"they dazzle with their light."*

**A fork, unlogged until now.** The Siku editors note on 王弼: 〔案昏昏**河上公注本作若昏**〕 — *"for 昏昏, Heshang Gong's commentary text reads 若昏."* Our base doubles the character; his hedges it to *as if 昏*. We keep the base. Recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`.

**Not changed, and worth seeing:** this chapter runs on **reduplication** — 昭昭 · 昏昏 · 察察 · 悶悶 · 沌沌 — and the English renders every one as a single plain word. Whether that doubling should show is unasked.

*End of chapter 20.*

## Chapter 21

*Heshang Gong's title: 虛心, "Emptying the heart".*

The greatest integrity follows only the Tao.
Whatever the Tao is, it is only vague, only elusive.
Elusive and vague, and within it there is an image.
Vague and elusive, and within it there is a thing.
Deep and dim, and within it there is vital essence.
Its essence utterly real, and within it there is trust.

From ancient times until today, the Tao's name has never been erased.
In this name, I observe the origin of the many.
How do I know the origin of the many is so? By this.

The Chinese:

孔德之容，
惟道是從。
道之為物，
惟恍惟惚。
惚兮恍兮，其中有象；
恍兮惚兮，其中有物。
窈兮冥兮，其中有精；
其精甚真，其中有信。
自古及今，其名不去，
以閱眾甫。
吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？
以此。

### Notes on chapter 21

**惟道是從 → "follows only the Tao."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`. Was: "simply follows the Tao.")* 惟 (*wéi*) is 唯 (*wéi* — only) written with the heart radical, and the next line already reads it *only*, twice: 惟恍惟惚, *"only vague, only elusive."* *Simply* restricted the verb, a manner of following. 惟 X 是 V (*wéi X shì V*) fronts the object and singles it out, the construction of ch 53's 唯施是畏 (*wéi shī shì wèi*), *"my only fear would be to stray."*

**以此 → "By this." — and every word we had added to it is gone.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-12.)* The line closed *"By this, here, now."* 以此 (*yǐ cǐ*) is 以 (*yǐ* — by means of) + 此 (*cǐ* — this): **two characters, two words.** The addition came from 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*), who glosses the phrase 此，今也 (*cǐ, jīn yě* — "'this' means **now**") and continues 以今萬物皆得道精氣而生 (*"because now the countless things all obtain the Tao's essence-breath and live"*). **A commentator's gloss is evidence for a rendering, not a rendering** — and this one had been lifted straight into the verse.

**It also picked a side the Chinese does not pick.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the same two characters the other way: 此上之所云也…言吾何以知萬物之始於無哉，以此知之也 — *"'this' is what was said above… it says: how do I know the countless things begin in no-thing? By this I know it."* That is **anaphora**, pointing back through the descent 象 (*xiàng* — image) / 物 (*wù* — thing) / 精 (*jīng* — vital essence) / 信 (*xìn* — trust). 河上公's *now* is **deixis in time**. The two are incompatible, and a bare *this* is the only English that leaves both standing. The note in `notes/manuscript.md` that claimed the old line "holds both" has been corrected; it held one.

***"Here, now" was also a date stamp.*** It is *Be Here Now* (Ram Dass, 1971) and the mindfulness literature after it — a register that postdates the text by twenty-three centuries and that this book helped create, so it reads back onto it invisibly. Now a standing principle: [`imported-register`](https://github.com/opencosmos-ai/taoteching/blob/main/process/principles/imported-register.md).

**Three chapters, one formula, one English.** 吾何以知…**然**哉？以此 closes ch 21, ch 54 and ch 57, and it had three Englishes — which meant `DISCOVERIES.md` §2, whose whole claim is that the *same* answer is given three times, was invisible in the manuscript it describes. All three now read **"By this."** 河上公 supports the unification from his own side: he glosses ch 21 and ch 57 with the **identical five characters**, 此，今也.

**The cost, accepted: the chapter now ends on two syllables and a full stop.** That thinness is the reading. The answer to the largest question in the book is a **gesture, not an explanation** — every word we were adding made the pointing finger talk.

*End of chapter 21.*

## Chapter 22

*Heshang Gong's title: 益謙, "The gain in humility".*

Bend, and stay whole. Be wronged, and be made straight.
Be hollowed out, and be filled. Be worn out, and be renewed.
Hold little and gain. Hold much and be confused.

Therefore the sage embraces one thing and serves as the world's pattern.

They do not show themselves off, and so they see clearly.
They do not insist they are right, and so their rightness shows.
They do not claim the work, and so the work is theirs.
They do not boast, and so they endure.

Only because they do not contend can no one in the world contend with them.
When the ancients said "bend, and stay whole," were those empty words?
These words hold. Return to them. Stay whole.

The Chinese:

曲則全，
枉則直，
窪則盈，
敝則新，
少則得，
多則惑。
是以聖人抱一
為天下式。
不自見，故明；
不自是，故彰；
不自伐，故有功；
不自矜，故長。
夫唯不爭，
故天下莫能與之爭。
古之所謂「曲則全」者，
豈虛言哉！
誠全而歸之。

### Notes on chapter 22

**夫唯不爭 → "Only because they do not contend can no one in the world contend with them."** *(2026-10-19, Shalom's call, `glossary/wei-唯.md`. Was: "Because they do not contend, no one in the world can contend with them.")* 唯 (*wéi* — only) restored. **It is now what separates this line from ch 66**, which closes on the same clause with 以其不爭 (*yǐ qí bù zhēng* — because they do not contend) and no 唯, and keeps its plain *"Because they do not contend."* One character apart in the Chinese, one word apart in the English.

**不自矜 → "They do not boast."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "They do not make themselves great.")* *Great* is 大 (*dà*)'s locked English and there is no 大 in the line. The old rendering took the commentary gloss 矜，大也 as its English. *Boast* is 矜's word at ch 30 (果而勿矜), and ch 24 mirrors this line, so the three now agree.

*Revised 2026-08-27, from the `WORKLIST.md` debt on 不自是. Full argument for all five decisions in `notes/translation.md` · Ch 22.*

**王弼 maps stanza three onto stanza one, one-to-one.** 不自見其明**則全**也 · 不自是**則其是彰**也 · 不自伐**則其功有**也 · 不自矜**則其德長**也 — the four 不自X (*bù zì X* — "does not self-X") lines are the four opening paradoxes restated as conduct. The chapter is one argument told twice, and **what you refuse to claim is what comes to you**. Note Wang Bi repeats the character: 不自是則其**是**彰也.

**抱一 → "embraces one thing," a deliberate de-mystification.** 王弼: **一，少之極也** — *"the one is the extreme of 少 (*shǎo* — few)"* — anchored in the line above, 少則得，多則惑. The least you can hold is one. *"The one"* now reads in English as a chosen-one trope, so the definite article was doing damage the Chinese never does; 一 (*yī*) is a single stroke, a tally mark. A **per-chapter call, not a lock** — 一 keeps *the one* at ch 14, 39, 42. See `glossary/yi-一.md`.

**明 → *see clearly*, retiring "luminous."** `glossary/ming-明.md` already used this line as its worked example; the verse was stale against its own entry. 河上公: 聖人**不以其目視**千里之外也，乃**因天下之目以視** — *"the sage does not see a thousand li with their own eyes; they see by means of the world's eyes."* Reception, not emission.

**式 (*shì*) is a template, not a moral example.** 弋 (*yì* — a driven stake) with 工 (*gōng* — a carpenter's square). 王弼: 式猶則之也. 河上公: 法式也. Ch 28's 常德**不忒** (*tè* — to deviate) proves it: you can only deviate from a standard.

**誠全而歸之 had no English at all** — the line read *"Try and see for yourself."* 全 (*quán* — whole) is the word the chapter opens on and quotes back, so restoring it forced 曲則全 → *"Bend, and stay whole."*

**誠 answers 虛言.** 豈**虛言**哉！**誠**全而歸之 — 虛言 (*xū yán* — empty words) answered by 誠, which is 言 (*yán* — words) + 成 (*chéng* — to complete): **words made good**. Hence *"These words hold,"* not a bare *in truth*.

**全 is preservation, not repair.** 河上公 on 曲則全: 則**全其身**也, *"then keeps their body whole."* The chapter is about not getting broken in the first place, so neither *makes you whole* nor *restores your wholeness* can stand — both presuppose the loss. **歸 → return**, the book's word for it in seven chapters, and the person is the one who moves (歸根 · 復歸於樸 · 復歸於嬰兒).

**之 → *them*, the words — and *home* was deliberately refused.** 歸 does carry homecoming; every destination this book gives it is the original state. But **home is not in the line**, and supplying it would hand the reader a conclusion the text lets them reach. The verse delivers the words; the depth belongs to the reader's own arrival. See `DISCOVERIES.md` §5. 河上公's filial reading (歸之於父母, from the *Xiaojing*) is declined as a Han Confucian import.

**Owed elsewhere:** ch 28 carries 為天下式 twice and needs the same 式 treatment; ch 24's 自伐 → *"boasts"* may want 伐 → *claim*. Both in `WORKLIST.md`.

**為天下式 → "serves as the world's pattern."** *(2026-09-01, with ch 28, closing `WORKLIST.md` T2-15.)* *(was: "sets a pattern for the world.")* The formula stands here and three times at ch 28, and the two chapters had rendered it two ways. **為 (*wéi*) is locked to *do / handle / serve as*** — *sets… for* read it as the other tone, 為 (*wèi* — for the sake of), which turns a role into an intention. The sage does not **make** a pattern for anybody; the sage **is** one.

*End of chapter 22.*

## Chapter 23

*Heshang Gong's title: 虛無, "Emptiness and absence".*

Brevity in speech happens of itself.
A squall does not last out the morning.
A downpour does not last out the day.
Who does this? Sky and earth.
Even sky and earth cannot make it last long.
How much less a person?

So one whose affairs follow the Tao is the same as the Tao.
One of integrity is the same as integrity.
One of loss is the same as loss.

Those the same as the Tao, the Tao too gladly gets them.
Those the same as integrity, integrity too gladly gets them.
Those the same as loss, loss too gladly gets them.
Where trust runs short, there is no trust.

The Chinese:

希言自然。
故飄風不終朝，
驟雨不終日。
孰為此者？天地。
天地尚不能久，
而況於人乎？
故從事於道者，
同於道；
德者，同於德；
失者，同於失。
同於道者，
道亦樂得之；
同於德者，
德亦樂得之；
同於失者，
失亦樂得之。
信不足焉，
有不信焉。

### Notes on chapter 23

**同 (*tóng* — the same) is the antonym of 異 (*yì* — different), and six lines of this chapter had made it a dissolution.** *(2026-09-03, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T2-25. Was: *"merges with the Tao / merges with integrity / merges with the loss,"* and *"Those merged with…"* three times more.)* **Chapter 1 prints the pair in one clause** — 此兩者，**同**出而**異**名, *"these two 同 emerge and 異 in name"* — and our ch 1 renders it correctly as *"the **same** origin."* Everywhere else 同 had drifted: *together* (1), *merges with* (4, 23 ×6, 56), *union* (56). **Five Englishes for one character.**

**Both commentators gloss 同 with 同, and neither describes a process.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 而物得其真，**與道同體**，故曰同於道 — *"things attain their genuineness, **of one body with the Tao**; therefore it says 同於道."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*), flatly: 同於道者，所謂**與道同**也 — *"'同於道' means what is called **being the same as the Tao**."*

**The chapter's claim is resonance, not union, and 河上公 says so in the 易經's own words.** His gloss on the closing 信 (*xìn* — trust) line: 物相歸，**同聲相應**，雲從龍，風從虎，水流濕，火就燥，自然之道也 — *"things return to their kind, **like sounds answer each other**: clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger, water flows to the damp, fire goes to the dry — this is the way of being so of itself."* **Every one of those is a pair, two things finding each other by kind.** 王弼 reaches the same place by a different road, glossing 樂得之 with 應 (*yìng* — to answer): 言隨行其所，故同而應之, *"it says: follow the conduct of what you belong to, and so, being the same, it answers you."*

**Identity would have collapsed the pair, which is why *"is the Tao"* was proposed and declined.** 同於道者，道亦樂**得之** needs a person and a Tao standing apart long enough for one to take up the other; read as *"the one who **is** the Tao, the Tao is glad to get,"* there is no one left to receive and no one to be received. A cloud that *is* the dragon has nothing to follow. **And 同 would have become a copula**, leaving ch 56's 玄同 (*xuán tóng* — dark sameness) with nothing to render. *(The proposal was consistent with ch 8's 幾於道 → *"nearly the Tao,"* and the asymmetry is this: 幾 (*jī* — nearly) survives in the English word *nearly*, where 同 would not survive in *is*.)*

***The third line is where the reading pays.*** 失者，同於失 had read *"Whoever loses merges with the loss"* — a mystical surrender. As **"One of loss is the same as loss"** it is the chapter's harder claim: **you are the same as what you keep company with, and that holds for loss exactly as it holds for the Tao.** 河上公 on 失者: 失謂任己失人也 — *"失 means relying on oneself and losing others."*

**事 (*shì* — affairs) is locked, and read *"actions."*** 從事於道者 had been *"the one who **aligns their actions** with the Tao"* and, in an intermediate draft, the clunky *"one who attends to affairs by the Tao."* It now reads ***"one whose affairs follow the Tao."*** **Both commentators define the phrase**: 王弼 從事謂舉動 (*"從事 means conduct, raising and moving"*), 河上公 從，為也。人為事當如道安静，不當如飄風驟雨 (*"從 means to handle; a person handling affairs should be like the Tao, still and calm, not like a squall or a downpour"*). And *aligns* rendered 從 (*cóng*), whose 說文解字 is 隨行也, *"to follow along"* — an alignment metaphor imported onto a following word.

***"One who follows the Tao"* was proposed and declined on the reverse check.** *(Shalom, 2026-09-03.)* **ch 21 already carries that exact English for a different grammar**: 惟道是從 reads *"The greatest integrity simply **follows the Tao**,"* and there 道 genuinely **is** 從's object. Here 從 governs 事 — 從事 is a set compound, 於道 its complement — so the same English would make two unlike constructions look identical. **And 從事 occurs exactly twice in the book**, here and ch 64's 民之從事, which we already render as *their affairs*. **The chapter is about conduct, not allegiance**: *follows the Tao* makes it a question of whose side you are on, where 河上公 makes it a question of how you go about your business.

***"Intensity" and "sustain" rendered nothing.*** 天地尚不能久 is *"even sky and earth cannot make it last long"* — 久 (*jiǔ*) is duration, 尚 (*shàng*) is *even*. **The invented *intensity* was 王弼's 暴疾** (*bào jí* — violent and rapid) lifted out of the commentary into the verse, the ch 24 *wart* error again: **a commentator's gloss is not the text.**

**人 (*rén* — a person) had become *"we."*** 而況於人乎 is *"how much less a person?"* — 河上公: 何况人欲為暴卒乎, *"how much less a person who wishes to act violently and abruptly."* The old *"how much less can **we**?"* invented a first person the line does not have. **This does not touch T4-1**, the deferred 民/人 call: *we* is neither candidate, and restoring *a person* is not choosing between *the people* and *a person*.

**為 (*wéi* — to do) had become *"acts."*** 孰為此者 is *"who does this?"* — 河上公: 孰，誰也。誰為此飄風暴雨者乎？天地所為, *"孰 means who. Who does this squall and downpour? What sky and earth do."* 為's lock is *do / handle / serve as*.

**希言自然 → "Brevity in speech happens of itself," and the 故 that follows is left unrendered.** *(Shalom's line and Shalom's call, 2026-09-03/04.)* The line is an equation — 希言 **is** 自然 — and the English had been *"Speak sparingly, for **things** go of themselves,"* which supplied 物 (*wù* — things), absent from the line. **Three intermediate drafts failed and each failure is worth keeping.** *"Speech barely heard"* named **volume**, which neither commentator does: 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) means quantity — 希言者是**愛言**也, *"being sparing with words"* — and 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) means unremarkable — 無味不足聽之言, *"speech with no flavour, not enough to hear."* **A whisper is neither.** *"Saying little is so of itself, and no one makes it so"* said something but did not earn the 故 (*gù* — therefore). And *"so a squall does not last out the morning"* asserted an inference the English could not carry.

**The chapter's weather decides 希 for 河上公's reading.** 飄風 (*piāo fēng* — a squall) and 驟雨 (*zhòu yǔ* — a downpour) are **too much at once**, and he draws the moral: 言疾不能長，暴不能久也, *"the rapid cannot be long, the violent cannot endure."* **Excess against sparseness, not loud against quiet.** 王弼's audibility reading is not lost to the book — it is 希's English at ch 14 (聽之不聞名曰希 → *"the inaudible"*) and ch 41 (大音希聲 → *"the great sound can barely be heard"*) — but it is not this chapter's argument.

**The storm is the counter-case, not a parallel instance, and both commentators say so.** 王弼: 言**暴疾**美興**不長**也 — *"violent, rapid, splendid arisings do not last long."* 河上公: 言**疾不能長**，**暴不能久**也. **A squall is not an example of natural brevity; it is the violent thing failing** — which is why the chapter closes the movement with a warning, 而況於人乎, *"how much less a person?"* *(An earlier draft of this note had it backwards, calling the storm "the thesis rather than its counter-example." Corrected.)* 王弼 sets the contrast up by glossing 希言 with the Tao's own speech, quoting 道之出言，淡兮其無味也。視之不足見，聽之不足聞 (*"the Tao's issuing forth in words is bland, without flavour; look, and there is not enough to see; listen, and there is not enough to hear"* — ch 35's line, which he calls 下章). **The self-so mode of speech is bland and barely there; a squall is its opposite, and it stops before noon.**

**故 is printed and not rendered, and the warrant is textual rather than stylistic.** The Siku 王弼 — our base — is the **only** witness that has it, and it says so itself: 〔案**河上公注本及各本俱無故字**〕, *"the Heshang Gong commentary edition and all editions lack the character 故."* Our vendored 河上公 confirms it; his lemma opens 飄風不終朝. **We print the base text and let the three statements stand in juxtaposition, as every other witness has them.** 說文解字 makes 故 unambiguously causal — **使爲之也。从攴古聲**, *"to cause something to be done,"* a hand holding a stick (攴 *pū*) over 古 (*gǔ* — old) — so it cannot be softened into a comparison. ***Likewise* was proposed and declined on exactly that**: it would give the book's causal particle, **63 lines across 42 chapters**, a comparative English in one place, and it would make the squall a parallel instance where both commentators make it the counter-case. **The second 故 in this chapter, at 故從事於道者, is rendered** — *So one whose affairs follow the Tao* — because there the inference is the chapter's own conclusion and the English carries it.

**自然 keeps the locked wording.** ch 17 (*by ourselves*) and ch 25 (*being what it is*) already depart from it, so **two of five occurrences do not show the phrase**; *on its own* would have made a sixth and produced exactly the invisibility `glossary/ziran-自然.md` exists to prevent. *Happens of itself* keeps the term visible and is its plain sense: 自 (*zì* — a nose, hence self) plus 然 (*rán* — so). ***"No one's doing"* was an earlier candidate and the reverse check killed it** — *doing* is 無為 (*wú wéi* — non-doing)'s declared rendering, backed by 無為 in ten lines, and there is no 無為 in ch 23.

**The glossary entry had argued for the old line, and it was half right.** `glossary/ziran-自然.md`'s register defended *"for"* on the ground that 自然 is **the ground, not the consequence** — 河上公's 愛言者自然之道. **That reasoning stands and is kept.** What it could not do was supply a subject without inventing 物, and the entry's own verdict on the line — *"English has no predicate slot that fits it; a strain case"* — was right. Per `CLAUDE.md`, when a decision and a file disagree, fix both and say which was wrong: **the diagnosis was right, the rendering was not.** Entry updated.

**得 (*dé* — to get) → *gets*, not *receives*.** 說文: **行有所得也**, *"walking and getting something,"* from 彳 (*chì* — a step) — active acquisition, not passive reception. And the plain word is what makes the third line land: **loss too gladly gets them.**

**Three textual facts, none of them previously logged.** 王弼's own lemma carries a 道者 our base text lacks; 河上公's third line reads 失亦樂**失**之 against our 失亦樂**得**之; and the Siku 王弼 reports a Ming witness without 樂 (*lè* — glad) in all three lines. See `notes/manuscript.md`.

**Contractions removed as incidental, not as a decision.** *doesn't* and *can't* became *does not* and *cannot* when the lines were rebuilt around them. Twelve chapters still carry contractions and none of them is touched here.

**信不足焉，有不信焉 → "Where trust runs short, there is no trust," matching ch 17.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14. Was: "Where trust is withheld, trust is withheld in return," and ch 17 had a different line again.)* **The waiver that stood here is gone with it.** It argued that ch 17 is a chapter about rulers while this one is about 同 (*tóng* — merging), so the two contexts wanted two Englishes. **The commentators cross that split in both directions**, which is what undid it: 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the line at **ch 17** as impersonal natural law — 信不足焉，則有不信，**此自然之道也** (*"where trust is insufficient, there is untrust; this is the way of things being so of themselves"*) — and 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplies a **ruler** here at ch 23: 君信不足於下，下則應君以不足也 (*"the ruler's trustworthiness is insufficient toward those below, and those below answer the ruler with insufficiency"*). Each frame appears in the chapter that was said to exclude it.

**河上公 also settles what the line is doing in this chapter, and it is not an appendix.** 此言物相歸，**同聲相應**，雲從龍，風從虎，水流濕，火就燥，自然之道也 — *"this says that things return to their kind, that **like sounds answer each other**: clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger, water flows to the damp, fire goes to the dry — this is the way of being so of itself."* That is the 易經 (*Yìjīng* — Book of Changes) formula for resonance, and it makes the 信 line **the fourth term of this chapter's 同 series** — 同於道者，道亦樂得之 (*"those who merge with the Tao, the Tao gladly receives them"*), and so on through 德 (*dé* — integrity) and 失 (*shī* — loss). Like joins like; trust is the fourth thing that does it.

***"In return" had taken a side.*** 王弼's shape is **emergence, not reciprocity** — his analogy is 御體失性則疾病生 (*"govern the body and lose its nature, and sickness arises"*), where nothing is given back and the deficiency simply produces its own consequence. The English is now agent-free, so both readings stand behind it.

**Bare 德 → "integrity," not "profound integrity."** *(2026-08-31, `WORKLIST.md` T1-5, closed with Pass C.)* Three lines here gave 德 (*dé*) the English that belongs to **玄德** (*xuán dé* — profound integrity), which stands at ch 10, ch 51 and ch 65 and **contains a 玄 this chapter does not have**. 德 is locked to *integrity*; `--english "profound integrity"` now returns only 玄德's four lines.

**It mattered structurally, not just lexically.** The stanza is a **three-term parallel** — 道者同於道；德者同於德；失者同於失 (*"the Tao-person merges with the Tao; the integrity-person merges with integrity; the loss-person merges with loss"*) — and giving the middle term an adjective the other two lack broke the symmetry the chapter is built on. It is the same fault this chapter had once before, when 信 (*xìn* — trust) was given 德's word.

**希 (*xī*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 聽之不聞，名曰希, which our English gives as *"its name is the inaudible."* The graph is 爻 (*yáo* — crossed threads) over 巾 (*jīn* — cloth): **loose-woven fabric you can see through**, which is why rarity and inaudibility are one property in Chinese and two words in English. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried in the notes — *the inaudible* there and this chapter's sparseness of speech are one character. Also ch 41 (大音希聲), 43, 70 and 74.

*End of chapter 23.*

## Chapter 24

*Heshang Gong's title: 苦恩, "Favour turned bitter".*

Those who stand on tiptoe do not stand.
Those who take long strides get nowhere.

Those who show themselves off do not see clearly.
Those who insist they are right convince no one.
Those who claim the work have none.
Those who boast do not endure.

Measured by the Tao, these are called leftover food and wasted motion.
Living things recoil from them.
Those who are with the Tao do not dwell among them.

The Chinese:

企者不立；
跨者不行；
自見者不明；
自是者不彰；
自伐者無功；
自矜者不長。
其在道也，
曰餘食贅行，
物或惡之，
故有道者不處。

### Notes on chapter 24

**自矜者不長 → "Those who boast do not endure."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "Those who make themselves great.")* The mirror of ch 22, changed with it; see that chapter's note.

*Rewritten 2026-08-28. Ch 24 is the exact negative of ch 22's 不自X (*bù zì X* — "does not X themselves") stanza, which was rebuilt 2026-08-27; the two had shared no English at all.*

**The mirror is in the four verbs, not in matching predicates.** 見 (*jiàn* — to display) · 是 (*shì* — to affirm as right) · 伐 (*fá* — to claim) · 矜 (*jīn* — to magnify oneself). Ch 22 has 不自X，故Y (*"does not X themselves, therefore Y"*); ch 24 has 自X者不Y (*"one who X's themselves does not Y"*). **The stanza's logic is: grasp at a thing and lose it.**

**The subjects genuinely differ between the two chapters, and an earlier draft of this repair forced them together with a colon.** In ch 22 what becomes evident is *their rightness* — 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) supplies it: 不自是則其**是**彰也 (*bù zì shì zé qí shì zhāng yě* — "not affirming themselves, then their rightness is made evident"). In ch 24 what fails to appear is **the person**: 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 衆共蔽之，使不得彰明 (*zhòng gòng bì zhī, shǐ bù dé zhāng míng* — "the crowd together obscures them, so they cannot be made evident"). Hence *"convince no one"* rather than a possessive.

***"Go unseen" was tried and rejected, because in this book it is praise.*** Ch 17's best rulers are barely known, ch 41 has 道隱無名 (*dào yǐn wú míng* — "the Tao is hidden and nameless"), ch 70's sage wears coarse cloth over jade. What this person grasps at is recognition, so the loss must read as failure. *(Caught by Shalom.)*

**跨 (*kuà*) is an overstretched step, not a stride.** 足 (*zú* — foot) beside 夸 (*kuā* — to boast): a step so long it straddles. *"Those who stride do not walk"* left a near-synonym of *walk* and the paradox evaporated. 河上公 supplies the fix by glossing 不行 (*bù xíng*) as 使不得行 (*shǐ bù dé xíng* — "so they cannot get anywhere"). 王弼 states the principle for both opening lines: 物尚進則失安 (*wù shàng jìn zé shī ān* — "a thing that presses forward loses its footing").

**餘食贅行 → "leftover food and wasted motion," and the commentators diverge here.** 贅 (*zhuì*) is 敖 over 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell); 說文 glosses it 以物質錢也 (*yǐ wù zhì qián yě* — "to pawn a thing for money"), hence **superfluous, an appendage**. 王弼 reads it physically — 肬贅 (*yóu zhuì* — a wart) — and 餘食 as 盛饌之餘也，本雖美，更可薉也 (*shèng zhuàn zhī yú yě, běn suī měi, gèng kě huì yě* — "the leftovers of a rich feast: fine to begin with, they turn foul"). 河上公 reads it morally: 贅，貪也 (*zhuì, tān yě* — "贅 means greed"). **Both are glosses, not the text**, and neither word is rendered here: *wasted motion* keeps 贅's plain sense and ties the summary back to the chapter's own opening, since tiptoe and overstretched steps *are* superfluous motion. 河上公's moral reading is declined on the naturalistic razor.

**物 → "living things," and 或 is dropped.** 物 (*wù*) cannot be inert here — 河上公: 物無有不**畏**惡也 (*wù wú yǒu bù wèi wù yě* — "there is nothing that does not **fear** and detest them"), and rocks do not fear. *The material world* was an import and ch 31's *all creatures* narrowed too far. 惡 read *wù* is aversion, not hatred, so **recoil**. 或 (*huò* — "perhaps, some") is a hedge we drop deliberately, on 河上公's near-universal reading.

**The last two lines are verbatim in ch 31 and were swept to match**, closing two `repeated-formula` warnings. 有道者 (*yǒu dào zhě* — "one who has the Tao") already read *"one who holds the Tao"* at ch 77.

**有道者 → "those who are with the Tao," and neither *have* nor *hold* survived.** 有 (*yǒu*) is 又 (*yòu* — a hand) over 肉 (*ròu* — flesh), a hand holding meat — but its force in 有道 is **existential, not possessive**: ch 46's 天下有道 (*tiān xià yǒu dào*) is *"there is Tao in the world,"* not *"the world owns the Tao."* Two things ruled out the obvious renderings. **The book refuses 有 as a way of relating** — 生而不有 (*shēng ér bù yǒu* — "bears and does not possess") stands in ch 2, 10 and 51 — so *have the Tao* sits one syllable from a contradiction. And **hold** was already doing duty for 守 (*shǒu* — hold fast to), 執 (*zhí* — grasp) and 保 (*bǎo* — keep) in four other chapters, including ch 15's 保此道者, which read *"one who holds the Tao"* for a different character. *With* claims nothing, and it survives ch 23's mutuality: 同於道者，道亦樂得之 (*tóng yú dào zhě, dào yì lè dé zhī* — "those who merge with the Tao, the Tao gladly receives them"). Swept to ch 31 and ch 77.

***"Dwell in the Tao" was proposed and refused on the hymn test*** — it is Psalm 23 and John 15 cadence — **and on placement**: 處 (*chǔ*) is the dwelling word and it belongs to the second clause, so moving *dwell* to 有's slot would spend the right word in the wrong place. *"Where there is Tao, these have no place"* was the strongest alternative and was declined because it drops 者 (*zhě* — "the one who"), and the chapter has spent eight lines contrasting two kinds of **person**. 河上公 keeps the person: 言有道之人不居其國也.

**故 (*gù* — therefore) is deliberately not rendered.** English carries the inference by adjacency, and the three closing lines read better as three flat verdicts than as a chain. The omission also travels: in ch 24 this is the final line, where *so* sums up what needs no summing; in ch 31 the same sentence sits third, where *so* would mark an inference the reader has not yet been given.

*End of chapter 24.*

## Chapter 25

*Heshang Gong's title: 象元, "Figuring the origin".*

Something mixed and complete, born before sky and earth.
Silent. Empty. Solitary. Unchanging.
It moves in a circle, never in danger,
and can be taken as the mother of the world.

I do not know its name.
Forcing a label on it, I call it the Tao.
Forcing a name on it, I call it great.

Great means departing,
departing means going far,
going far means returning.

Therefore, the Tao is great, the sky is great, the earth is great, and humans are also great.
Within all bounds there are four great things, and one of them is human.

Humans model themselves on the earth,
Earth models itself on the sky,
The sky models itself on the Tao,
The Tao models itself on being what it is.

The Chinese:

有物混成，
先天地生。
寂兮寥兮，
獨立而不改，
周行而不殆，
可以為天下母。
吾不知其名，
強字之曰道，
強為之名曰大。
大曰逝，
逝曰遠，
遠曰反。
故道大，天大，地大，王亦大。
域中有四大，
而王居其一焉。
人法地，
地法天，
天法道，
道法自然。

### Notes on chapter 25

**On 人 in the four greats — an editorial call, not a manuscript one.** Our base text reads 王 (*wáng* — king) and we render **human**. Every excavated witness reads 王, Guodian (~300 BCE) included; the human reading is transmitted, from 傅奕 (Tang) and 范應元 (Song), and rests on the seam in the received text itself — the next line is 人法地, *humans follow earth*. Corrected 2026-08-20 from an earlier note that had the manuscript evidence backwards. Apparatus: `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 25.

**周行而不殆 → "It moves in a circle, never in danger" — a dropped clause restored and a borrowed word returned.** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "Inexhaustible, it can be considered the mother of the world.")* Two faults in one line. **周行 (*zhōu xíng* — "moves in a circle") was not translated at all**, a debt `WORKLIST` already carried. And 不殆 was given *inexhaustible*, which belongs to 窮 (*qióng*) at ch 6 and ch 35.

**殆 (*dài*) is peril, not exhaustion.** 說文解字: 危也. The graph is 歺 (*è*), the bare-bone radical — the death element in 死 (*sǐ* — to die) and 殃 (*yāng* — calamity). 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the line 周行無所不至而**免殆** — *"it circulates and reaches everywhere, yet **escapes peril**"* — with the Siku compilers' collation note 〔案免永樂大典作危〕, *"for 免, the Yongle Dadian reads 危."* **Peril under either reading; exhaustion under neither.**

**The circle matters to the chapter.** 周行 is the motion the next movement names — 大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反 (*"Great means departing, departing means going far, going far means returning"*) — so dropping it left the return with nothing to return along.

**大 (*dà*) → "great," replacing *"vast"* on all four lines.** *(2026-09-06, Shalom's call.)* 大 occurs **seven times in this chapter** — it is the chapter's own name for the Tao — and ch 25 was the only place in the book rendering it *vast*. Everywhere else 大 is **great**, across 41 lines. **The decisive comparison is ch 34, which makes the identical move:** 可名為大 reads *"it can be called great"* while ch 25's 強為之名曰大 read *"I call it the vast"* — the same claim, twice, invisible to a reader. It failed in the other direction too: *vast* was also carrying 廣 (*guǎng* — broad) at ch 41 and 恢 (*huī* — vast) at ch 73, so one English wore three characters while 大 answered to two. Ch 25's *vast* also predates every Pass D decision, all of which landed on *great* — 大象 → *the great image* (35), 大制 → *the great carving* (28), 大丈夫 → *the great person* (38).

**⚠ The sweep is incomplete, deliberately. Ch 67 still reads 大 as *vast* twice**, and swapping it there would expose rather than fix a fault: 天下皆謂我**道**大 (*"everyone says my **Tao** is great"*) is rendered *"Everyone says **I** am vast"* — **道 dropped, and the line handed to the speaker.** *"Everyone says I am great"* would read as boasting the Chinese does not contain. That is a line rewrite, not a term swap. `WORKLIST.md` T2-42.

**混 (*hùn*) → "mixed," settled across ch 14, 15 and 25.** *(2026-09-06.)* Three chapters had three Englishes — *"they **blend** into one"* (14), *"**Blended**, like muddy water"* (15), *"formed in the **undifferentiated**"* (25). 說文: 豐流也。从**水**昆聲 — *"**abundant flow**. From 水 (*shuǐ* — water)."* **混 is a water word**, and the mixing sense comes from a full river carrying everything along, which is what muddy water is. 王弼 here: 混然不可得而知而萬物由之以成 — *"混-ly, it cannot be known, yet the countless things come to completion through it."* This line's 有物混成 is now *"Something mixed and complete"* — undifferentiated and already whole, which is the paradox 混成 states. **Not yet a glossary entry** (`WORKLIST.md` T2-40), so the rendering is settled but unenforced.

**A rider the reverse search exposed: *blend* was also 沖's word.** Ch 42's 沖氣以為和 reads *"**blending** the vital breath into harmony,"* where 沖 (*chōng*) is the character ch 4's Pass D work settled as **empty** — 道沖, *"The Tao is empty."* Freeing *blend* from 混 does not fix ch 42; it isolates it. `WORKLIST.md` T2-41.

**大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反 → three lines, and 逝 → "departing."** *(2026-09-06. Was: "The vast means expanding, expanding means going far, going far means returning" — one line.)*

**逝 is not size, and all three sources say so.** 說文: **往也**, *"to go."* 王弼: **逝行也**…不守一大體而已，周行無所不至，故曰逝也 — *"逝 is 行 (*xíng* — to go)… it does not hold to one great body only; it circulates and reaches everywhere."* 河上公 supplies what the word is doing here: 非若天常在上，非若地常在下，乃復**逝去无常處所**也 — *"not like the sky always above, nor the earth always below; it **goes away and has no constant dwelling place**."* ***Expanding* is growth in place, which is the one thing the line denies.**

**Why *departing* over the plainer *going* (Shalom's call).** The three steps are a journey with three legs — departure, distance, return — and *departing* names its leg where *going* leaves it unspecified, which is exactly 河上公's 无常處所. An earlier objection that English *departed* suggests death was **weak and is withdrawn**: as a gerund inside a travel sequence it carries no such reading, and 逝's own commentary is about ranging, not ending.

**反 → "returning," to match ch 40.** 遠曰反 is the same claim as 反者道之動 (*"Returning is the Tao's movement"*), the book's most famous statement of this idea, and *turning back* would hide the link. 說文 反: 覆也 — *to overturn*, on 又 (*yòu* — a hand). **⚠ *Return* is overloaded book-wide** — it currently carries 反 (25, 40, 65), 復 (16, 28, 52, 59) and 歸 (14, 34), which 說文 keeps distinct: 復 is 往來也, *"going and coming"*, on the step radical 彳; 歸 is 女嫁也, *"a woman marrying in"* — going where one belongs. Three motions, one English. `WORKLIST.md` T2-44.

**遠 → "going far," not bare "far."** *(Shalom's call.)* Bare *far* left the middle step without a verb — *"departing means far"* strands it, the same fault the no-em-dash rule exists to prevent — and it broke the parallel with the gerunds on either side. **The cost, stated:** both commentators gloss 遠 as **extent** rather than travel. 王弼: **遠極也**，周無所不窮極，不偏於一逝 — *"遠 is 極 (*jí* — the utmost); it circles with nothing it does not reach to the utmost, not partial to any one departing."* 河上公: 言遠者**窮乎無窮**，布氣天地無所不通也 — *"far means exhausting the inexhaustible, spreading breath through sky and earth with nothing it does not get through."* *Going far* tilts a reach word slightly toward motion. It is defensible against the chapter's own frame — 周行 (*zhōu xíng* — "moves in a circle") makes the whole sequence a circuit, and 遠 is its far leg — but the tilt is real and is recorded here rather than smoothed over.

**The three lines are three lines in the Chinese, and the chain is anadiplosis** — each opens on the word the last one closed with, 大 → 逝 → 遠 → 反. Run onto one English line, the steps were invisible. This is the circuit 周行 promised nine lines earlier, so the return now has something to return along.

**The naming block rebuilt.** *(2026-09-06. Was: "Its true name, I will never know. Forcing a label upon it, I call it the Tao. / Forcing a description for it, I call it great." — two English lines for three Chinese ones.)*

**說文 explains why a name is the wrong instrument here.** 名: 自命也。从**口**从**夕**。夕者，冥也。**冥不相見，故以口自名** — *"to name oneself. From 口 (*kǒu* — mouth) and 夕 (*xī* — dusk); 夕 means 冥 (*míng* — dark). **In the dark you cannot see one another, so you use the mouth to name yourself.**"* **A name is what you reach for when sight fails.** 王弼 states the chapter's problem in four characters — **名以定形**, *"a name fixes a form"* — and draws the conclusion: 混成無形，不可得而定，故曰不知其名也, *"the mixed-and-complete has no form, cannot be fixed, therefore 'I do not know its name.'"*

**So 吾不知其名 is not a confession of ignorance.** *"Its **true** name, I will **never** know"* invented a true name existing somewhere out of reach, and turned a claim about formlessness into one about the speaker's limits. Both the *true* and the *never* are gone: 不知 is **do not know**.

**名 (*míng*) occurs twice in three lines and had two Englishes** — *"true name"* then *"description."* It is **name** in every other chapter, including ch 1's 名可名，非常名, and runs 21 lines across 9 chapters.

**字 (*zì*) → "label," and 王弼 distinguishes it from 名 outright:** 夫**名以定形，字以稱可言** — *"a 名 fixes a form; a 字 designates what can be spoken."* He then applies it: 吾所以**字**之曰道者，取其可言之稱**最大**也 — *"the reason I 字 it 'Tao' is that I take the greatest of speakable designations"* — and warns that forcing a 名 costs more: 大有繫則必有分，有分則失其極矣, *"大, being tied, must have divisions; having divisions, it loses its utmost."* **字 occurs once in the whole book**, so nothing constrains the choice. *Word* and *speak* were both unavailable — 言 (*yán*) holds those across 11 lines — and *designation*, which is 王弼's own 稱 and exact, is bureaucratic. **Label is plain, free, and deflationary, which is the argument**: *Tao* is only the largest thing that can be said, not the thing. 說文 on 字 is 乳也, *"to nurse"* — 子 (*zǐ* — a child) under 宀 (*mián* — a roof); the designation sense is later and is not read into the line.

**曰 (*yuē*) is "call" in both lines, as it is twice in the Chinese.**

**Left open, deliberately: 強為之▢ is a frame shared with ch 15**, whose 強為之容 reads *"I force a likeness."* Here 強為之名 reads *"Forcing a name on it."* Same frame, two English shapes — raised rather than matched, since ch 15's line closes a movement and this one does not.

**故道大，天大，地大，人亦大 is written almost entirely in one figure.** *(2026-09-08, raised by Shalom.)* 說文 defines 大 as 象**人形**, *the human form* — a person seen head-on, arms and legs spread — and it is a **radical** whose family is made by marking that same body: **天** is a line **above the head** (顛也。从一大, *"the crown of the head"*), **亦** is marks at **both sides** (人之臂亦也, *"a person's armpits,"* borrowed for *also*), **立** is a line **beneath the feet**, and **夫** a line **through the topknot** — a hairpin, the 夫 inside ch 38's 大丈夫.

**So this line holds three members of the family — 天, 大, 亦 — and 說文's entry for 大 quotes the line itself.** 人亦大 is close to tautological in the graphs: 大 *is* a picture of a person and 亦 *is* that person's armpits. **A person is also what the picture of a person means.** The tautology is the argument — **scale here is measured outward from a body, not downward from a heaven**, which is why 天 is locked to *sky* and 大 to the ordinary *great*. Full family in `glossary/da-大.md`; reader-facing in `notes/reading.md` · *Thread · the standing figure*.

**⚠ Two limits, since 說文 rationalises elsewhere.** 大 is **not** 人 with a stroke added, though it looks like it — 說文 makes them independent pictographs of the same subject, 人 in profile (象臂脛之形, *arms and shins*) and 大 head-on. And whether Laozi's readers saw any of this is unknowable; that the characters are built this way is not.

*End of chapter 25.*

## Chapter 26

*Heshang Gong's title: 重德, "The weight of integrity".*

The heavy is the root of the light.
Stillness is the ruler of the agitated.

Therefore, the noble travels all day without leaving the baggage wagons.
Even where the sights are glorious, they dwell at ease and stay apart.

How can the lord of ten thousand chariots
make their own body light in the world?
Lightness loses the root.
Agitation loses the ruler.

The Chinese:

重為輕根，
靜為躁君。
是以君子終日行不離輜重。
雖有榮觀，
燕處超然。
奈何萬乘之主，
而以身輕天下？
輕則失本，
躁則失君。

### Notes on chapter 26
