**君子 (*jūn zǐ*) → "the noble," swept with ch 31 on 2026-09-07.** *(Was "the sage.")* **聖人 (*shèng rén*) is the sage** and carried 38 English lines; 君子 is literally *a ruler's child*, the **Confucian** honorific, and giving it 聖人's word made Laozi's figure and Confucius's the same person. Full argument in ch 31's notes. **Note the seam:** 君子 named a male class and *the noble* is deliberately neutral. **君 (*jūn*) now reads *ruler* in both places** *(closed 2026-09-20, T2-6)* — it had been *ruler* at 靜為躁君 and *mastery* at 躁則失君, three lines apart in a chapter whose last two lines are a matched pair.

**The whole chapter reworked, 2026-09-20** *(T2-1 · T2-5 · T2-6)*.

**輕 (*qīng* — light) had three Englishes and the chapter turns on it.** 重 (*zhòng* — heavy) against 輕 is the first line's pair and the last two lines' verdict, and *ungrounded* had replaced *light* at all three, hiding the pair. **輜重 (*zī zhòng* — the heavy baggage train) had become *sustenance***, losing the 重 that line 1 depends on; 王弼 reads it plainly, 以重為本故不離, *"takes the heavy as root, therefore does not leave it."*

**靜 (*jìng*) → *stillness*, closing T2-5.** It read *Silence* here alone against seven lines elsewhere (16 ×2, 45 ×2, 57, 61 ×2).

**奈何萬乘之主，而以身輕天下 had lost three of its parts.** 萬乘 (*wàn shèng* — ten thousand chariots) went to *a great ruler*; 身 became *their being*; and **天下 (*tiān xià* — the world) was deleted outright.** That line is one of only three in the book where 身 and 天下 stand together — with ch 13's 以身為天下 twice and ch 54's ladder — and `chapters/013.md` cites this line as the support for its own closing couplet. 河上公: 王者至尊，而以其身行輕躁乎. See `glossary/shen-身.md`.

**燕處超然 → *they dwell at ease and stay apart*.** *Their equanimity is undisturbed* rendered no character; 燕處 is dwelling at ease and 超然 is standing clear.

*End of chapter 26.*

## Chapter 27

*Heshang Gong's title: 巧用, "Deft use".*

Masterful traveling leaves no tracks.
Masterful speaking is flawless.
Masterful calculating uses no counting rods.
Masterful security uses no locks, yet cannot be breached.
Masterful tying uses no ropes, yet cannot be untied.

Therefore the sage is always masterful at rescuing people, and so no one is abandoned.
Always masterful at rescuing things, and so nothing is abandoned.
This is called clarity worn covered.

Therefore, the masterful one naturally teaches the novice.
And the novice is the raw material of the master.

Not valuing the master and not loving their raw material is a sign of great confusion.
Even those who appear intelligent are lost. This is the essential secret.

The Chinese:

善行無轍跡，
善言無瑕謫，
善計不用籌策，
善閉無關楗而不可開，
善結無繩約而不可解。
是以聖人常善救人，
故無棄人；
常善救物，
故無棄物。
是謂襲明。
故善人者，
不善人之師；
不善人者，
善人之資。
不貴其師，
不愛其資，
雖智大迷，
是謂要妙。

### Notes on chapter 27

**籌策 → "counting rods."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "abacus.")* 籌策 (*chóu cè*) are counting rods and tally sticks, bamboo laid out to reckon. The abacus is attested centuries after the text.

**是謂襲明 → "This is called clarity worn covered."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-10.)* *(was: "This is called inherited clarity.")* **襲 (*xí*) is grave-clothes.** 說文解字: **左衽袍** — *"a robe with the lapel closed to the left."* The living close a robe right over left; the dead are dressed left over right. The graph is 衣 (*yī* — clothing) with 龖 abbreviated for sound, and every later sense — *to double, to succeed to, to fall upon* — descends from **one garment put on over another**. Inheritance is a derived sense (you "put on" what was worn before), and taking it as the primary one lost the layering.

**The chapter is built on marks not left.** It opens 善行無轍跡 (*shàn xíng wú zhé jì* — "masterful traveling leaves no tracks") and runs five masteries that leave nothing behind, then closes here. **The summary line says the clarity is under something** — the same gesture as 被褐懷玉 (*bèi hè huái yù* — "wears coarse cloth, carries jade at the breast," ch 70) and 光而不耀 (*guāng ér bù yào* — "bright but not dazzling," ch 58).

**Paired with ch 52's 是謂襲常, and the pair is why we keep 襲 there.** 明 (*míng* — clear-seeing) and 常 (*cháng* — the ever-present) are bonded by 知常曰明 (*"knowing the ever-present is called clarity"*), verbatim at ch 16 and ch 55; 是謂襲X is one gesture applied to both halves. See `notes/manuscript.md` — ch 52's text is contested and its English had been following the other character.

*End of chapter 27.*

## Chapter 28

*Heshang Gong's title: 反朴, "Back to uncarved wood".*

Know the rooster, hold to the hen,
serve as the world's ravine.
Serve as the world's ravine, and the ever-present integrity never leaves you.
Return again to the infant.

Know the white, hold to the black,
serve as the world's pattern.
Serve as the world's pattern, and the ever-present integrity never varies.
Return again to the endless.

Know the glory, hold to the disgrace,
serve as the world's valley.
Serve as the world's valley, and the ever-present integrity is enough at last.
Return again to the uncarved wood.

The uncarved wood scatters, and becomes vessels.
The sage puts them to use and becomes chief of the officers.
So the great carving severs nothing.

The Chinese:

知其雄，守其雌，
為天下谿。
為天下谿，常德不離，
復歸於嬰兒。
知其白，守其黑，
為天下式。
為天下式，常德不忒，
復歸於無極。
知其榮，守其辱，
為天下谷。
為天下谷，常德乃足，
復歸於樸。
樸散則為器，
聖人用之，則為官長，
故大制不割。

### Notes on chapter 28

**The chapter is a chain of things you could point at, and the English had been a chain of concepts.** *(2026-09-01, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T1-7, T1-15, T1-16, T3-5, and the last of T2-15.)* 說文解字 makes almost every term here a physical object — a bird's father and a bird's mother, a mountain watercourse with no outlet, a spring that runs through to a river, a carpenter's square, a roof's ridgepole, vessels, a knife — and the old English read *assertive energy · yielding energy · deep ravine · **reservoir** · pattern · the limitless · **master orchestrator** · **the great orchestrator***. **The pointing test failed on nearly every line**, and the replacements sat in one register: the mechanistic, with the modern spiritual idiom beside it. ***"Energy" renders no character at all*** — 氣 (*qì* — vital breath) is not in this chapter.

**雄 and 雌 are a rooster and a hen, and the reason is not the graph alone — it is that 牝/牡 have already taken *male* and *female*.** 說文 defines the two pairs in exactly parallel words in two different animal classes: 雄 **鳥父**也 / 雌 **鳥母**也, from 隹 (*zhuī* — a short-tailed bird); 牡 **畜父**也 / 牝 **畜母**也, from 牛 (*niú* — cattle). Our English gives 牝/牡 *the female* and *the male* at ch 6 (是謂玄牝), 55 and 61, so 雌/雄 must have their own words, and the graph says which. **In English ornithology *cock* and *hen* are precisely this pair** — the male and female of any species, as in *a cock pheasant* — and *cock* is unusable in modern English. **The cost: *rooster* is more specific than 雄, which is any male bird.** The pairing is what carries the sense.

**Both commentators read the pair as *position*, not species** — a reading for this note, not a rendering. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 雄先之屬，雌後之屬也。知為天下之先也，必後也。是以聖人後其身而身先也 — *"雄 belongs to the class of going first, 雌 to the class of coming after. To know how to be first in the world, one must be behind. This is why the sage puts their person behind, and their person comes first."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 雄以喻尊，雌以喻卑 — *"雄 figures the honoured, 雌 the lowly"* — 就雌之柔和，如是則天下歸之，如水流入深谿也, *"come to the hen's softness, and the world returns to you as water flows into a deep ravine."*

**谷 → "valley," and *reservoir* was backwards.** 說文: 谷 is 泉出**通川**為谷 — *"where a spring comes out and **runs through to a river***" — while 谿 is 山瀆**無所通**者, *"a mountain watercourse with **no outlet**."* **The two are distinguished on whether the water gets out**, and a *reservoir* is a man-made tank that holds it in. **谷 is already *valley* in six other chapters** — 6, 15, 32, 39 ×2, 41 — so ch 28 alone was the outlier. 谿 keeps **ravine**; English cannot carry 說文's outlet distinction, and that is what this note is for.

**The template is the chapter, and ours broke it at every joint.** Three stanzas of 知其X，守其Y / 為天下Z / 為天下Z，常德不W / 復歸於V, with only the variables moving. Ours gave **守 three Englishes and then a fourth** (*"attune to"* ×3, then *"we must welcome"*), **復歸於 three shapes** (*"Become like an infant again" · "Return to the limitless" · "Return to the uncarved wood"*), invented ***we must***, and **dropped 常 — a locked term — from all three 常德**. The template now runs unbroken, which is T3-5.

**為天下X → "serve as the world's X," which is 為's own locked English** (*do / handle / serve as*), and it closes the last of T2-15's formula pairs: **ch 22 read *"sets a pattern for the world"*** for the identical 為天下式 and now reads *"serves as the world's pattern."* *Embody* rendered nothing.

**守 → "hold to,"** matching ch 32 (侯王若能守之) and ch 37, and **not pre-empting T2-19**, the holding family. 說文: **守官也。从宀从寸** — *"to hold an office; from 宀 (a roof) and 寸 (a rule of measure)"* — **keeping a charge you are answerable for.** *"Attune to"* inverted the grammar as well as the register: you attune yourself **to** something; you 守 something **as a duty**.

**白/黑 → "the white" and "the black," not *light* and *darkness*.** 光 (*guāng*) already holds **light** at ch 4, 52 and 56, and 明 (*míng*) is locked to **clarity**. 河上公 keeps the pair visual: 白以喻昭昭，黑以喻默默 — *"white figures the bright-bright, black the silent-silent"* — 當復守之以默默，如闇昧無所見, *"one should hold to the silent, as if dim and seeing nothing."*

**常德's three predicates, one at a time.** **不離** → *never leaves you*; 離's own graph is an oriole (說文: 黃倉庚也，鳴則蠶生, *"the oriole; when it sings the silkworms hatch"*) and the parting sense is a loan. **The *you* is supplied because English 離 needs an object, and 河上公 supplies exactly that**: 德常在，不復離於己. **不忒** → *never varies*; 說文 忒，更也 (*"to change"*), 王弼 忒，差也 (*"to err"*) — *varies* takes the graph and leaves the verdict out. **乃足** → *is enough at last*, where **乃 is the *only then*** that marks the triad closing; 足 is 知足's own word. *(河上公 reads 足 as 止: 足，止也。人能為天下谷，德乃止於己 — "integrity then comes to rest in them." A second reading, noted rather than merged.)*

**無極 → "the endless," not "the limitless."** *Limitless* is currently wearing 淵 (*yuān* — a deep pool) at ch 8, and both commentators gloss 無極 by **exhaustion**, not by extent: 王弼 不可窮也 (*"it cannot be exhausted"*), 河上公 歸身於無窮極也 (*"return the body to what has no exhausting limit"*). 說文 on 極 is worth keeping even though no English can carry it: **棟也**, *"the ridgepole of a roof"* — 無極 is a roof with no topmost beam.

**器 → "vessels," which is its lock** (*vessel / tool / implement*) and its English at ch 11, 29, 41 and 67; *"various tools"* invented *various*. **散 → "scatters,"** matching ch 64's 易散, and not *"is carved"* — the carving is 割's job three characters later. 王弼: 樸真也。真散則百行出，殊類生，若器也 — *"樸 is the genuine; when the genuine scatters the hundred conducts come out and different kinds are born, like vessels."*

**則為官長 follows 河上公 on the grammar, and 王弼 diverges.** 河上公: 聖人升用則為百官之元長也 — *"the sage, raised to use, **becomes** head chief of the hundred officers."* 王弼 reads 為 as *wèi*, "for them": 聖人因其分散，故**為之立**官長 — *"the sage, following their dispersion, **establishes** officers and chiefs for them."* **The line above settles it:** 樸散**則為**器 is the identical 則為 construction one line up, and if that is *becomes vessels*, this is *becomes chief*. **The grammar decides where the commentators split** — the ch 4 lesson, run the other way. 長 → *chief* also matches ch 67's 成器長.

**故大制不割 → "So the great carving severs nothing," and it is a paradox that had been erased.** **制 also carries this chapter's word at ch 32** (始制有名 — *"When the carving begins, there are names"*), and 說文 makes it a knife on timber: **裁也。从刀从未** — *"to cut out; from 刀 (a knife) and 未 (a grown tree)."* *(制 read *cutting* in both places until 2026-09-07, when it moved to **carving** so that 樸 — the **uncarved** — and the blade that ends it share one English root. Full argument in ch 32's notes.)* **割 is a different cut** — 說文 剥也, *"to flay, to strip"* — so it takes **sever**; 河上公 has 无所傷割, *"nothing wounded or cut."* The old *"the great orchestrator itself does not carve"* put **one mechanistic English on two different characters** (官長 and 大制) and lost the knife inside both. 王弼: 大制者，以天下之心為心，故無割也 — *"the great carving takes the world's heart as its own heart, and so there is no cutting."*

**The two em-dashes are gone as a side effect, not as a decision.** They stood in *"Embodying the deep ravine of the world — this is where…"* and its twin, both lines now rewritten. **T4-3 stays deferred**; ch 28 simply no longer appears on its list.

**Not attested at Guodian** (~300 BCE), and **the stanza order is an editorial restoration** — the Yongle Dadian puts the 雄/雌 stanza second. See `notes/manuscript.md`.

*End of chapter 28.*

## Chapter 29

*Heshang Gong's title: 無為, "Non-doing".*

Those who would take the world and handle it,
I see they will not succeed.
The world is a sacred vessel. It cannot be handled. It cannot be grasped.
Those who handle it ruin it. Those who grasp it lose it.

So among things, some go ahead, some follow;
some sigh, some blow;
some are strong, some are frail;
some are carried, some are toppled.

Therefore the sage lets go of excess, lets go of extravagance, lets go of grandeur.

The Chinese:

將欲取天下而為之，
吾見其不得已。
天下神器，
不可為也，不可執也。
為者敗之，執者失之。
故物或行或隨；
或歔或吹；
或強或羸；
或挫或隳。
是以聖人去甚，
去奢，去泰。

### Notes on chapter 29

**為 (*wéi*) → "handle," three times, and the last formula pair closes.** *(2026-09-07, Pass D. Was *force* in all three: 而為之, 不可為也, 為者敗之.)* `glossary/wei-為.md` locks 為 to **do / handle / serve as** — the most frequent word in the glossary, 113 lines across 48 chapters — and **no check could see the breach**, because 為's forbidden list holds only *execute* and *function as*. **為者敗之，執者失之 is verbatim at ch 29 and ch 64**, which already read *"Those who handle it ruin it. Those who grasp it lose it."* The two now match, closing `WORKLIST.md` T2-15.

**What *force* cost was the chapter's argument.** 王弼: 萬物以自然為性，故**可因而不可為**也；可通而不可執也 — *"the countless things take 自然 (self-so) as their nature, therefore they **can be gone along with but not handled**; they can be passed through but not grasped."* **因 (*yīn* — to go along with) is permitted; 為 is not.** *Force* turns that into a warning against violence and lets a gentle manager pass, which the Chinese does not. 河上公 agrees from his side: 欲以**有為**治民, *"wanting to govern the people by having-something-to-do."* **And *force* was already spoken for** — it renders 力 (*lì*) at ch 33 and ch 68, a character covered by `glossary/qiang-強.md`, and **強 stands in this chapter** at 或強或羸.

**取 (*qǔ* — to take) restored.** 將欲**取**天下而為之 had read *"Those who wish to force their will upon the world"*, which dropped the taking and doubled the forcing. The em-dash went with the rewrite, not by decision on `WORKLIST.md` T4-3.

**物 (*wù* — things) restored to block 2.** 故**物**或行或隨 opens with its subject; the English began *"Therefore, sometimes leading."* 王弼 reads the whole series through it: 凡此諸或，言**物事**逆順反覆 — *"all these 'sometimes' speak of things and affairs going against and along, reversing and returning."* That gloss is also what settles the fourth pair, below.

**或▢或▢ four times, four matching lines.** `--formulas 29` shows the frame is the block's entire structure, and the English had varied its shape.

**羸 (*léi*) → "frail."** 說文: **瘦也。从羊** — *"thin; from 羊 (*yáng* — a sheep."* A gaunt animal, not an abstraction. Pairs with 強, locked to *strong*.

**去 (*qù*) → "lets go of," three times.** 說文: **人相違也** — *"people parting from one another."* The manuscript already reads 去 as *let go of* at ch 12, 38 and 72 (去彼取此); ch 29 had one *removes* for three 去.

**甚 · 奢 · 泰 take three distinct words, because 說文 makes them three distinct things.** 甚 is 尤**安樂**也, on 甘 (*gān* — sweet) — **excessive comfort**, not abstract extremity. 奢 is **張也**, on 大 — *stretching wide*, **display**. 泰 is 滑也 — smooth, and by the Warring States **grandeur**. *"The extreme, the extravagant, the excessive"* gave three near-synonyms where the Chinese climbs a scale.

**Two forks recorded, and one is followed against our base — see `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 29.** 或挫或隳 reads 或**載**或隳 in 河上公, and we follow him: 挫 is 說文 摧也 (*to break*) beside 隳 (*to ruin*), which gives **two wrecking words where every other pair in the series is an opposition**. 載 is 乘也。从**車** — *to carry*, on the cart radical — so *carried* against *toppled* restores it, and 王弼's own 逆順反覆 gloss demands one. **Both witnesses here are transmitted, not excavated** — Guodian does not carry this chapter — so this is an editorial call on internal grounds and is logged as such. 或歔或吹 keeps the base: 河上公 reads 呴 and glosses the pair 呴溫也，吹寒也 (*warm against cold*), where our 歔 is 說文 欷也…一曰出气也, *to sob; to let out breath*. **"Some sigh, some blow"** takes the base; the temperature reading is recorded, not adopted. *(The old *"breathing heavily / breathing easily"* also had the effort backwards — 吹 is the forceful one.)*

*End of chapter 29.*

## Chapter 30

*Heshang Gong's title: 儉武, "Sparing with arms".*

One who supports a ruler with the Tao does not use military force to dominate the world.
Such undertakings tend to come back on you.
Where armies camp, thorns and brambles grow.
After a big military campaign, a year of disaster follows.

The masterful one halts after succeeding and never pushes on to seize dominance.
They succeed without boasting, succeed without bragging, succeed without arrogance.
They succeed because their actions are unavoidable. They succeed without using excessive force.

When things reach their prime, they decay.
This is called not-Tao. Not-Tao comes to an early end.

The Chinese:

以道佐人主者，
不以兵強天下。
其事好還。
師之所處，荊棘生焉。
大軍之後，必有凶年。
善有果而已，
不敢以取強。
果而勿矜，
果而勿伐，
果而勿驕。
果而不得已，
果而勿強。
物壯則老，
是謂不道，
不道早已。

### Notes on chapter 30

**以道佐人主者 → "One who supports a ruler with the Tao."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "One who rules in alignment with the Tao.")* 佐 (*zuǒ*) had been dropped, which moved the line from the minister to the ruler. 說文 defines its root 左 as 手相左助也, *"one hand helping the other"*: 佐 is the ruler's other hand. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads the line as an argument from the lesser case: 以道佐人主尚不可以兵强於天下，况人主躬於道者乎 — *"even one who supports a ruler by the Tao must not force the world with arms; how much less a ruler who embodies the Tao."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) reads 佐 reflexively (人主能以道自輔佐, *"the ruler supports themselves with the Tao"*), which the old English followed. *Advises* was weighed and declined: it narrows a helping hand to speech. **Cost, accepted:** *supports* is also 輔 (*fǔ*)'s word at ch 64. The two are the ordinary compound 輔佐, and 河上公 glosses this line with it, so the shared English reflects the language. It also makes ch 30 and ch 64 echo: support, never force.

*End of chapter 30.*

## Chapter 31

*Heshang Gong's title: 偃武, "Laying arms down".*

Fine weapons are tools of ill omen.
Living things recoil from them.
Those who are with the Tao do not dwell among them.

The noble at home prizes the left;
using weapons prizes the right.
Weapons are tools of ill omen, not the noble's tools.
Used only when unavoidable, calm detachment is best.

Win, but do not glorify it.
To glorify it is to delight in killing people.
And those who delight in killing people cannot get their will in the world.

Auspicious occasions honor the left; inauspicious occasions honor the right.
The deputy general takes the left, the higher general the right,
which is to say they are placed by the rites of mourning.
For the crowd of people killed, weep with sorrow and grief.
A victory in battle is placed by the rites of mourning.

The Chinese:

夫佳兵者，不祥之器，
物或惡之，
故有道者不處。
君子居則貴左，
用兵則貴右。
兵者不祥之器，
非君子之器，
不得已而用之，
恬淡為上。
勝而不美，
而美之者，是樂殺人。
夫樂殺人者，
則不可得志於天下矣。
吉事尚左，凶事尚右。
偏將軍居左，上將軍居右，
言以喪禮處之。
殺人之眾，以悲哀泣之，
戰勝以喪禮處之。

### Notes on chapter 31

*物或惡之 and 故有道者不處 swept 2026-08-28 to match ch 24, which carries both verbatim. Full argument in `chapters/024.md` · Notes.*

**君子居則貴左，用兵則貴右 → "The noble at home prizes the left; using weapons prizes the right."** *(2026-09-07, Pass D. Was: "In times of peace, the sage chooses creation. When the military must be used, they choose destruction.")*

**左 (*zuǒ* — left) and 右 (*yòu* — right) had been deleted and replaced with an interpretation** — while the same two characters four lines later were rendered literally, 吉事尚左，凶事尚右. One chapter, one pair of characters, read twice on opposite principles. `WORKLIST.md` T1-9.

**And the old English reversed the argument.** It has the sage *choosing destruction* once war comes. 河上公 says the opposite in seven characters: 此言**兵道與君子道反**，所貴者異也 — *"this says the way of arms and the way of the 君子 are **opposed**, and what they prize is different."* The very next line agrees — **非君子之器**, *not the 君子's instrument*. **The noble does not switch sides; weapons belong to a different way entirely.**

**左 and 右 are this book's own pair, which is why deleting them cost so much.** 河上公 glosses them with the locked vocabulary: 貴左 is **貴柔弱也** (*prizes the soft and **yielding***, 弱 locked to *yielding*) and 貴右 is **貴剛強也** (*prizes the hard and **strong***, 強 locked to *strong*). He also gives the ritual sense at 吉事尚左: **左生位也**, *"the left is the position of life"*, against 凶事尚右: **陰道殺人**, *"the yin way kills."*

**君子 (*jūn zǐ*) → "the noble," not "the sage."** *(Shalom's call: the neutral word, over *the gentleman*, which would make the Confucian borrowing visible at the cost of the male default.)* **聖人 (*shèng rén*) is the sage**, and *the sage* carried 38 English lines before this sweep. 君子 is literally *a ruler's child* and is the **Confucian** honorific — handing 聖人's English to it makes Laozi's figure and Confucius's the same person, which is the overlay this edition exists to strip. **Swept at ch 26 with this chapter**, its only other appearance. **Note the seam:** 君子 named a male class and *the noble* is deliberately neutral. `WORKLIST.md` T4-7.

**The general-seating passage carries its point again.** 河上公: 偏將軍**卑**而居陽者，**以其不專殺也** — *"the deputy general is **lower in rank** yet occupies the yang side, **because he is not the one in charge of killing**"* — and 上將軍**尊**而居右者，**言其主殺也** — *"the higher general is **honoured** yet occupies the right, **meaning he presides over the killing**."* **The senior officer takes the inferior seat because he is the one who kills**, which is why the sentence closes 言以喪禮處之: this is a funeral seating. **偏 is a deputy, off to one side; 上 is *higher*** as at ch 8, 38 and 41 — the old *"lieutenant general"* and *"supreme commander"* imported modern ranks, and *supreme* is now forbidden for 大 besides.

**Five characters that repeat, and had two Englishes: 以喪禮處之.** It closes both 言以喪禮處之 and 戰勝以喪禮處之, and read *"placed by the rites of mourning"* then *"treated like a funeral rite."* Both now read **placed by the rites of mourning**.

**Three more terms brought back to their locks.** **器** ran *instruments* once and *tools* twice in one chapter; it is locked *vessel / tool / implement*, so **tools** throughout. **美 (*měi*)** ran *revel* then *glorify* in adjacent lines; **glorify** both times, and it answers 佳 (*jiā* — fine) in the chapter's first line, which 河上公 reads as the same warning: 不當**修飾**之, *"one should not embellish them."* **眾** → **the crowd**, per its lock, where 殺人之眾 had read *"when many have been killed."*

**兵 (*bīng*) → "weapons" throughout, and "arms" was not available.** *Arms* renders 臂 (*bì* — the body's arms) at ch 38, 42 and 64. **兵 still reads *military force* at ch 30**, so the character owes a check of its own. `WORKLIST.md` T2-49.

**夫 (*fú*) is a topic particle and had twice been inflated into an imperative** — *"Understand that…"* opened two lines that begin with nothing of the kind.

**⚠ Part of this chapter may not be Laozi, and the Siku editors say so — see `notes/manuscript.md` · Ch 31.** 王弼 leaves **no commentary at all** on ch 31, alone among the chapters vendored here.

*End of chapter 31.*

## Chapter 32

*Heshang Gong's title: 聖德, "The integrity of the sage".*

The Tao is ever nameless, uncarved.
Though small, nothing in the world can make it a subject.
If rulers are able to hold to this, the countless things will submit of themselves.
Sky and earth join together to send down sweet dew.
No one commands the people, and they even out of themselves.

When the carving begins, there are names.
Since names already exist, one must know when to stop.
Knowing when to stop, you come to no danger.

The Tao in the world is like streams and valleys to the river and the sea.

The Chinese:

道常無名。
樸雖小，天下莫能臣也。
侯王若能守之，萬物將自賓。
天地相合，以降甘露，
民莫之令而自均。
始制有名，
名亦既有，夫亦將知止，
知止可以不殆。
譬道之在天下，
猶川谷之於江海。

### Notes on chapter 32

**知止可以不殆 — we follow 所以, and the English stands.** *(2026-10-14.)* Our base prints 可以 (*kě yǐ* — can), which would make the line *"knowing when to stop, you **can** come to no danger"*: an opening, not a guarantee. **The base is alone.** The Siku editors' note on this line in our vendored 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads 〔案河上公注本及各本俱作所〕, *"Heshang Gong's edition and all editions read 所"*; 王弼's own comment closes 故知止**所以**不殆也; and Mawangdui A, where the characters survive, reads 所以不. 所以 (*suǒ yǐ*) is *that by which*: knowing when to stop **is how** you come to no danger. *"Knowing when to stop, you come to no danger"* already says that, and it now matches ch 44's 知止不殆, *"know when to stop, and you come to no danger,"* as the witnesses do. Same shape as ch 21's 然 / 狀. Logged in `sources/variants.yaml` and `notes/manuscript.md`.

**知止可以不殆 → "Knowing when to stop, you come to no danger."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "one avoids depletion.")* 殆 (*dài*) is **peril**: 說文解字 危也, the graph 歺 (*è* — the bare-bone radical, as in 死 *sǐ* "to die") with 台 for sound. **Depletion is an energy metaphor**, this edition's named besetting temptation, and it renders no character at all. The same line stands at ch 44 and now reads alike; 殆's five occurrences (16, 25, 32, 44, 52) all read *danger*, and *danger* renders nothing else.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) on the parallel line at ch 44** gives the sense plainly: 知可止則財利不累身…則身**不危殆**也 — *"knowing when one can stop, wealth and profit do not burden the body… then the body is not in peril."*

**制 (*zhì*) → "carving", at ch 32 and ch 28**
*(2026-09-07, Shalom's call. Was *cutting* in both.)*

**The change exists to make one thread visible in English.** This chapter opens 道常無名**樸** — *"the Tao is ever nameless, **uncarved**"* — and six lines later says 始**制**有名. Those two lines are the same argument arriving and departing: the uncut thing has no name; **the moment the blade goes in, names exist.** With 樸 as *uncarved* and 制 as *cutting*, an English reader had two different roots and no way to see that the second line undoes the first. **Uncarved / carving shows it.**

**説文 makes 制 a knife on timber, not a metaphor.** 裁也。从**刀**从**未**。未，物成有滋味，可裁斷 — *"to cut out. From 刀 (*dāo* — a knife) and 未 (*wèi*). 未 means things have matured and have flavour, so they can be cut through."* **未 is a tree with grown branches.** So the chain the chapter runs on is entirely woodwork: 樸 (uncarved timber) → 制 (the blade) → 器 (the vessel it becomes, ch 28's 樸散則為器) → 名 (the name that vessel now has).

**Why a cut produces a name.** A name needs a separate thing to attach to. While the timber is whole there is nothing to point at; cut it into a bowl and a spoon and there are two things, and two things need two names. **Naming is the receipt for a cut already made** — which is ch 1's 無名天地之始，有名萬物之母. `glossary/pu-樸.md` already reached this independently: *"Naming **is** carving… The book is a carving that argues against carving."*

**⚠ The loss, and it is a real one: 制 is a tailor's word as much as a carpenter's.** 說文's defining gloss is **裁** (*cái*) — to cut cloth to a pattern — and 制 also means to regulate and to govern, which is the sense 河上公 takes here (道無名，能**制**於有名, *"the nameless can govern the named"*). **"Carving" narrows a word that cuts cloth, timber and states down to timber alone.** That narrowing was accepted deliberately, because without it the line about names does not make sense in English: the reader cannot see what is being cut, and the chapter's central move goes silent. The wider sense is recorded here and in `glossary/pu-樸.md`.

*(A second English carries "carv-": 斫 (*zhuó* — to hew) at ch 74, 代大匠斫. The two characters never share a chapter, so no check will fire — but they now share a root, and 斫 is axe-work where 制 is a fitted cut. `WORKLIST.md` T2-50.)*

**說文 hides the chapter's answer inside the character of its problem**
制's entry closes **一曰止也** — *"one definition: **to stop**."* The very next line of this chapter is 知**止**, **know when to stop**. The chapter is not saying *do not carve* — there are no officials without titles and no bowl without a blade. It is saying that the word for the cut already contains the word for the halt.

**王弼 gives the social reading and names the danger:** 始制謂樸散始為官長之時也。始制官長，不可不立**名分**以定尊卑，故始制有名也。過此以往，將**爭錐刀之末** — *"始制 means the moment the uncarved scatters and first becomes officials and chiefs. Once you institute officials you cannot avoid setting up **name-and-role** to fix high from low… **Go on past this and they will fight over the tip of an awl.**"* That is 樸散則為器 at ch 28, in the same words.

**河上公 parses the line differently and it is worth keeping.** 始，道也。有名，萬物也。道無名，能制於有名；無形，能制於有形也 — *"始 is the Tao; 有名 is the countless things. The nameless Tao can govern the named, the formless can govern the formed."* He reads 始 as the **Tao** and 制 as **govern**, where 王弼 reads 始制 as *when cutting begins*. **We follow 王弼**, because his reading is what ties the line to 樸 three lines above and to ch 28; 河上公's is recorded, not adopted.

**The rest of the chapter**
**譬道之在天下，猶川谷之於江海 → "The Tao in the world is like streams and valleys to the river and the sea."** *(Was: "In this world, with its high streams and valleys, the Tao is like the river and the deep sea.")* **高 and 深 are not in the line** — *high* and *deep* were both invented — and the 譬…猶 simile frame had been dissolved into a description. `WORKLIST.md` T1-14.

**王弼's gloss is the finest thing in the chapter, and it ties the ending to the middle:** 川谷之求江與海，**非江海召之**，不召不求而自歸者世。行道於天下者，**不令而自均**，不求而自得 — *"the streams and valleys seek the rivers and the sea; **it is not that the rivers and sea summon them**. Unsummoned and unseeking they return of themselves. One who practises the Tao in the world **does not command, and things even themselves**; does not seek, and gets of themselves."* **不令 and 自均 are quoted verbatim from 民莫之令而自均**, four lines earlier. *(His 召 — to summon — is also ch 73's word at 不召而自來, *"It does not summon, yet things come of themselves."*)*

**The English keeps the Chinese's ambiguity deliberately.** Grammatically 道之在天下 : 川谷之於江海 maps the Tao onto the **streams**; both commentators read it the other way, the Tao as the **sea** that things come to unbidden. *"Like streams and valleys to the river and the sea"* preserves the order and lets both stand.

**自均 → "even out of themselves," not "naturally harmonize."** **Harmonize is 和's word** (ch 2), where 均 (*jūn*) is to **level** — 河上公: 皆**自均調若一**也, *"all even themselves out, as if one."* And **自 occurs twice in three lines** (自賓, 自均) and had *of themselves* against *naturally*; 自然's lock is *of itself / of themselves*, so both now read alike. *"Without any external command"* had also invented the **external**.

**侯王若能守之 is verbatim at ch 32 and ch 37, and 能 had been dropped here.** Ch 37 reads *"If rulers are able to hold to this"*; this chapter read *"If rulers hold it."* Now matched.

**賓 (*bīn*) → "submit of themselves," and it is the chapter's weakest joint.** A **hapax** — one occurrence in the book — so nothing constrains it. 賓 is a **guest**, and 河上公 glosses it 賓服, *submit and follow*. *Submit* carries a compulsion this chapter spends its length denying, and *guest* is taken by 客 (ch 15, 35). **"Defer of themselves" is the live alternative** and is free.

*End of chapter 32.*

## Chapter 33

*Heshang Gong's title: 辯德, "Telling integrity apart".*

One who knows others is intelligent.
One who knows themselves sees clearly.

One who overcomes others has force.
One who overcomes themselves is strong.

One who knows they have enough is wealthy.
One who forces themselves onward has will.

One who does not lose their rootedness, endures.
One who dies but does not perish has long life.

The Chinese:

知人者智，
自知者明。
勝人者有力，
自勝者強。
知足者富。
強行者有志。
不失其所者久。
死而不亡者壽。

*End of chapter 33.*

## Chapter 34

*Heshang Gong's title: 任成, "Letting things complete".*

The great Tao overflows. It can go left or right.
The countless things rely on it to live, yet it refuses none.
It works without claiming to be the owner.

The Tao clothes and nourishes the countless things, yet it claims no ownership.
Ever desireless, it can be called small.
The countless things return to it. Without acting as their master, it can be called great.

It never makes itself great,
and so completes its greatness.

The Chinese:

大道汎兮，其可左右。
萬物恃之以生而不辭，
功成而不名有。
衣養萬物而不為主，
常無欲，可名於小；
萬物歸焉而不為主，可名為大。
以其終不自為大，
故能成其大。

### Notes on chapter 34

**大道汎兮，其可左右 → "The great Tao overflows. It can go left or right."** *(2026-10-14, with the 可 lock. Was "The great Tao overflows to the left and to the right.")* The old line dropped 可 (*kě* — can) and stated as a fact what the Chinese gives as a possibility: the Tao *can* go either way, and nothing prevents it. Both commentators read it that way. 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 言道氾濫無所不適，可左右上下周旋而用 — *"the Tao floods and there is nowhere it cannot go; it can be turned left, right, up and down, all the way round, and used."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 道可左右，无所不宜 — *"the Tao can go left or right; there is nowhere it does not suit."* *Or* rather than *and*, because the claim is that either way is open to it. See `glossary/ke-可.md`.

*End of chapter 34.*

## Chapter 35

*Heshang Gong's title: 仁德, "Humane integrity".*

Grasp the great image, and the world comes to you.
It comes unharmed, at rest, and utterly even.

Music and food bring a passing guest to a halt.
The Tao is bland in the mouth. It has no flavor.
Look at it. There is not enough to see.
Listen for it. There is not enough to hear.
Use it. It never runs out.

The Chinese:

執大象，天下往。
往而不害，安平太。
樂與餌，過客止。
道之出口，淡乎其無味。
視之不足見，
聽之不足聞，
用之不可既。

### Notes on chapter 35

**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D35 · T1-12; the 執 rider opened at ch 28 on 2026-09-01). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; the two forks in `notes/manuscript.md` and `sources/variants.yaml`.

- **The chapter is one argument.** 王弼 runs 樂與餌 straight into 道之出口 — music and food stop a passer-by, the Tao stops nobody. The old stanza break severed the comparison. 不足 → *there is not enough*, its sense in all six other chapters, not *cannot* (which is ch 14's 不見, without 足). 河上公 reads 足 as 得 and takes the other side; we follow 王弼.
- 執大象 → **grasp the great image**, restoring the mirror with ch 29's 不可執也 — you cannot grasp the world; grasp the image and the world comes. Does not close **T2-19** (the 守/執/保 family, Pass E).
- 大象 → **the great image**, matching ch 41's 大象無形. *Form* is 形's.
- 往 → a verb of going, as at ch 80. *Routes* was mechanistic.
- 安平太 → **at rest, utterly even**. 太 never stands alone in this book, so 安平 is the pair and 太 the intensifier.
- **Open, not closed here:** ch 69 deletes 主/客 entirely, rendering 河上公's gloss (主，先也) as *move first / move second*; and ch 12's 口 → *palate*, which picks eating over speech.

*End of chapter 35.*

## Chapter 36

*Heshang Gong's title: 微明, "Subtle clear-seeing".*

If you would draw it in, you must first stretch it out.
If you would weaken it, you must first strengthen it.
If you would bring it down, you must first raise it up.
If you would take from it, you must first give to it.

This is called the hidden clarity.
The soft and yielding overcome the unbending and strong.

A fish cannot leave deep water.
A state's tools of advantage cannot be shown.

The Chinese:

將欲歙之，必固張之；
將欲弱之，必固強之；
將欲廢之，必固興之；
將欲奪之，必固與之。
是謂微明。
柔弱勝剛強。
魚不可脫於淵，
國之利器不可以示人。

### Notes on chapter 36

**剛 → "unbending."** *(2026-10-14, Shalom's call. Was: "the hard and strong.")* 堅 (*jiān*) keeps *hard*; 剛 is the edge that will not give. `glossary/ruo-弱.md`.

**國之利器不可以示人 → "A state's tools of advantage cannot be shown."** *(Shalom's call, 2026-10-14. Was "must never be shown.")* The two clauses are one parallel, 魚不可脫於淵 and 國之利器不可以示人, and the English had split them into *cannot* and *must never*. **王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) reads both as one consequence:** 魚脫於淵則必見失矣。利國器而立刑以示人，亦必失也, *"a fish that leaves the deep is surely lost; to show the state's tools to people is also surely lost."* 亦 (*yì* — also) joins them and 必 (*bì* — surely) makes both predictions. A fish is not forbidden to leave the water. It dies. **The cost, named:** 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) and 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*) hear advice to a ruler (不可以示執事之臣, *"must not be shown to the ministers"*), and *must never* was honest to that reading. The chapter's other *musts* stay, because 必 prints them. Full argument: `glossary/ke-可.md`.

**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D36 · T3-4). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; three forks in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **The four clauses are conditional instructions, not abstract laws.** 將欲X之，必固Y之 ×4 — the frame repeats and the English must. 將欲 and both 之 had been deleted, the verbs nominalized, and **固 turned from an adverb into the adjective *"firm."*** 河上公 glosses 固 with 先 (*xiān* — first) all four times, and 韓非's worked examples are sequences in time.
- 利器 → **tools of advantage**, not *sharp instruments*. All three commentators read an instrument of governing: 韓非 賞罰 (reward and punishment) · 王弼 利國之器 · 河上公 權道. *advantage* is 利's covered lock in `wu-you-無有.md`; *edge* was already 銳's at ch 9.
- 淵 → **deep water**, not *the deep abyss*. 說文 回水也…左右，岸也 — circling water, banks left and right. **Closes T2-24's ch 36 half.**
- 示人 → **shown**. 說文 defines 示 with the phrase 所以示人也, so the audience is inside the verb; *to others* restated it.
- **Open, not settled here:** 微 (*wēi*) reads *hidden* here against **faint** at ch 15 and 64 · T2-34. And 利器 as a compound also stands at ch 57 · T2-33.

**微 (*wēi*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 是謂微明 renders **微** as *hidden*. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 搏之不得，名曰微, given there as *"its name is the intangible."* 說文解字 has 微 as 隱行也, *"to move concealed,"* on 彳 (*chì* — the step radical) — which is this chapter's word almost exactly, since 微明 is clarity that does not announce itself. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 15 and ch 64, where 微 reads *faint*.

*End of chapter 36.*

## Chapter 37

*Heshang Gong's title: 為政, "Handling government".*

The Tao is ever non-doing, yet nothing is left undone.
If rulers are able to hold to this, the countless things will transform of themselves.

When the countless things urge action, I will stabilize them with the nameless uncarved wood.
The nameless uncarved wood is without desire.

Relinquishing desire, being still, the world rights itself.

The Chinese:

道常無為而無不為。
侯王若能守之，萬物將自化。
化而欲作，吾將鎮之以無名之樸。
無名之樸，夫亦將無欲。
不欲以靜，天下將自正。

*End of chapter 37.*

## Chapter 38

*Heshang Gong's title: 論德, "On integrity".*

The highest integrity does not do integrity, and so it has integrity.
The lowest integrity does not lose integrity, and so it has none.
The highest integrity is non-doing, and has nothing it acts for.
The lowest integrity acts, and has something it acts for.

The highest humaneness acts, and has nothing it acts for.
The highest duty acts, and has something it acts for.
The highest ritual acts, and no one answers,
so it bares its arms and drags them along.

So when the Tao is lost, then integrity is lost.
When integrity is lost, then humaneness is lost.
When humaneness is lost, then duty is lost.
When duty is lost, then ritual is lost.
Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust, and the head of disorder.
Knowing in advance is the blossom of the Tao, and the beginning of foolishness.

This is why the great person dwells in the thick, not the thin,
dwells in the substance, not the blossom.
They let go of what is out there and take what is here.

The Chinese:

上德不德，是以有德；
下德不失德，是以無德。
上德無為而無以為；
下德為之而有以為。
上仁為之而無以為；
上義為之而有以為。
上禮為之而莫之應，
則攘臂而扔之。
故失道而後德，
失德而後仁，
失仁而後義，
失義而後禮。
夫禮者，忠信之薄，
而亂之首。
前識者，道之華，
而愚之始。
是以大丈夫處其厚，
不居其薄；
處其實，不居其華。
故去彼取此。

### Notes on chapter 38

**失道而後德 → 失道而後失德: the ladder is a cascade, and we follow 韓非.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-24. `WORKLIST.md` T1-25.)* *(was: "So when the Tao is lost, then integrity. / When integrity is lost, then humaneness…")* **We depart from the base.** Our base prints 失 (*shī* — to lose) once per clause: 失道而後德 (*shī dào ér hòu dé* — "lose the Tao, and after it, integrity"). 韓非 (*Hán Fēi*, d. 233 BCE), the oldest witness to this text, prints it twice, four clauses running: 失道而後失德，失德而後失仁，失仁而後失義，失義而後失禮 (*"lose the Tao, then lose integrity; lose integrity, then lose humaneness; lose humaneness, then lose duty; lose duty, then lose ritual"*).

**Ours was a descent and his is a cascade.** In the descent, each rung *appears* as the one above it goes, so the lesser virtues are what remains after a loss. In the cascade nothing appears and everything is forfeited in turn. **And 韓非 argues his reading rather than just quoting it.** Just before the quotation, in 解老 (*Jiě Lǎo* — "Explaining Laozi"), he gives the chain: 德者，道之功…仁者，德之光…義者，仁之事也…禮者，義之文也, *"integrity is the achievement of the Tao; humaneness is the radiance of integrity; duty is the business of humaneness; ritual is the pattern of duty."* **Each rung is made from the one above it, so it cannot outlast it.** That is why losing the Tao loses integrity.

**It also sharpens the chapter's spine.** Pass D rebuilt ch 38 around 失 (T1-4), and 失 now carries all four clauses of the ladder, as it carries 下德不失德 (*xià dé bù shī dé* — "the lowest integrity does not lose integrity") above. The source table keeps the base text, as every chapter's must. The departure is recorded in `sources/variants.yaml` and `notes/manuscript.md` → *The 韓非 harvest*, as ch 39's 輿 (*yú* — cart) is.

**故去彼取此 → "They let go of what is out there and take what is here."** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-13.)* *(was: "Rejects surfaces and embraces life's thickness.")* The same five-character closing tag ends ch 12, ch 38 and ch 72, and 彼 (*bǐ* — that, yonder) occurs nowhere else in the book. All three now read alike.

**The old line restated; the Chinese points.** It repeated *thickness* from the line directly above, so nothing was lost in the change — 彼 and 此 (*cǐ* — this) are **deictic**, and their four referents are already on the page: 厚 (*hòu* — thick) and 實 (*shí* — fruit) against 薄 (*bó* — thin) and 華 (*huá* — flowery display). 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) sorts them flatly: 去彼華薄，取此厚實 — *"let go of that flowery thinness; take this thick substance."*

**The spatial English fits this chapter best of the three, because the two lines above are already locational** — 處 (*chǔ* — to dwell) and 居 (*jū* — to reside), each used twice. The 大丈夫 (*dà zhàng fū* — the fully grown person) is being placed somewhere, and the closing line says which of the two places. **A bare *"that / this"* was not an option here either**: four referents cannot be sorted into two pairs by English *that/this*, the same structural reason the bare draft was killed at ch 72.

***"Embraces" freed.*** The word had been rendering **four characters** — 抱 (*bào* — to embrace: ch 19, 22, 42, 54), 守 (*shǒu* — hold fast: ch 16), 有 (*yǒu* — there is: ch 46), and 取 (*qǔ* — to take: here). This was the loosest of the four and comes off free; the remaining two belong to `WORKLIST` T2-19, the holding family.

**Still owed on this stanza, not fixed here.** *"The thickness **of being**"* invents *of being* for 厚, and *"**life's** fruit"* invents *life's* for 實. That is Pass D, and `WORKLIST` T1-4 already carries this chapter.

---

**失 (*shī* — to lose) is this chapter's spine, and the English had deleted it from the one line where it does the work.** *(2026-08-31, Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` T1-4.)* *(was: "Lesser integrity clutches at integrity, therefore it lacks integrity.")* 失 occurs **five times in ch 38 — more than in any other chapter in the book**: 下失德 at the top, then 失道 · 失德 · 失仁 · 失義 down the whole descent. With 失 gone from line 2, the chapter's argument had nothing to stand on — **that the refusal to lose is what produces the losing.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) threads it through his longest commentary in the book: 下德求而得之，為而成之… **求而得之，必有失焉；為而成之，必有敗焉** — *"lower integrity seeks and gets it, acts and completes it… seek and get it, and there must be loss; act and complete it, and there must be failure"* — closing 所謂**失道而後德**也, *"this is what is meant by 'lose the Tao, and then integrity.'"*

**And the word that replaced it renders a character that is not in the chapter.** 執 (*zhí* — to grasp) appears **zero times in ch 38**. *Clutches at* came from 王弼's gloss on the line **above** — 無執無用, *"without grasping, without using"* — describing what 上德 **lacks**. That is the *commentaries are evidence, never candidate renderings* rule, and the class of error only `--english` finds. 執 is also unsettled (`WORKLIST` T2-19), and ch 64 pairs it with 失 in one line: 無執故無失.

**河上公 does not read grasping here at all**, which is the second reason the word had to go. For him the difference is **visibility**: of 上德, 其德不見 (*"its integrity is not seen"*); of 下德, 其德可見，其功可稱 (*"its integrity can be seen, its merit praised"*). Two commentators, and *clutches* picked a third thing.

**The mirror it destroyed.** 上德不德 / 下德不失德 is **a matched pair of negatives** — *does not do integrity* / *does not lose integrity* — one letting go, one holding on, both stated as a **not**. *"Isn't concerned with"* made the first an attitude and *"clutches at"* made the second an assertion, so there was no mirror left. ***"Does not do integrity" stays strange on purpose***: 上德不德，是以有德 puts 德 three times in six characters, and smoothing that is how the line was lost.

**無為 → "takes no action" was a forbidden-register breach no check could see.** The lock renders 無為 *non-doing*; the forbidden list held `"non-action"` and `"inaction"` but not `"takes no action"`, so `check_locks --chapter 38` reported **0 errors and 0 info** on this chapter. `"takes no action"` is now on the list and verified firing — the third near-synonym hole in two days, after `"effortless"` and `"without effort"`.

**上 (*shàng* — upper / highest) had two Englishes and one of them a capital.** Five occurrences — 上德 ×2, 上仁, 上義, 上禮 — read *"highest"* twice and ***"Ultimate"*** three times, a capital that standing rule 5 forbids, on **the rung-marker of a ladder**, changing halfway down. **Ch 41 already renders 上德 *"the highest integrity"* and 上士 *"the highest student,"* and `glossary/wei-為.md`'s own table prints *"上仁 highest humaneness."*** The chapter was contradicting its own glossary entry. 下 → *lowest*, and 禮 reads *ritual* in all three places (it had been *"ritualism"* once).

**以為 → "has something it acts for," because both commentators read it concretely and *"deliberate motive"* pointed at neither.** 王弼: **無以為者，無所偏為也** — *"無以為 means there is nothing it acts partially for"* — and of 上仁, 愛之無所偏私, *"it loves without partiality or private favour."* 河上公 is blunter: 無以為 is 言**無以名號為**, *"it does not act for the sake of name and title,"* and 有以為 is 言**以為己取名號**也, *"it acts to get name and title for itself."* The four lines are a 2×2 grid on two axes — *does it act?* and *is there something it acts for?* — and the English now shows the grid. *(The seam I trust least: the Chinese pairs 無為 / 為之 evenly and *"is non-doing" / "acts"* does not. 無為 is a technical term here and 為之 is not, which is the reason, not an excuse.)*

**The 禮 rung breaks the pattern in the Chinese, and now in ours.** 上仁 and 上義 get one line each; **上禮 gets two** — 上禮為之而莫之應，/ 則攘臂而扔之。 The overflow *is* the content: ritual is the rung that cannot stay in its slot. Ours had fused them into one long line.

**扔 → "drags them along," not "forces them."** 說文解字 glosses 扔 as **因也**, *"to draw along"*; 河上公's text reads 仍 and he glosses **攘臂相仍引**, *"bare their arms and pull at one another."* *Forces* renders neither graph — both are about pulling. Fork recorded in `sources/variants.yaml` and `notes/manuscript.md`.

**而後 → "then," not "follows," and *"pure"* is gone.** *"Pure integrity"* invented a word for 德 on the first rung only, breaking the chain. *Follows* was unavailable: it is 從 (*cóng*)'s English at ch 21. The verbless *"when X is lost, then Y"* also lands the descent at roughly one English word per character, which is the shape 失X而後Y has. **The English is agent-free on purpose** — 失 has no subject, and the commentators supply different ones: 河上公 impersonal (道衰而德化生也, *"the Tao declines and the transforming power of integrity is born"*), 王弼 with an implied human agent (不能無為而貴博施, *"unable to be non-doing, they prize broad bestowal"*).

**首 and 始 are two characters and had one English, in adjacent lines.** 而亂之**首** / 而愚之**始** both read *"the beginning of."* **始 (*shǐ*) is *beginning* everywhere in the book** — ch 1, 39, 64 — so ch 38 was borrowing it. 首 (*shǒu*) occurs only twice in the whole book, and 說文 draws it as **a head with the hair on it** (巛象髪). *The head of disorder* keeps it strange in the direction the character points, and *head* was free in the English. *(說文 on 始 is worth keeping for elsewhere: 女之初也 — "a woman's beginning.")*

**華 and 實 are a bonded pair running across two stanzas, and had three Englishes.** 華 (*huá*) read *"flowery imitation"* and *"flowery display"*; 實 (*shí*) read *"life's fruit."* 說文 on 華: **榮也**, *"blossoming."* On 實: **富也。从宀从貫** — *"abundance; a roof over strung cowrie-shells,"* a full house. 河上公 sets them against each other on the 前識 line itself: **失道之實，得道之華** — *"loses the Tao's substance, gets the Tao's blossom."* Both invented words are gone. ***"The fruit, not the blossom" was the better music and was refused***: 華/實 is genuinely the botanical pair and 華而不實 is a classical idiom, but *fruit* against *flower* is heavily churched in English (Matthew 7:16) and that is the hymn test firing. **Substance** is what 華而不實 means, what 說文's full house shows, and what 河上公 glosses (處其實 = 處忠信也).

**前識 → "knowing in advance," because the commentators openly diverge.** 王弼: 前識者，**前人而識**也 — *"to know ahead of others"* — real but premature knowing, 竭其聰明以為前識 (*"exhausting one's hearing and sight to make foreknowledge"*). 河上公: **不知而言知**為前識 — *"to speak as knowing what one does not know."* One genuine, one bogus. *"Predicting the future"* picked neither and narrowed it to prophecy. The English names the practice; the line's own verdict does the judging.

**處 / 居 — one English verb for two, and a Ming collation note licenses it.** Our 王弼 carries 〔案焦竑云古本四句並作處〕, *"Jiao Hong says the old text has 處 in all four,"* so the alternation may not even be original. See `notes/manuscript.md` for why it is **not** in `sources/variants.yaml`.

**大丈夫 → "the great person," and the gendered reference is removed deliberately.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-08-31. Standing rule 2 — this is the rule's default, not a `shaloms-call`; what was missing was the note.)* *(was: "the mature person.")* **The word is emphatically male and there is no gender-neutral reading of it in the Chinese.** 說文 defines 夫 (*fū*) by a ruler and a hairpin: **丈夫也。从大，一以象簪也…人長八尺，故曰丈夫** — *"an adult male; from 大 (a standing person) with the single stroke depicting a hairpin… a person stands eight 尺 tall, therefore we say 丈夫,"* the hairpin being the 冠禮, the capping at twenty. And 丈 is **十尺也。从又持十**, *"ten 尺; a hand holding ten."* **The word is a measurement and a social marker: full height, publicly grown.**

***"The mature person" failed on two counts.*** *Maturity* in English is an **inward** achievement; 丈夫 is **outward and measurable**, and nothing in the character is about an inner state. And it **fails the 1968 test** — it is Allport-and-Maslow vocabulary and would sit unremarked in a paperback with a lotus on the cover. *(Register — no modern spiritual idiom, `notes/translation.md`. *Matures* also already serves 亭之毒之 at ch 51.)*

**Why *great person* and not *a person of full stature*.** 大丈夫 is **a title in an honour system, not a description of a psychological type** — and you cannot tell a personality trait to move somewhere else. *A person of full stature* was still a description. 大 → *great* is this book's own intensifier (大道, 大器, 大象, and the whole 大X若Y series at ch 45), and 說文 on 大 is **大象人形**, *"大 depicts a human form"* — so both content graphs in 大丈夫 are the **same standing figure**, one of them pinned as an adult. *The great person* renders the picture and universalises the marker.

**The seam, named rather than erased.** There is a real reading on which this chapter **borrows the opposition's vocabulary**: 大丈夫 is a **hapax** here; 聖人 (*shèng rén* — the sage) appears in 25 of 81 chapters and **not once in ch 38**; and ch 38 is where the Confucian ladder lives — 禮 in only two chapters book-wide, 義 in three. On that reading Laozi reached for their word for their ideal man and told it where to stand instead, and 孟子's own 大丈夫 turns on exactly that (居天下之廣居，立天下之正位). **It is a reading, not a fact** — 河上公 goes the other way, glossing 大丈夫 as 得道之君, *"the ruler who has attained the Tao,"* our figure and not theirs; and ch 4 taught that a distributional argument is a reason to look, not to conclude. **No English noun can carry the borrowing in any case**, because it rests on a register contrast an English reader has no ear for. **What the English can do is not fight the frame the fourteen lines above have already built** — which a modern psychological category does. **`WORKLIST` now carries a row for the whole family**: 大丈夫 here, 君子 (*jūn zǐ*) at ch 26 and 31, 士 (*shì*) at ch 15, 41 and 68.

*End of chapter 38.*

## Chapter 39

*Heshang Gong's title: 法本, "Following the root".*

These received the one long ago:
Sky received the one, and so became clear.
Earth received the one, and so became settled.
Spirit received the one, and so became numinous.
The valley received the one, and so became full.
The countless things received the one, and so came to life.
Rulers received the one, and so serve as the world's standard.

Follow it through:
Sky with no way to be clear is likely to split.
Earth with no way to be settled is likely to burst.
Spirit with no way to be numinous is likely to cease.
The valley with no way to be full is likely to run dry.
The countless things with no way to live are likely to die out.
Rulers with no way to be prized and high are likely to topple.

So the prized takes the cheap as its root,
and the high takes the low as its footing.
This is why rulers call themselves orphaned, alone, and unworthy.
Is this not taking the cheap as the root? Is it not?

So reduce a cart to the count of its parts, and there is no cart.
Do not want to be gleaming like jade,
or common like stone.

The Chinese:

昔之得一者：
天得一以清；
地得一以寧；
神得一以靈；
谷得一以盈；
萬物得一以生；
侯王得一以為天下貞。
其致之。
天無以清，將恐裂
地無以寧，將恐發；
神無以靈，將恐歇；
谷無以盈，將恐竭；
萬物無以生，將恐滅；
侯王無以貴高，將恐蹶。
故貴以賤為本
高以下為基。
是以侯王自謂孤、寡、不穀。
此非以賤為本邪？非乎？
故致數譽無譽。
不欲琭琭如玉，
珞珞如石。

### Notes on chapter 39

**Rewritten 2026-09-05** (Pass D, `WORKLIST.md` D39 · T3-6). Full reasoning in `notes/translation.md`; five forks in `notes/manuscript.md`.

- **得一 means holding what makes you what you are**, not living off the quality it produces. 王弼: 用一以致清耳，非用清以清也 — *"it is by using the one that clarity is brought about, not by using clarity to be clear."* 得 → **received** (Shalom's line): 王弼 calls the one 其母, *its mother*.
- **The mirror was inverted.** It broke at pair five, where the Chinese holds (生/生, read *"come into being"* / *"lacked **presence**"* — 有's locked word, and 有 is absent), and was smoothed at pair six, where the Chinese breaks (為天下**貞** / 無以**貴高**, both *"anchor"*). 貴高 is the hinge into 故貴以賤為本，高以下為基.
- 為天下貞 → **serve as the world's standard**, matching ch 22 and ch 28 ×3 (T2-15, settled 2026-09-01). We had a fourth rendering of a settled formula. 貞 is 說文 卜問也 — what is consulted to know what is right.
- 無以X → **with no way to be X**: the loss is of the *means*, not the quality.
- 貴/賤 → **prized / cheap**, not *noble / humble*. Both are 貝 (cowry) graphs: 說文 物不賤也 and 賈少也. **Price words, not moral ones.**
- **故致數譽無譽 → the cart.** We depart from the base: the Siku editors call 譽 a scribal error and both commentaries explain a vehicle. Lands ch 11's image.
- **The close is *neither* jade *nor* stone**, not *"not jade but stone."* One 不欲 governs both clauses, and both commentators say so outright. *Instead* was supplied.
- **Two strains, named:** 琭琭/珞珞 have no 說文 entries; 靈 → *numinous* fails the pointing test. 神 and 靈 want an entry together · T2-37.

*End of chapter 39.*

## Chapter 40

*Heshang Gong's title: 去用, "Putting use aside".*

Returning is the Tao’s movement;
Yielding is the Tao’s use.
The countless things of the world are born from presence;
Presence is born from absence.

The Chinese:

反者道之動
弱者道之用。
天下萬物生於有，
有生於無。

*End of chapter 40.*

## Chapter 41

*Heshang Gong's title: 同異, "Same and different".*

Those highest in service hear the Tao and practice it with diligence.
Those middling in service hear the Tao and keep some, forget some.
Those lowest in service hear the Tao and laugh aloud at it.
If it weren’t laughed at, the Tao wouldn’t be what it is.

Therefore, as the established sayings have it:
The clear Tao seems murky.
The advancing Tao seems to retreat.
The level Tao seems rough.
The highest integrity seems a valley.
The whitest white seems soiled.
Boundless integrity seems not enough.
Sturdy integrity seems slack.
Substantial truth seems to waver.

The great square has no corners.
The great vessel is never completed.
The great sound is barely heard.
The great image has no form.

The Tao is hidden and nameless.
Only the Tao is masterful at lending, and at completing.

The Chinese:

上士聞道，勤而行之；
中士聞道，若存若亡；
下士聞道，大笑之。
不笑不足以為道。
故建言有之：
明道若昧，進道若退，夷道若纇。
上德若谷，大白若辱，
廣德若不足，建德若偷，質真若渝。
大方無隅，大器晚成，
大音希聲，大象無形。
道隱無名。
夫唯道，善貸且成。

### Notes on chapter 41

**昧 (*mèi*) → *murky*, not *dark*.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-20. `WORKLIST.md` T2-54.)* 說文 gives the character both senses — 昧爽，旦明也 for the compound (*daybreak*), 一曰**闇**也 for the graph alone (*shut-in dark*) — so *dark* was defensible about 昧 and **unavailable** all the same: it is 玄 (*xuán*)'s English across six lines, including ch 1's 玄之又玄, *"dark, and dark again."* There is no 玄 in this chapter, so the old line made a reader hear the book's deepest word where the text has only the plain antonym of 明. *Dim* is 和 (*hé*, ch 4 and 56) and 冥 (*míng*, ch 21); *faint* is 微 (*wēi*); *dull* is 爽 and 悶. **The chime with 濁 (*zhuó* — *muddy*, ch 15 and 49) was weighed and accepted as resonance rather than an invented link** — the two are distinct enough to stand apart. 雲 (*yún* — cloud) occurs nowhere in the book, so *clouded* was free too and was declined for this.

**And the English must not settle the commentators, who diverge here.** 王弼: 光而不耀, *"bright but not dazzling"* — the light is present and merely unshowy, and he is quoting ch 58 at it. 河上公: 明道之人若**闇昧**，無所見, *"one of the clear Tao seems dark and obscure, as if seeing nothing"* — genuine obscurity. *Murky* holds both: a murky light is still light, and you cannot see through it.

**大器晚成 — our base prints 晚成, and the English follows the witnesses.** 王弼's text reads 晚成 (*wǎn chéng* — "completed late"); Mawangdui A reads 免成 and Guodian 曼成, both **"never completed."** We follow the witnesses, because *never* completes the parallel the other three lines make — 無隅 (no corners), 希聲 (barely heard), 無形 (no form) — each *"the great X lacks its defining mark."* Recorded in `sources/variants.yaml`; reasoning in `notes/manuscript.md`.

**The 建言 catalogue rebuilt, one saying per line.** *(2026-09-06.)* 故建言有之 (*gù jiàn yán yǒu zhī*) introduces a **quotation** — 河上公: 建設也，設言以有道, *"建 is to set up; sayings set up so as to have the Tao"*; 王弼: 建猶立也. What follows is twelve proverbs, and our English had packed them onto five lines while changing shape as it went: *"Bright Tao seems dark"* with no article against *"The highest integrity seems **like** a valley"* with one and an inserted *like*. **`--formulas 41` shows the chapter is almost nothing but frames** — ▢士聞道 ×3, ▢道若▢ ×3, ▢德若▢ ×2, 大▢無▢ ×2, and 大▢若▢ five times across **this chapter and ch 45 together**. A catalogue rendered as prose stops being a catalogue.

**大白若辱 → "The great white seems disgraced."** *(Was: "true purity seems soiled.")* Three faults in four characters. **大 had been replaced by *true***, which is a breach of the lock at `glossary/da-大.md` that **no check can catch** — every rule keys off a forbidden word, and this one is an absence. **白 (*bái*) is *white*, not *purity*** — an abstraction where the Chinese has a colour, and *purity* is separately forbidden for 樸 (*pǔ*). And **王弼 reads the line straight into ch 28**: 知其白守其黑，大白然後乃得 — *"know the white, hold to the black; only then is the great white attained"* — quoting 知其白，守其黑 verbatim. Ch 28 renders those *"Know the white, hold to the black,"* so *"true purity"* had severed a link the commentator states outright. 辱 (*rǔ*) → **soiled** here, against *disgrace* at ch 13 and ch 28 — a licensed split, argued below.

**大白若辱 → "The whitest white seems soiled" — an English overlay removed**
*(2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)* An intermediate rendering read **"The great white seems disgraced."** It was right about the Chinese and wrong about the English.

**The Chinese carries no racial content, and the question is worth answering with evidence.** 白 and 黑 meet in only one place in the book, ch 28's 知其白，守其黑, and 河上公 glosses the pair outright: 白以喻**昭昭**，黑以喻**默默** — *"白 figures **being conspicuous**; 黑 figures **being unnoticed**."* **It is a figure for visibility, and the instruction is 守其黑 — hold to the black.** 說文 agrees on both graphs: 白 is 西方色也。**陰**用事 (the **yin** colour, of autumn and the west), and 黑 is 火所熏之色也, *"the colour of what fire has smoked"* — **soot**. **There is also no 大黑, and could not be:** the 大▢若▢ frame never pairs opposites, it pairs a thing with the look of its own deficiency — 大方無**隅**, 大成若**缺**, 大白若**辱**. 黑 is not a positive in the frame; it is the hiding place.

**But *"the great white"* is a fixed phrase in English** — *great white hope*, coined for a white challenger to Jack Johnson, and *great white hunter* — and it imports to the reader a reading the Chinese does not contain. This edition exists to strip overlays the English adds; the hymn test and the pointing test both missed this one because both are aimed at theology.

**"The whitest white"** removes the phrase, reads naturally, and doubles 白 the way English intensifies a colour. **The cost, which is real and is the reason this note exists: 大 reads as an intensifier here and as *great* in the four lines of block 3** — 大方, 大器, 大音, 大象 — eleven lines below, inside the same catalogue. A reader cannot see that all five share a character. **That is a deliberate exception to the lock at `glossary/da-大.md`, taken because the alternative ships a line that says something the text never said.** It also touches the question that entry leaves open — whether the whole 大▢若▢ frame wants a superlative — which must still be settled across ch 41 and ch 45 together, not from this line.

**辱 → "soiled" here** rather than *disgrace*, on 河上公's warrant in this very line: 大潔白之人若**汙辱**，不自彰顯 — *"a person of great cleanness-and-whiteness is as though **soiled**, not displaying themselves."* At ch 28 辱 pairs with 榮 (*róng* — glory) and is social standing; here it is a mark on a surface. 說文 gives 恥也, shame, from a graph about **missing the ploughing season** and being punished at the field's boundary.

**夷 (*yí*) → "level," not "smooth."** 王弼: 大夷之道因物之性，**不執平以割物**，其平不見，乃更反若纇㘨也 — *"the great level Tao follows the nature of things and does not grasp levelness to cut them; its levelness is not visible, so it looks instead like unevenness."* 割 (*gē* — to sever) ties this to ch 28's 大制不割. **夷 is polysemous across the book** and this is not ch 14's 夷, which is the unseeable one of the three (名曰夷).

**建 flexes, and this is the argument — do not relitigate it**
**建 (*jiàn*) occurs twice in this chapter and takes two Englishes on purpose:** 故**建**言有之 → *"the **established** sayings"*, and **建**德若偷 → *"**Sturdy** integrity."* *(Settled 2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)*

**The character is one thing.** 說文: **立朝律也**。从**聿**从廴 — *"to establish the laws of the court,"* from 聿 (*yù* — a writing brush) and 廴 (*yǐn* — to stride). 王弼 glosses it plainly: 建猶立也, *"建 is 立 — to set up."* 河上公 reads 建言 compositionally too: 建設也，設言以有道, *"建 is to set up; sayings set up so as to have the Tao."*

**They were unified to *established* first, and the unification had to be undone**, because it made the second line unreadable. *"Established integrity"* collapses in English into **long-standing** — a reputation, which is the opposite of what the line says. The saying needs *fully built* against *looks idle*; **建言** needs *received body of maxims*. One English cannot be both, and the consistency was bought at the price of the sense.

**The grammar differs, which is what licenses the flexion.** 建言 is a **fixed compound** — maxims, a received corpus — where 建德 is 建 **modifying a noun**. This is the same licensed-flexion pattern as 事 (*shì* — affairs / to attend to) and 弱 (*ruò* — yielding / weaken): the register holds, the word bends with the grammar.

**The cost, recorded rather than hidden:** a reader cannot see from the English that these two lines share a character. The chapter notes are where that lives; the verse cannot carry it.

**廣 → "boundless," not "broad."** *(2026-09-07, Shalom's call.)* *Broad* states a width without implying abundance, so *broad → not enough* read as no paradox at all. **Boundless says why it seems insufficient: there is no edge to arrive at** — which is 王弼's argument exactly, 廓然無形，**不可滿也**. *(Runner-up: **ample**, which literally means more-than-enough, so *"ample… not enough"* is a flat contradiction — sharper as wordplay, but it only states the paradox where *boundless* explains it.)*

**建德 → "sturdy," and the reason is in the section below.** *Sturdy* sets a solidly-built thing against *slack* and the tension reads at once. **Its cost:** 建 is the **act** of erecting and *sturdy* is the resulting property, so the building is implied rather than named.

**廣德若不足 and 建德若偷 are a matched pair, and the pairing is architectural.** 說文 on 廣: **殿之大屋也**。从**广**黃聲 — *"a great hall of a palace,"* on 广 (*yǎn* — a roof). **Both characters build.** One is the span of the hall, the other the setting-up of the code, and each saying pairs the thing with the look of its own deficiency. **廣 — the hall so wide it can never be filled looks empty:** 王弼, 廣德**不盈**，廓然無形，**不可滿也**, *"broad integrity does not fill; open and formless, it cannot be filled"* (不盈 is ch 15's word, and 盈 is 滿器, a filled vessel); 河上公, 德行廣大之人**若愚須不足**也. **建 — the code so well established that nobody enforces it looks unenforced:** 王弼, 建德者因物自然，**不立不施**, *"sets nothing up and dispenses nothing"*; 河上公, 建設道德之人**若可偷引使空虛**也, *"as though one could rob them and empty them out."* **Extent produces the appearance of deficiency; structure produces the appearance of sloth.** With 上德若谷 above them the 德 sayings are three, not two.

**⚠ `--formulas` missed the third one.** ▢德若▢ reported ×2 (上/谷, 建/偷) and did not catch 廣德若不足, because 不足 is two characters and the finder matches whole comma-segments. That is `WORKLIST.md` T5-13, confirmed here on a live line.

**不足 → "not enough,"** carrying ch 35's settled rendering rather than *insufficient*.

**質真 → "substantial truth."** *(Was "the most solid truth" — the superlative was invented.)* 王弼: 質真者**不矜其真**，故渝 — *"the substantially true does not boast its truth, and so seems to change."*

**Open, and not settled here**
**明 (*míng*) reads "clear," which the lock does not license in so many words.** `glossary/ming-明.md` locks 明 to *clear-seeing / clarity* and lists ch 41 among its chapters — and the entry's own body glosses this very line as *"the clear path seems dim."* *Bright* was worse: it is 皦 (*jiǎo*)'s word at ch 14 (*"a bright top"*), so the old line had two characters wearing one English. **The entry needs an adjectival flexion stated in its frontmatter, or this line needs a different word.** *(That entry also glosses 道 as **path** here, which `glossary/dao-道.md` rejects — the glossary-self-check hole, `WORKLIST.md` T5.)*

**夷 and 希 both run back to ch 14, which is where the book names them.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* 視之不見，名曰夷 and 聽之不聞，名曰希 give the two as *"the invisible"* and *"the inaudible"* — the meanings rather than the words, chosen for that chapter's legibility, with 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) supplying both readings (無**色**曰夷 · 無**聲**曰希). **This chapter is the strongest argument against that choice, and it was made anyway:** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*) defines 希 here by quoting ch 14 outright, 聽之不聞名曰希, so 大音希聲 and 名曰希 are one word by his own hand. The connection is carried in the notes instead of in ch 14's verse.

**希 (*xī*) is left as "barely heard."** 王弼 defines it by quoting ch 14 outright — 聽之不聞名曰希 — so 大音希聲 and ch 14's 名曰希 are **the same word**, and ours reads *the inaudible* there. 希 runs six chapters with four Englishes and is TRIAGE 14b; the graph is 爻 (crossed threads) over 巾 (cloth), **loosely woven fabric you can see through**. Not settled inside a chapter review.

**廣 (*guǎng*) → "broad" here and "reach far" at ch 67.** Two chapters, two Englishes. *Vast* is now free of 大 and could take it, but 廣 owes a decision of its own.

**王弼 explains 大音 and 大象 with the same mechanism he uses for 大 at ch 25.** 有聲則有分，有分則不宫而商矣 — *"if it has sound it has divisions, and divided it is either the note 宫 or the note 商"*; 有形則有分 — *"if it has form it has divisions."* At ch 25 he argued 大有繫則必有分，有分則失其極矣, *"大, once tied, must have divisions; having divisions, it loses its utmost."* **One argument, three places:** whatever is fully itself cannot be a particular instance of itself.

**士 → "in service", settled across 15, 41 and 68**
*(2026-09-07, Shalom's call. Was "student" here, "warrior" at 68, "masters" at 15 — three Englishes for one character, two of them on the **identical phrase** 善為士者.)*

**"Student" fails on the evidence.** 說文: **士，事也** — *"a 士 is one who handles **affairs**."* Service, not study. 河上公 reads them as governors: the middle 士 治身以長存，**治國以太平** — *"governs the body for long life, governs the state for great peace"* — and the lowest as 貪狼多欲, *"greedy as wolves and full of desire."* Nobody in this chapter is at school. Historically a 士 was the **lowest rank of Zhou nobility**, a person with a sword and a post, between the 大夫 (*dà fū* — grandee) and the commoner.

**Why "in service" and not "officer."** *Officer* was the stronger English — concrete, it takes 上/中/下 naturally, and it repairs ch 68, where *"The master warrior is not martial"* cancels itself. It was declined because **it reads as bureaucratic and carries a negative valence for many readers**, where 士 covers the swordsman and the gentleman-in-waiting as well as the official. *(It also collided with 官 at ch 28, *"chief of the officers."*)* **"In service" is wider and costs only compactness** — five English words for two characters, and a weaker noun.

**Note the seam, per standing rule 2:** 士 named a **male** class, and *in service* is deliberately neutral. The male-default is not erased silently; it is recorded here.

**⚠ Ch 68 now has a seam of its own.** 善為士者 is verbatim at ch 15 and ch 68, so all three must read alike — but ch 68's other three lines run the frame 善▢者 as *"The master fighter,"* *"The master of overcoming enemies,"* *"The master of using people."* Its first line now breaks that shape. `WORKLIST.md` T2-47.

**The closing line**
**夫唯道，善貸且成 → "Only the Tao is masterful at lending, and at completing."** *(Was: "Yet the Tao alone masterfully provides for the countless things and brings them to completion.")*

**萬物 is not in the line.** *"The countless things"* was supplied by the English.

**貸 (*dài*) is to lend.** The graph is 貝 (*bèi* — a cowrie shell, money) with 代 phonetic; 說文 glosses it 施也 (*to bestow*), but 王弼 rules out exactly the reading our English had: **貸之非唯供其乏而已**，一貸之則足以永終其德，故曰善貸也 — *"as for its lending, **it is not merely supplying what they lack**; one lending suffices to complete their integrity forever, hence 'masterful at lending.'"* *Provides for* **is** 供其乏. **Things hold what they have on loan** — one that never runs out and is never called in. 善 governs both verbs, since 王弼 glosses 善貸 and 善成 separately.

**道隱無名 keeps "hidden," and the character is ch 15's.** 說文 defines 隱 as **蔽也** — the graph we settled at ch 15 as *stay covered*. The Tao does at the end of this chapter what the ancients do in that one.

**⚠ 大笑之 renders 大 adverbially as "aloud,"** which `glossary/da-大.md` does not license among its flexions. The entry needs it added. `WORKLIST.md` T2-48.

*End of chapter 41.*

## Chapter 42

*Heshang Gong's title: 道化, "The Tao transforming".*

The Tao births the one, the one births the two, the two births the three, the three births the countless things.
The countless things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang with their arms, blending the vital breath into harmony.

What most people hate is to be called orphaned, meager, or unworthy,
Yet rulers and lords take these very descriptions for themselves.

For so it is: what is decreased is thereby increased, and what is increased is thereby decreased.

What others teach, I also teach:
The strong and rigid do not die a natural death.
I take this as the root of learning.

The Chinese:

道生一，一生二，二生三，三生萬物。
萬物負陰而抱陽，沖氣以為和。
人之所惡，唯孤、寡、不穀，
而王公以為稱。
故物或損之而益，或益之而損。
人之所教，我亦教之。
強梁者不得其死，
吾將以為教父。

*End of chapter 42.*

## Chapter 43

*Heshang Gong's title: 徧用, "Use that reaches everywhere".*

The softest thing in the world gallops over the hardest thing in the world.
The formless enters the seamless.
This is how I know the benefit of non-doing.

The wordless teaching, the benefit of non-doing —
few ever reach this.

The Chinese:

天下之至柔，馳騁天下之至堅。
無有入無間，
吾是以知無為之有益。
不言之教，無為之益，
天下希及之。

### Notes on chapter 43

**希 (*xī*) — the thread from ch 14.** *(Shalom's call, 2026-09-10 — `WORKLIST.md` T2-52.)* *"Few ever reach this"* renders **希**. **Chapter 14 is where the book names this character**: 聽之不聞，名曰希, given there as *"its name is the inaudible."* The graph is 爻 (*yáo* — crossed threads) over 巾 (*jīn* — cloth), **loose-woven fabric you can see through** — so *scarce among people* and *barely audible* are the same property in Chinese, read across a crowd or across a sound. Ch 14 renders the meaning rather than the word for that chapter's legibility, so the link is carried here. Also ch 23, 41, 70, 74.

*End of chapter 43.*

## Chapter 44

*Heshang Gong's title: 立戒, "A standing caution".*

Reputation or your body — which is dearer?
Your body or goods — which is worth more?
Gain or loss — which does more harm?

Therefore, extreme attachment inevitably brings great cost
And hoarding inevitably brings heavy loss.

Know when you have enough, and you are never disgraced.
Know when to stop, and you come to no danger.
And so you can last long.

The Chinese:

名與身孰親？
身與貨孰多？
得與亡孰病？
是故甚愛必大費，
多藏必厚亡。
知足不辱，
知止不殆，
可以長久。

### Notes on chapter 44

**貨 → "goods," swept.** *(2026-08-30, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-14.)* 身與貨孰多 (*shēn yǔ huò shú duō*) read *"Your self or **wealth** — which is worth more?"* **Wealth belongs to 富 (*fù*)** — *wealth · wealthy · enrich* at ch 9, 33 and 57 — and 富 does not appear in this chapter, so nothing licensed the word here. 貨 (*huò* — goods) is now locked: `glossary/huo-貨.md`. The line's three pairs are 名 (*míng* — name, reputation), 身 (*shēn* — the self), 貨 (goods), and *goods* is the plainest thing the third can be.

**知止不殆 → "Know when to stop, and you come to no danger."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-11.)* *(was: "you avoid depletion.")* The same clause stands at ch 32 and the two now read alike. 殆 (*dài*) is **peril** — 說文解字 危也, built on 歺 (*è*), the bare-bone radical that carries 死 (*sǐ* — to die) and 殃 (*yāng* — calamity). *Depletion* is an energy metaphor and renders no character.

**河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*) on this line:** 知可止則財利不累身，聲色不亂於耳目，則身**不危殆**也 — *"knowing when one can stop, wealth and profit do not burden the body, sounds and colours do not disorder the ears and eyes; then the body is not in peril."* Note that it is **the body** that is spared, which ties the line back to this chapter's opening question, 身與貨孰多 (*"the self or goods, which is worth more?"*).

*End of chapter 44.*

## Chapter 45

*Heshang Gong's title: 洪德, "Vast integrity".*

Great completeness seems deficient, yet when used, it never wears out.
Great fullness seems empty, yet when used, it never runs dry.

Great straightness seems crooked.
Great skill seems clumsy.
Great argument seems halting.

Movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat.
Clear stillness brings order to the world.

The Chinese:

大成若缺，其用不弊。
大盈若沖，其用不窮。
大直若屈，
大巧若拙，
大辯若訥。
躁勝寒，靜勝熱。
清靜為天下正。

### Notes on chapter 45

**大辯若訥 → "Great argument seems halting."** *(2026-08-31, Pass C, `WORKLIST.md` T2-9. Closes Pass C.)* *(was: "Great eloquence seems awkward.")* 辯 (*biàn*) read *eloquence* here and *argue* at ch 81, and ch 81's Notes had licensed the split on the grounds that **辯 is praised here**. It is not.

**The 大X若Y frame does not endorse its X — it says the greatest form of X is unrecognizable as X.** The proof is one line up. **大巧若拙** puts 巧 (*qiǎo*) in the frame, and 巧 is condemned twice elsewhere: ch 19's 絕巧棄利 (*jué qiǎo qì lì* — "cut off cunning, abandon profit") and ch 57's 人多伎巧 ("the more cunning people become, the more strange contrivances appear"). Nobody read that line as praise either.

**The commentators put 大辯 and ch 81's 不辯 almost on top of each other.** 王弼 (*Wáng Bì*): 大辯**因物而言**，己**無所造**，故若訥也 — *"great 辯 speaks according to things; the self **invents nothing**, and so it seems halting."* 河上公 (*Héshàng Gōng*): 大辯者智無疑，如訥者口尤辭 — *"one of great 辯 knows without doubt, and like a halting person has few words."* Against ch 81's 善者以道修身，**不綵文**也 — *"the masterful do not **ornament** their words."* **The paradox is that the greatest arguing looks like inarticulacy because it is not arguing.**

***Eloquence* is also not what 辯 means.** 說文解字: 治也。从言在辡之閒 — *"to put in order; from 言 (*yán* — words) placed between 辡."* 辡 is two 辛 (*xīn* — tattooing knives, the convict's mark) facing each other: **words between two disputants.** Fine speech is 美言 (*měi yán* — "pretty words"), ch 81's opening.

**訥 → "halting," not "awkward."** 說文: **言難也**, *"difficulty in speech"* — specifically speech, where *awkward* is generic and overlaps 拙 (*zhuō* — clumsy) in the line above.

**Still owed here: 巧 reads *skill* in this chapter and *cunning* at ch 19 and ch 57** — the same fault as 辯, one line up. `WORKLIST` T2-20.

*End of chapter 45.*

## Chapter 46

*Heshang Gong's title: 儉欲, "Sparing desire".*

When the world embraces the Tao, swift horses are retired to work the fields.
When the world lacks the Tao, war horses are bred in the borderlands.

There is no greater disaster than discontent,
No greater fault than craving to acquire.
And so the contentment of knowing you have enough is ever-present contentment.

The Chinese:

天下有道，卻走馬以糞。
天下無道，戎馬生於郊。
禍莫大於不知足；
